entry.title: Microsoft’s 21-hour outage: How its fallout cascaded into lives of users worldwide
entry.content:
Written by: Arav Shah8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 10:55 PM IST A computer screen shows the Microsoft support page in London (AP Photo) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Between the hours of 2300 to 2330 IST on November 12, users across India began to flag login issues with Microsoft 365 applications. The mailbox and accessibility issues affected applications ranging from Outlook — Microsoft’s primary workspace tool — to CoPilot AI, Teams.

Third party products like Anthropic’s Claude AI also appeared among the services flagged, though a connection between Microsoft’s outage has not yet been explained.

Initially, the issues were logged on the website Downdetector — an online platform providing real-time status tracking for websites. As of 1607 IST on November 13, Downdetector continued to list Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, Claude AI, and CoPilot as the most reported sites.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

On the other side of the globe, the United States and Canada felt the brunt of the outage on November 12 in the midst of their workday, and according to Downdetector, the outage affected “74 countries and territories in an hour” — including the UK, Japan, Singapore, Australia, and New Zealand.

By 1630 on November 13, the outage was still being reported. Why has the outage taken so long to fix despite the scale of the issue? And, how did the cloud-service infrastructure system hosting the 3rd largest company in the world’s enterprise data cascade across regions? We explain.

First, what exactly happened? And, what has Microsoft officially said till now?

The position enjoyed by Microsoft’s cloud-hosted service is a vital element of operations around the world for businesses and institutions alike.

Exchange Online – a cloud hosted email service – was identified as the first to experience intermittent connectivity issues in the Americas. The service is, in fact, integrated into several other 365 functions, which makes its availability important beyond just communicating.

According to Microsoft’s incident updates, the service issue was linked to incident ID EX1550543 and Microsoft’s engineering teams were actively working to resolve the issue.

Also Read | Microsoft offers voluntary exit to 60,000 employees: What it means for India staff

Microsoft, however, subsequently identified a wider problem affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services according to Jose Benjamin Solis, a volunteer moderator on the official Q & A site.

Users were advised that they may be unable to connect to services including Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR. Microsoft, however, specified that only features dependent on interaction with Exchange Online were affected.

In its explanation, Microsoft said that a number of servers had unexpectedly become unavailable placing additional load on the remaining infrastructure. They stressed that the increased load was not the result of an increase in user traffic or more importantly, born of malicious activity.

Microsoft has not officially disclosed the number of people affected. BBC reporting, however, stated that roughly 430 million people use their services worldwide with tens of thousands of complainants across 70 countries.

How did it spread across services? And, does it extend beyond just Microsoft?

As mentioned above, Exchange Online is an integrated service with other offerings across Microsoft 365.

Microsoft’s own advisory stated that users could experience difficulties accessing certain features of Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR. The company clarified that this did not mean the entirety of these services had stopped functioning, only features dependent on Exchange Online were affected.

The main takeaway to keep in mind is that the dependence of these services on a common element means that a disruption originating in one part of Microsoft’s ecosystem could affect multiple applications simultaneously.

The Microsoft services affected. Also Read | Explained: From the cloud, computing moves to the edge

The effects of the disruption were not confined to Microsoft’s own applications. Businesses, government departments and institutions across different countries that relied on Microsoft 365 for their daily operations also reported difficulties accessing their digital workplace infrastructure.

This is significant because these organisations operate independently of one another, across different jurisdictions and sectors. Their reliance on a common technology provider meant that a disruption within Microsoft’s ecosystem could affect their operations simultaneously.

For a multinational corporation, for instance, employees working across different countries may use the same Microsoft-hosted email and collaboration services. Similarly, government departments and businesses may rely on the same provider for communication, document management and other administrative functions.

Their recovery efforts till now have involved returning affected servers to service, applying changes to the infrastructure and gradually expanding those changes across affected regions.

Why then, have services not resumed completely yet?

The answer lies partly in the interconnected nature of cloud computing infrastructure.

Cloud-hosted services operate through a network of interconnected servers, data centres, and backend processes that work together. These components are not independent of one another and applications may rely on the same infrastructure to authenticate users and maintain connectivity.

When a section of this infrastructure becomes unavailable, the remaining components may have to absorb additional traffic and workloads. This stresses the total capacity.

Restoring the initial servers that were not able does not necessarily restore all services disrupted. That is because Microsoft must test that the restored infrastructure can accommodate the renewed volume of requests. The distinction can be equated to an athlete that is returning from injury. While he may be free of injury, his suitability as “match-fit” may not have necessarily been restored.

Simply fixing the intially affected servers does not remedy the outage.

Restoring infrastructure capacity does not, therefore, equate to the resumption of services for the million of users affected. This was visible when Microsoft announced earlier today that some recovery measures had not delivered the expected improvement.

Not the first 365 Suite outage this year

Between August 31 and September 3 2026, Microsoft had recorded a disruption involving Exchange Online — and other services — to an issue with an authentication configuration used by these services.

An authentication configuration is basically the setup in an application which dictates how a user’s identity is verified and what responses for unauthenticated users are used. Users had then experienced access issues with Outlook, Sharepoint online and Onedrive for Business among others.

The November disruption also affected other firms. Anthropic, the company behind Claude AI, reported that its Microsoft 365 connector was experiencing elevated errors because of the incident. The connector’s mail, calendar and search functions were failing for most requests, while Claude for Outlook was also affected. Basically, the ability to access information through Microsoft.

According to the BBC , Microsoft puts the number of people using Microsoft 365 applications at approximately 430 million. Separately, Microsoft’s FY2026 annual filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reported that its Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services generated $101.997 billion in revenue, an increase of 16% over the previous FY.

The company also reported a 6% increase in commercial seats, which it defines as paid users covered by a Microsoft 365 Commercial subscription. In a bid to assess whether Microsoft should be given strategic market status (SMS), the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) found that 60–70% of global revenue in the productivity software suite market could be attributed to Microsoft.

The consequences of this dependence are not limited to lost access to emails or workplace applications.

Reuters reported in November that stock-exchange operator Euronext faced email communication problems within its listing teams, while British insurer Aviva began putting backup arrangements in place for its earnings calls. In India, IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India reported disruptions to their email support services and certain flights were grounded due to this.

These incidents do not establish that these sectors ceased functioning. The takeaway, instead, is that the failure of a single provider translates into a halt in operations across sectors that seem disparate.

entry.title: Paytm wallet to be back? What RBI’s initial nod means, and why it restricted Paytm Payments Bank
entry.content:
Written by: George Mathew, Sukalp Sharma7 min readMumbai, New DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 08:16 PM IST In April this year, the RBI scrapped Paytm Payments Bank’s banking licence. (File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Over two-and-a-half years after placing debilitating restrictions on Paytm Payment Banks, which effectively shut down Paytm’s various services including prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) like digital wallets, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Friday (November 13) granted in-principle authorisation to Paytm Payments Services Ltd (PPSL) to set up and operate a payment system for issuing and operating PPIs in India.

While a final approval from the central bank is still awaited, the development paves the way for Paytm — once the poster boy of India’s fintech revolution — to again offer its once popular wallet services and other prepaid instruments. Before its wallet services — then housed under Paytm Payments Bank — were effectively suspended, Paytm had become India’s largest digital wallet provider. If the in-principle approval from RBI culminates into a final authorisation, Paytm wallet and other prepaid instruments will be back, this time under PPSL.

In April this year, the RBI scrapped Paytm Payments Bank’s banking licence, over two years after barring it from offering all its core services, which included accepting deposits or top-ups in any customer account, prepaid instruments, wallets, FASTags, National Common Mobility Card (NCMC), etc. While cancelling the license, the central bank said the bank’s operations were conducted in a way that was “detrimental to the interest of the bank and its depositors.”

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Paytm had transferred its prepaid instruments business to Paytm Payments Bank in 2017 due to RBI guidelines governing payments banks and prepaid payment instrument issuers. The norms required Paytm to restructure its digital payments ecosystem and migrate mobile wallet users into the RBI-licensed payments bank.

Even as it was certain that the Paytm Payments Bank’s license was going to be scrapped, PPSL — a wholly-owned arm of Paytm parent One 97 Communications — had applied in December 2025 for setting up a payment system for issuance and operation of prepaid payment instruments, shows the RBI’s in-principle authorisation, which was shared by One 97 Communications with the stock exchanges on Friday. The company’s share rose on the development, closing 1.1% higher at Rs 1,945 apiece on the BSE.

What does the RBI’s in-principle approval for Paytm say?

The RBI’s in-principle approval does not allow PPSL to immediately commence wallet operations. The company can issue prepaid payment instruments, including wallets, only after receiving final authorisation or a Certificate of Authorisation from the central bank.

The RBI has laid down certain conditions that PPSL must fulfil before securing final approval. It has advised the company to undertake a system audit, including a cyber security audit, through an auditor empanelled with CERT-In or a qualified information systems auditor.

From the archive | Trouble in a wallet: What’s behind the Paytm storm

The audit must cover the requirements specified under the RBI’s Master Directions on Cyber Resilience and Digital Payment Security Controls for non-bank Payment System Operators, dated November 5, 2026. The company has also been asked to ensure compliance with the RBI’s April 6, 2018, circular on storage of payment system data.

The RBI has stipulated a six-month deadline from the date of its letter for submission of the system audit report. Failure to submit the report within this period will result in the in-principle authorisation automatically lapsing. In such a situation, the central bank will not consider granting final authorisation thereafter.

The RBI has further advised PPSL that any change in the company’s shareholding or ownership should be guided by its July 4, 2022, directions on obtaining prior approval in cases involving the takeover or acquisition of control of non-bank payment system operators, and the sale or transfer of payment system activities.

 RBI actions against Paytm (2018-2024)

Paytm Payments Bank was under regulatory scrutiny since 2018 due to various compliance-related concerns. The central bank identified violations related to know-your-customer (KYC) norms — rules designed to verify customer identities and prevent financial fraud. One of the key issues flagged by the RBI was that the bank had linked a single Permanent Account Number (PAN) to multiple customer accounts.

This raised serious red flags, as such practices can potentially be used to bypass regulatory safeguards. Additionally, the RBI observed that the bank was allowing transactions beyond the prescribed limits for certain accounts, which heightened concerns around possible money laundering risks.

In June 2018, the RBI conducted an audit of the bank’s onboarding processes and found significant gaps in how new customers were being verified. The audit revealed that proper KYC procedures were not consistently followed during customer acquisition. As a result, Paytm Payments Bank was directed to halt the onboarding of new customers until it strengthened its compliance systems and addressed the identified deficiencies. These developments marked the beginning of sustained regulatory oversight, with the RBI closely monitoring the bank’s operations to ensure adherence to financial and compliance norms.

The bank was directed to stop onboarding new customers with effect from March 11, 2022. On January 31, 2024, the RBI barred Paytm Payment Bank from accepting deposits or top-ups in any customer account, prepaid instruments, wallets, FASTags and NCMC card after February 29, 2024 in the wake of persistent non-compliances and material supervisory concerns. The RBI had also imposed a penalty of Rs 5.39 crore on the bank in October 2023.

Also Read | Why RBI cancelled Paytm Payments Bank’s banking licence

The actions were taken due to non-compliance of various regulatory guidelines including those related to know-your-customer (KYC) and not maintaining a Chinese wall with the group company, One 97 Communications.

The RBI action against Paytm Payments Bank triggered a sharp but uneven impact on One 97 Communications: its stock plunged 40–50% while its integrated payments ecosystem broke down, disrupting wallets, merchant settlements and services like FASTag and autopay.

Paytm was forced to partner with banks such as Axis Bank and YES Bank, migrate users and infrastructure and absorb higher compliance costs, leading to temporary user and merchant attrition to rivals like Google Pay and PhonePe, ultimately causing short-term disruption but a longer-term shift toward a leaner, partner-driven model.

Scrapping of Paytm Payments Bank license

While scrapping the Paytm Payments Bank’s license in April this year, the RBI said that the general character of the management of the bank is prejudicial to the interest of depositors as also the public interest. “Thus, the bank is not complying with provisions of Section 22 (3) (c) of the BR Act. No useful purpose or public interest would be served by allowing the bank to continue as envisaged in Section 22 (3) (e) of the BR Act,” the RBI said.

Also Read | After RBI action, when will Paytm Payments Bank customers get their money back?

Section 22(3)(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, stipulates that a banking license is granted or maintained only if the general character of a bank’s proposed or existing management is not prejudicial to the public interest or the interests of its depositors.

The central bank said Paytm Payments Bank was prohibited from conducting the business of ‘banking’ as defined in Section 5(b) or any additional business specified under Section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 with immediate effect.

entry.title: Flight tickets, food and more: 5 charts that explain what’s driving inflation higher, wider
entry.content:
Written by: Siddharth Upasani4 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 11:40 AM IST The first thing that households notice getting expensive is food items: in October, food inflation jumped to 8.94%. (Magnific) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

October saw, for the first time in two years, household prices in a month rise more than 6% compared to the same month a year ago. The 6% figure is significant for one reason and one reason only: it is the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s legally mandated tolerance range.

By law, if average inflation — as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) — is above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters, then the central bank is deemed to have ‘failed’ in achieving its mandate.

Three quarters is a long time. But some are already sounding warning signs: according to Tanay Dalal, an economist at Axis Bank, inflation is “likely to print above 6% until June 2027”. But what is driving inflation so hard that economists think prices will keep rising rapidly? We break it down here.

‘Don’t travel by air’

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Anyone who has tried to book flight tickets to go home for Diwali would have noticed just how much prices have risen. And while the war in West Asia has made jet fuel very expensive, flying became sharply more expensive in October.

Rising airfares over time.

In October, average airfares were a massive 43% higher compared to the same month last year. More importantly, of all the 358 goods and services in the CPI basket, airfares saw the largest increase in price (13.36%) from the previous month.

Flying has become so expensive that the matter even reached the Supreme Court this month, with an application seeking a cap on fares ahead of the festival season. The court, however, declined to grant an urgent hearing, with Justice Vikram Nath saying ‘don’t travel by air’.

All about chips

As this newspaper has been pointing out for the better part of a year, the spiralling price of memory chips used in the manufacture of consumer electronics — or ‘chipflation’ — is increasingly becoming a driver of household inflation.

In October, pen drive inflation jumped to 22%, phones and laptops to 9%, and other major electronic appliances to 4-5%.

What will worry policymakers is that the global chip shortage, manufacturers say, is not going to end for several years.

Explained | Inflation generalisation: Why price pressures are spreading, and what it means for interest rates

Eat at home or out?

The first thing that households notice getting expensive is food items: in October, food inflation jumped to 8.94%. And if you want to dine out, throw in costlier cooking gas for restaurants.

“The surge in food prices continues, reflecting the impact of a weak monsoon as well as the festival season,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, IDFC FIRST Bank’s Chief Economist.

Core inflation rising

Prices of food and fuel items can be volatile — they can rise and drop sharply from one month to the next if supply suddenly improves for one reason or another. This is why, to understand the underlying price pressures, economists and policymakers like to also see how inflation is evolving by excluding food and fuel. This is called ‘core’ inflation.

Even more refined versions of core inflation, which economists call ‘core-core inflation’, are rising. It excludes food, fuel, and jewellery.

All measures of underlying inflation show prices are rising.

The problem, however, is that core inflation is also rising. The RBI predicted last month that core inflation will average 4.4% in 2026-27. With the October core inflation print already at 4.5%, the average for the first seven months of the fiscal year is 3.9%.

Higher… and wider

The RBI will not just be worried about inflation rising, but also spreading to more and more items in the CPI basket, like consumer goods and services: 95 of the 358 items of the consumption basket recorded 6%-plus inflation in October versus 40 in January. Other measures also point to price pressures spreading wider.

“The latest CPI data show that inflationary pressures are spreading beyond energy-related sectors,” ANZ economist Dhiraj Nim said. “Acute pipeline price pressures are also likely feeding through to consumer prices more visibly, beyond energy-sensitive CPI. With WPI (wholesale) and PPI (producer price) inflation still in double digits and growth broadly resilient, further passthrough to consumer prices is highly likely.”

entry.title: From Jensen Huang to India-Pakistan and beyond, the long history of honeytrapping
entry.content:
Written by: Abhinav Chakraborty9 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 08:20 PM IST Mata Hari (left) is considered among the most famous and controversial examples of honeytrapping, now in focus because of reports surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang. (Wikimedia Commons, File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

At the height of World War II, a charming, six-foot-six former British Royal Air Force pilot became the life of America’s cocktail party circuit. He built connections with American politicians, journalists and business tycoons. And he wooed some of the country’s most influential socialites, including oil heiress Millicent Rogers and Congresswoman Clare Boothe Luce.

All this was part of an undercover effort to detect any potential anti-British sentiment circulating in the US government’s corridors of power. We know the man better as the beloved children’s author Roald Dahl. And he was what those in the intelligence community would call a classic case of a “honeypot”.

The tactic, long used in spycraft, has recently been in the news after it emerged that Jensen Huang, CEO of the high-profile US technology firm Nvidia, had an extramarital affair with a woman suspected to be working on behalf of Chinese intelligence agencies. The latest case of an Indian Air Force (IAF) Wing Commander allegedly sharing classified operational information with a suspected Pakistani agent in exchange of “nude pictures” also highlights its present-day relevance. We explain the meaning of the term and its history of deployment in the world of espionage

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is a honeypot or honeytrap?

While the Oxford English Dictionary lists the earliest usage of the term “honeypot” in the English-Latin wordbook Catholicon Anglicum in 1475 CE, it came to describe anything irresistible or something that drew people towards it — as idioms such as “like flies to a honey pot” in mid-19th-century newspapers indicate. On the other hand, “honeytrap” had a literal meaning — as in any type of insect trap that uses honey as bait — before both terms became prevalent in spycraft.

Now, a honeypot or a honeytrap refers to an espionage tactic that involves an attractive person promising or using romantic or sexual relations to lure individuals possessing valuable, classified information into revealing it. A deeply invasive and controversial tactic, it aims to extract sensitive information such as State or military secrets or even gain access to embassies and consulates.

Poster from World War II, depicting an attractive woman speaking to a Royal Air Force sergeant. (Wikimedia Commons)

Traditionally, this involved physical relationships. But the Internet’s ever-growing reach since the turn of the millennium has led to rising cases of cyber-honeytrapping, where victims are enticed through false social media profiles or even AI deepfakes.

How are honeypots used in spying?

Some claim that the earliest recorded instance of honeytrapping exists in the Bible’s Book of Judges, where a woman named Delilah is bribed by the Philistines to discover the source of the Israelite judge Samson’s superhuman strength. Samson eventually falls in love with Delilah (who might not have reciprocated his feelings) and gives away his secret to her, who then betrays him to his enemies.

But its deployment as a stratagem in a systematic manner began only in the 20th century. One of the earliest and contentious examples is the Dutchwoman Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod, better known as the exotic dancer Mata Hari. She gained fame in Paris, but she was constantly on the radar of French intelligence during World War I, given her numerous relationships with military officers, some involving money.

Also in Explained | A short history of spies and spying, from the earliest times to present

After intercepted communications showed her receiving money from a German consul, she was convicted of being a German spy by a French military court and executed by firing squad in 1917. Decades later, many have raised questions about her guilt, while some have suggested that she had either been a scapegoat for officials seeking to blame someone for France’s wartime failures or that her blatant disregard for societal norms led to her conviction.

Another prominent example from the early 20th century was Yakov Agranov, a high-ranking deputy of the Soviet intelligence service NKVD, who was responsible for political repression and the Stalinist show trials during the 1920s and 1930s. He organised sex spy operations (also called “sexpionage”) to target members of the Russian intelligentsia using Bolshoi ballerinas as well as movie and theatre actresses.

Agranov was also responsible for establishing what would serve as a blueprint for Russia’s “sexpionage schools” — Jason Matthews, a former CIA officer-turned-novelist, depicted one such real-world school in the Russian city of Kazan in his award-winning 2013 novel Red Sparrow (later adapted into a 2018 Hollywood film starring Jennifer Lawrence).

During WWII, the Anglo-American spy Betty Pack (whose maiden name was Amy Elizabeth Thorpe) played a key role in extracting naval code ciphers of France’s Nazi collaborator Vichy regime by seducing a French embassy official. Her deception facilitated the successful US invasion of parts of Vichy-held North Africa in late 1942.

It’s not just women

As WWII ended and the Cold War began, Germany had already been divided into two: West and East. In the early 1950s, the East German spymaster Markus Wolf established a new department in his country’s security service, the Stasi, and filled it with good-looking, well-mannered male agents called “Romeo spies”.

The department stemmed from Wolf’s realisation that since WWII had cost thousands of German lives (mostly men), many women in West Germany — especially some powerful and influential ones — were seeking company. The Romeo spies exploited this enforced solitude to obtain valuable intelligence and infiltrated West Germany’s government and key industries.

The same Stasi, in the 1960s, would also use women, nicknamed “Mielke’s Maidens” after the Stasi chief Erich Mielke, to carry out sexpionage operations against Western diplomats and businessmen to entrap and compromise them. The Stasi even identified and targeted gays and lesbians perceived as susceptible to blackmail.

Express Investigation | IAF officer shared war plans, deployment details with Pak operative: Police to court

A 2002 report in The Scotsman on a 2,500-page declassified Stasi dossier revealed the extent of these operations. “Officially, prostitution was a western bourgeois ailment that had no place in the socialist Utopia of the German Democratic Republic. Unofficially, it was an important tool in the war against the class enemies beyond the Berlin Wall,” the report said.

While some intelligence agencies would use honeypotting to recruit an adversary as a double agent, those at the KGB, the Russian spy agency, were known to use kompromat — that is, the use of incriminating material (such as illicit sexual encounters) to blackmail or pressurise the targeted individual.

That didn’t mean honeytraps were out of the KGB playbook, as it showed in the case of Clayton Lonetree, a Marine guard supervisor at the US Embassy in Moscow during the 1980s. A Russian agent who worked as a translator at the embassy seduced Lonetree, and then put him in touch with a KGB handler. He continued to spy for the Russians even after being transferred to Vienna, though he subsequently surrendered — becoming the first Marine to be convicted of spying against the US.

But even the Americans didn’t shy away from such tactics, as William Sullivan, a former assistant director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, would testify in front of a US congressional committee in November 1975: “The use of sex is a common practice among intelligence services all over the world. This is a tough, dirty business. We have used that technique against the Soviets. They have used it against us.”

Although there have been cases of honeypots in recent years, the tactic doesn’t appear to have the institutional backing it once enjoyed during the Cold War.

Have Indians been targets of honeypotting?

Closer to home, there have been several cases of Indian officials, military officers, and employees in domestic defence companies whom Pakistani spies have allegedly targeted in honeytrap operations. These cases, however, are notable for being instances of cyber-honeytrapping.

On Friday (November 13), The Indian Express reported that a Wing Commander of the IAF, arrested five months ago and booked under the Official Secrets Act, allegedly shared classified operational information including war-plan documents, drone capabilities, military deployment locations, movements of frontline combat aircraft, and coordinates of sensitive installations with a suspected Pakistani intelligence agent.

The IAF officer, according to the police charge sheet, had been in communication over WhatsApp with the suspected operative between January and April this year until he was stopped. The charge sheet says that the officer “uploaded” a page of a “secret war plan” after receiving “a nude picture” from the suspected Pakistani operative and “even stated that for each nude pic he will provide a new page of (the) war plan”.

In May 2023, Maharashtra’s anti-terrorism squad arrested Pradeep Kurulkar, an Indian scientist who headed the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Research and Development Establishment (Engineers) laboratory at the time. He was accused of sharing information about sensitive defence projects with a woman who identified herself as Zara Dasgupta — an alleged Pakistani intelligence agent — in exchange for nude pictures and sexting. His trial finally began in July 2026.

In one case involving military personnel, the Indian Army’s Shantimay Rana was arrested in July 2022 for allegedly leaking classified information after he was honeytrapped by Pakistani spies posing as women through fake social media profiles.

These incidents led the Indian armed forces to issue guidelines to its personnel, warning them against excessive use of social media platforms. The Indian Army, for instance, began setting up a new, dedicated information warfare team at its headquarters — in April 2026, then Army chief General Upendra Dwivedi confirmed that the unit had been operationalised and would play a critical role in countering adversary narratives and managing perceptions.

entry.title: Microsoft global outage: How one cloud failure disrupted businesses worldwide
entry.content:
Written by: Soumyarendra Barik5 min readNew DelhiNov 13, 2026 07:41 PM IST The disruption, which began on Thursday (November 12) and continued into Friday, hit some of Microsoft’s most widely used products, including Outlook, Teams, Microsoft 365 and its artificial intelligence (AI) assistant Copilot. Photo: AP/Kirsty Wigglesworth Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

A massive global outage at Microsoft disrupted email services, workplace communication tools, and several cloud-based applications for nearly a day, affecting businesses, government agencies, airlines, and millions of users across countries. The disruption, which began on Thursday (November 12) and continued into Friday, hit some of Microsoft’s most widely used products, including Outlook, Teams, Microsoft 365 and its artificial intelligence (AI) assistant Copilot.

The outage also affected government communication systems in Japan, Singapore and Australia, while Indian airlines IndiGo and Air India reported problems with their email services. AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic also faced disruptions to their Microsoft 365 integrations. In the US, outage tracking website Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook-related problems at the peak of the disruption.

Microsoft said it was gradually restoring services but warned that recovery remained uneven across regions. The incident has once again exposed the extent to which critical institutions and businesses depend on a handful of technology companies to keep their operations running. We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What caused the Microsoft outage

The disruption appears to have originated in Microsoft’s Exchange Online infrastructure, which powers email and calendar services for businesses. Microsoft initially identified an unusually high load on parts of its infrastructure before finding that several servers had unexpectedly become unavailable, putting additional pressure on the remaining systems.

In its service updates, Microsoft said its engineers were restarting affected servers, redistributing traffic, and applying configuration patches. However, some servers became unresponsive again after traffic was restored, complicating recovery efforts.

Also read | Microsoft outage: Company reports positive results as it works to restore services

Microsoft subsequently reported positive results from a patch addressing an authentication and routing configuration component. In a later update, it said recovery was progressing across regions, although “service health remains variable” and infrastructure capacity had not returned to normal.

The company extended its email delivery timeout window to 48 hours to help preserve delayed messages while clearing backlogs. It also said there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident”, and promised a detailed post-incident report once services were restored.

Services and institutions impacted by Microsoft outage

Microsoft said the disruption affected services relying on Exchange Online, although several functions remained operational. Exchange Online is Microsoft’s cloud-based email and calendar service for businesses and organisations, powering email communication, scheduling and contact management through applications such as Outlook.

Outlook users experienced difficulties accessing mailboxes and sending or receiving emails. Microsoft Teams users faced problems scheduling meetings, managing calendars and creating certain events, although core messaging, calls, and meetings largely continued working.

The consequences extended beyond Microsoft’s customers. British police forces reported difficulties receiving online crime reports, while the UK’s National Health Service faced email disruptions that could delay prescriptions. Government email systems were affected in Singapore and Japan, while the Philippines’ Supreme Court also reported operational difficulties.

In India, IndiGo warned that its email support services were disrupted, while Air India temporarily rerouted customer emails. Both airlines said flight operations remained unaffected. OpenAI and Anthropic separately reported problems with connectors linking their AI services to Microsoft applications.

Why Microsoft outages matter

Microsoft is among the world’s largest technology companies, with its products embedded in the everyday operations of corporations, governments, educational institutions, and critical infrastructure providers.

In January 2026, Microsoft said its Microsoft 365 commercial business had crossed 450 million paid seats worldwide. Its annual revenue reached approximately $332 billion in FY2026, reflecting the scale of its software and cloud businesses.

This dependence also means failures in shared infrastructure can spread across otherwise unrelated organisations, disrupting communications and business operations simultaneously.

Also in Explained | Microsoft outage: How its fallout cascaded into lives of users worldwide

The latest disruption recalls July 2024, when millions of Windows computers displayed the dreaded “blue screen of death”, grounding flights, disrupting hospitals, and affecting banking, retail, and government services worldwide. That incident, however, was different. It was triggered by a faulty software update from cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, rather than a failure in Microsoft’s own cloud infrastructure.

Microsoft estimated that around 8.5 million Windows devices were affected, representing less than 1% of all Windows machines. Nevertheless, their importance to critical services meant the consequences were felt globally.

Microsoft’s workforce reductions amid rising AI investments

The outage also comes against the backdrop of significant workforce reductions at Microsoft as the company reorganises operations while spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

Microsoft eliminated more than 15,000 jobs in 2025, followed by another 4,800 positions in July 2026 and further cuts in September. On October 26, the company announced a voluntary exit programme covering approximately 60,000 eligible employees across the US, the UK, Canada, and India. Microsoft employs around 23,000 people in India, although it has not disclosed how many would qualify for the programme.

The company has maintained that these measures reflect changing business priorities and workforce requirements, rather than suggesting it no longer needs employees. As of now, there is no established link between the reductions and the latest outage.

entry.title: Jensen Huang-Alice Huang affair: How the Nvidia scandal became a US security concern
entry.content:
Written by: Abhishek Chakraborty9 min readNov 13, 2026 04:09 PM IST Jensen Huang during his China visit in May 2026 (left); Alice Huang at a dinner hosted by the erstwhile Nvidia CEO at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, in May last year (AP). Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang Thursday resigned as its chief executive officer after a controversy over his extramarital affairs, two of which reportedly involved company colleagues.

But the affair that triggered his ouster was with a Chinese woman named Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), who has been accused of passing on intelligence to China. Adding to the concerns was the fact that Huang has lobbied for easing America’s restrictions on sales of artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China in the past.

Alice Huang is a former executive from the Singapore-registered data centre operator Megaspeed, which American authorities have separately investigated since 2024 over suspicions that it was helping China access restricted AI chips.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

This is why the extramarital affair goes well beyond his personal life or his company’s future.

What’s the Jensen Huang-Alice Huang Scandal?

The Nvdia CEO’s scandal broke on October 29, when The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials were examining Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang admitted to having the affair over the following weekend. US President Donald Trump then said the FBI was investigating the matter, but backed the Nvidia co-founder.

Nobody has been charged with any offence so far, and as per Nvidia board of director’s last statement on the matter, the company had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

How an affair went beyond Nvidia CEO’s marriage and became a national security risk

A CEO’s private life is normally his own business. It stops being so when he is involved with a person of interest who is under surveillance by intelligence agencies. And if the CEO’s company makes the chips at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and US-China tech race, he will be scrutinised for sure.

Also Read | Jensen Huang resigns: Why his exit from Nvidia will be a test for the AI boom

While Jensen Huang himself was not a suspect, Alice Huang and Nvidia’s deals with Megaspeed — and by extension China — have come under scrutiny.

Essentially, the concern is over how much leverage, access and influence Alice Huang had over Nvidia’s operations and decisions. Investigators reportedly wanted to know whether Chinese intelligence was using an executive relationship to learn about Nvidia’s hardware allocation, supply timelines and lobbying on export rules.

Happier Times: Jensen Huang and his wife Lori Huang walk to the White House to attend a state dinner hosted for China’s President Xi Jinping on September 24, 2026 (AP Photo)

US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of working for China’s Ministry of State Security, according to the Financial Times and The New York Times. Chinese state media, however, has called the claims baseless. Singapore’s Home Affairs ministry said that in February 2025, the Singapore Police Force and Singapore Customs initiated an independent investigation into several companies and their key officers, including Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, and its controllers.

“The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences… Alice Huang (otherwise known as Huang Le), a Hong Kong resident, was investigated for suspected involvement in the possible offences in Singapore, given her position as then-CEO,” the Singapore government said in a statement on Thursday.

It, however, clarified that Alice Huang was not investigated for espionage.

The US House Select Committee on China called Alice Huang a “publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset” and asked her to attend a November 18 briefing.

. WORLD · NVIDIA · US–CHINA TECH Nvidia’s CEO resigned. What is confirmed, alleged and denied Jensen Huang quit as CEO and board member on Nov 12 after reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials reportedly suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. The two are not related. Nvidia says he went at Trump’s invitation. NOV 6–7Reports (NYT, FT) on a US intelligence memo alleging China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to spy on him. NOV 8 · SUNNvidia’s board opens an independent investigation. Huang tells staff he “was unfaithful to my wife.” NOV 9 · MONTrump says the FBI is looking into it, and says he believes Huang did not know she was a spy. NOV 12 · THUNvidia announces the resignation; Kress named interim CEO. Singapore publishes its Megaspeed findings. Reuters reports a third relationship, with another employee. CONFIRMED · ALLEGED · DENIED CONFIRMED Huang resigned as CEO, president and board member; Kress is interim CEO (Nvidia). Huang admitted to staff that he was unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia’s board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and opened an independent probe. ALLEGED (PER REPORTS) US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang works for China’s Ministry of State Security (NYT, FT). A House committee called her a “publicly reported” Chinese intelligence asset. The Information reported her relationship helped steer at least $7.5bn in Nvidia sales to Chinese buyers; CNBC said it could not verify this. NYT: a relationship with VP Kimberly Powell. Reuters: a third, with another employee. Neither has been confirmed; Nvidia declined to comment on Reuters. Reports do not allege security wrongdoing by Powell. DENIED OR DISPUTED China’s foreign ministry calls the spy claim unsubstantiated and “smears.” Huang denied compromising national security or Nvidia secrets. Nvidia said his dealings with her were “not unusual” and it shares no classified information with customers. Nvidia says it found no evidence of chip diversion and cut off Megaspeed in June 2025. Megaspeed denies illegal transfers to China. WHY WASHINGTON IS WATCHING The question: lawmakers want to know whether sensitive information was compromised and whether the administration responded properly (Reuters). The access: Trump approved H200 chip sales to China in Dec 2025, with 25% of proceeds going to the US government. About 10 Chinese firms were cleared, but none had shipped by mid-May as Beijing held orders back (Reuters). Critics such as Sen. Warren say Huang lobbied for looser curbs; Nvidia says H200 sales need a US licence. Both parties: Republicans Brian Mast and John Moolenaar want testimony; Democrats Warren and Schumer say the resignation does not end the matter. MEGASPEED AND ALICE HUANG MEGASPEED Singapore-based firm that rents out computing power built on Nvidia chips; customers include Alibaba. One of Nvidia’s biggest foreign buyers (NYT, CBS). Short-seller Culper says its balance sheet jumped from about $33m to about $3bn in 2024. The source of that money is unconfirmed. NYT reports a US trade official saw unopened Nvidia chip boxes at a Megaspeed affiliate, raising re-export fears. Megaspeed says checks by US and Malaysian authorities and Nvidia found no violations. Renting chips in third countries is not itself barred. ALICE HUANG (A.K.A. HUANG LE) Former Megaspeed CEO, chair and key controller; a Hong Kong resident, per Singapore. NYT describes her as a Chinese citizen. Singapore investigated possible false declarations on server purchases from Feb 2025. In Feb 2026 police found insufficient evidence of offences, but said she gave information she knew to be inaccurate. She got a stern warning and a re-entry ban. WHAT TO WATCH Huang has agreed to brief Congress before Thanksgiving (Nov 26), per Rep. Mast; the closed-door date is still being set. Nvidia’s board is weighing internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. Trump and Xi are expected to meet around the APEC leaders’ meeting, Nov 18–19 (CNBC). Who is Alice Huang, and what is Megaspeed?

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who worked as a state-media TV reporter and then as a private banker. She was Megaspeed’s CEO, Chairperson, and one of the key controllers. She is no longer associated with the Singapore-based data centre operator with Chinese origins. Its genesis can be traced to 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud-computing company that US lawmakers have described as having links to the Chinese government.

While American export controls prohibit the unauthorised shipment of certain advanced chips to China, Chinese companies can potentially obtain access to comparable computing power by renting infrastructure housed in other countries.

Also Read | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

Megaspeed rents out computing power from Nvidia chips housed in data centres outside China, according to Fortune. In fact, Nvidia’s biggest customer of chips in Southeast Asia was Megaspeed, a 2025 Bloomberg report said. This is why the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

According to The New York Times, Nvidia has said its checks show Megaspeed has no Chinese shareholders and that it has no evidence of chip diversion to China.

But Megaspeed’s business dealings have raised questions about the extent of its links with Chinese technology companies. According to trade records cited by The New York Times, a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. The company has reportedly supplied computing capacity to Alibaba and other Chinese businesses, allowing them to access Nvidia-powered infrastructure located outside China.

Megaspeed’s Southeast Asia footprint

The company grew fast. South China Morning Post, citing Singapore corporate records, reports that Megaspeed’s assets jumped roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion. Revenue went from nothing in 2023 to more than $294 million in 2024.

Bloomberg reported that Megaspeed rents out Nvidia chips at several Southeast Asian facilities to Alibaba. Its data centres are in Malaysia and Indonesia. This setup is what Washington is worried about. Chinese firms can use computing power in Singapore and Malaysia without importing the restricted chips themselves, according to a experts quoted by Fortune and Forbes. Such arrangements may be legal if the operator isn’t acting on behalf of a Chinese entity.

 

The timeline raises questions. Alice Huang was photographed with Jensen Huang at Taiwan events in 2024 and 2025. Megaspeed was placing huge orders during the same period. The Information reported that she used her relationship with him to help Megaspeed secure $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chip sales for China.

A US Commerce Department investigation in late 2024 reportedly reportedly found unopened boxes of brand new Nvidia chips at a facility operated by Speedmatrix, a subsidiary of Megaspeed. This gave rise to suspicions of the chips being smuggled to China. According to CNBC, Speedmatrix was substantially funded in “secret” by Chinese ecommerce giant Alibaba through “shell companies”.

After the 2024, Megaspeed paused direct orders, but Speedmatrix continued to acquire Nvidia chips. According to New York Times, between 2024 and February 2026, Speedmatrix acquired at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment, Nvidia chips-enabled systems.

Huang’s Beijing visit with Donald Trump

Jensen Huang had immense access to Trump, serving on the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and accompanying him on high-level diplomatic trips, including a May 2026 visit to Beijing. As head of Nvidia and a presidential advisor, Huang had deep insight into next-generation semiconductor roadmaps, US’s own supply chain vulnerabilities, and high-level government deliberations regarding AI competition with China.

Counterintelligence experts raised alarms over exactly over this and flagged concerns regarding what sensitive information Alice might have procured during her relationship with Jensen.

Jensen Huang and Donald Trump during a White House event in September 2026 (AP Photo)

Huang reportedly lobbied fiercely with the administration to take a lighter regulatory approach to AI and successfully pushed for approvals to sell advanced chips to China. Officials feared foreign intelligence could have used the relationship to indirectly shape US trade and technology policy.

Huang’s trip to Beijing with Trump wasn’t on the original itinerary. Trump called and invited him, and he joined the plane in Alaska. Nvidia said he attended at Trump’s invitation.

The big prize was already in hand. Trump approved H200 chip exports to China in December, and formal licences followed. Just before the summit, Reuters reported that the US had cleared about 10 Chinese firms, including Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and JD.com, to buy H200s. The Beijing trip itself delivered little. The Reuters report stated that no H200 chips had been delivered at that point because Beijing was holding back.

With Nvidia chips being used in global AI technologies as well as US military equipment, Chinese extortion or coercion, too, remains a major worry. 

The Kimberly Powell report

On November 11, The New York Times again reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, who reported to him. In the report, NYT cited five people who had worked at the company. Reuters on Thursday reported a third affair by Jensen, again with a company executive.

Nvidia is yet to comment on the allegations. Powell has not been accused of any security wrongdoing, and the board’s announced investigation does not mention her.

entry.title: Blue Flag beaches: What it takes to earn this global tag, held by just 22 in India
entry.content:
Written by: Zeeshan Shaikh5 min readMumbaiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 02:05 PM IST Shrivardhan beach in Maharashtra's Raigad district. (Wikimedia Commons) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

In a first for Maharashtra, three of its beaches have been awarded an international certification that recognises beaches meeting stringent standards of environmental protection, water quality, safety and tourist facilities.

The Ladghar and Guhagar beaches in Ratnagiri district, and the Shrivardhan beach in Raigad district, have earned the international Blue Flag certification. Only 22 beaches in India carry the certification, awarded by a Denmark-based non-governmental organisation. What does it take to earn the tag, and what do its standards entail?

 What is the Blue Flag tag?

The Blue Flag is an internationally recognised voluntary eco-label awarded to beaches, marinas and tourism boats that meet prescribed standards of environmental management, water quality, safety, accessibility and environmental education.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The programme is run by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), an international non-governmental, non-profit organisation headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. It began in France in 1985 and has since grown into a global certification programme.

Also Read | 7 Blue Flag beaches in India worth exploring

Unlike awards that recognise a destination’s popularity or tourism potential, the Blue Flag assesses how a beach is managed. The emphasis is on whether its bathing water is safe, waste is disposed of responsibly, the surrounding ecosystem is protected and visitors have access to basic safety and other facilities.

Who decides which beaches get the Blue Flag?

The certification process is overseen by the FEE, which works through national operators in participating countries. Applications are first examined at the national level before being sent to the International Blue Flag Jury for a final decision.

The international jury includes representatives of organisations and experts working in environmental protection, tourism, water quality, coastal management and accessibility. These include the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), UNESCO, UN Tourism and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Guhagar beaches in Ratnagiri district. (Wikimedia Commons)

In India, a National Blue Flag Jury comprising experts, government representatives and members of civil society examines applications and recommends beaches for international consideration. The final decision rests with the FEE’s International Jury.

What does a beach have to do to qualify for a Blue Flag tag?

India’s Blue Flag programme prescribes 33 criteria, grouped under four broad heads: environmental education and information, water quality, environmental management, and safety and services.

Environmental education and information: Beaches must display information about the local ecosystem, bathing water quality, available facilities and appropriate visitor conduct. They are also required to organise activities to raise awareness about the coastal environment.

Water quality: This is among the most critical requirements. Beaches must undergo regular water sampling and testing and meet prescribed standards for microbiological contamination, including E. coli and intestinal enterococci. Sewage, industrial waste and other discharges must not contaminate bathing waters.

Ladghar beach in Ratnagiri district. (Wikimedia Commons)

Environmental management: Authorities must ensure regular cleaning, proper waste collection and segregation, and adequate sewage disposal. They must also protect sensitive habitats and local biodiversity. Tourism infrastructure and other activities should not come at the cost of the surrounding ecosystem.

Safety and services: Beaches must have first aid facilities and emergency arrangements, along with appropriate public safety measures. Basic visitor amenities include drinking water and toilets. Accessibility for persons with disabilities is also part of the assessment.

Does a beach get to keep the tag permanently?

No. The Blue Flag is awarded for a particular season and has to be renewed. Beaches must continue to meet the prescribed criteria throughout the certification period.

National operators carry out monitoring and control visits, while the international programme also provides for inspections. If a beach fails to maintain the required standards, authorities can be asked to take corrective measures. The certification can also be suspended or withdrawn.

How many beaches worldwide and in India have the Blue Flag tag?

According to the FEE’s announcement for the 2026 Northern Hemisphere season, 5,274 sites across 53 countries had received Blue Flag recognition. These included 4,371 beaches, 745 marinas and 158 tourism boats.

In India, 22 beaches have received the certification for the 2026 to 2027 season. Of these, 13 are renewals and nine are new additions. The three Maharashtra beaches are among the new entrants.

India’s first eight beaches received the Blue Flag certification in 2020. Since then, the programme has expanded to cover more coastal destinations across the country.

What does the recognition mean for Maharashtra?

Ladghar, Guhagar and Shrivardhan are the first beaches in Maharashtra to make it to the Blue Flag list. Their inclusion gives the state’s coastline international recognition for environmental management and sustainable tourism.

The state government intends to use the programme to bring more eligible beaches along the Maharashtra coast up to international standards. The certification could also improve the visibility of these destinations among tourists and provide a boost to local tourism related businesses.

entry.title: How does Parliament convene special sessions, and what sets them apart?
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk5 min readNew DelhiNov 13, 2026 12:47 PM IST The power to convene a session of Parliament rests with the government. (File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The Indian Express reported on Friday (November 13) that a special session of Parliament could be convened before the regularly scheduled Winter Session this year. The Centre is planning to do so to secure passage of its legislative agenda on delimitation of electoral constituencies and implementation of women’s reservation.

Sources said this could be the last window to advance the implementation of women’s quota to 2029, when the Lok Sabha elections are scheduled to be held.

In the ordinary course, Parliament holds three sessions: the Budget Session, Monsoon Session and the Winter Session. Here are the provisions that govern them, and what entails a special session.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Sessions of Indian Parliament

The power to convene a session of Parliament rests with the government. The decision is taken by the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs, which currently comprises 10 ministers, including those for Defence, Home and Finance. The committee’s decision is formalised by the President, in whose name MPs are summoned to meet for a session.

India does not have a fixed parliamentary calendar. The Constitution specifies that six months should not elapse between two parliamentary sessions. The framers of the Constitution borrowed it from the Government of India Act of 1935.

By convention, Parliament meets for three sessions in a year. The longest, the Budget Session, starts towards the end of January and concludes by the end of April or the first week of May. The session has a recess so that Parliamentary Committees can discuss the budgetary proposals.

Research | The historical journey of parliamentary sessions in India

The second session is the three-week Monsoon Session, which usually begins in July and finishes in August. The parliamentary year ends with a three-week-long Winter Session, which is held from November to December. This Winter Session is expected to begin in late November or early December.

Notably, as of November 12 this year, the Monsoon Session of Parliament has not been prorogued for 91 days since being adjourned sine die (postponed without a new day for reconvening) on August 13. This is the longest such adjournment in history, and it means Parliament can be convened any day without the mandatory 14-day notice required before the House is called into session, government sources said.

What the Constitution says on Parliament sessions

The summoning of Parliament is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution. Like many other Articles, it is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935. This provision specified that the central legislature had to be summoned to meet at least once a year, and that not more than 12 months could elapse between two sessions.

Dr B R Ambedkar’s drafting of the provision reduced the gap between sessions to six months, and specified that Parliament should meet at least twice a year. He argued that “The clause as it stands does not prevent the legislature from being summoned more often than what has been provided for in the clause itself. In fact, my fear is, if I may say so, that the sessions of Parliament would be so frequent and so lengthy that the members of the legislature would probably themselves get tired of the sessions.”

Over the years, governments have shuffled around the dates of sessions to accommodate political and legislative exigencies. In 2017, the Winter Session was delayed on account of the Gujarat Assembly elections. In 2011, political parties agreed to cut short the Budget Session so they could campaign for Legislative Assembly elections in five states.

Sessions have also been cut short or delayed to allow the government to issue Ordinances. For example, in 2016, the Budget Session was broken up into two separate sessions to enable the issuance of an Ordinance.

Special session of Parliament

The Constitution does not use the term “special session”. The term sometimes refers to sessions the government has convened for specific occasions, like commemorating parliamentary or national milestones.

For the two Houses to be in session, the presiding officers (the Lok Sabha Speaker and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) should chair their proceedings. The presiding officers can also direct that the proceedings of their respective Houses be limited, and procedural devices like Question Hour would not be available to MPs during the session.

While Article 85 empowers the President to summon Parliament, the convention is to give around 15 days’ notice for a regular session. A special session, however, can be convened at shorter notice. If a session has been adjourned sine die but not prorogued (meaning formally ending a session), it technically remains alive, and the Lok Sabha can be reconvened at short notice by the Speaker under Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure.

However, Article 352 (Proclamation of Emergency) of the Constitution does refer to a “special sitting of the House”. Parliament added the part relating to the special sitting through the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978. Its purpose was to add safeguards to the power of proclaiming an Emergency in the country, after the events of 1975 under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It specifies that if a Proclamation of Emergency is issued and Parliament is not in session, then one-tenth of Lok Sabha MPs can ask the President to convene a special meeting to disapprove the Emergency.

entry.title: Can divorce abroad end an Indian marriage? What SC said in bigamy case
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 07:25 PM IST In the present case, the dispute arose after the marriage was solemnised under Hindu rites and customs in 2003. Photo: Pixabay Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The Supreme Court has held that a person who is married under Indian law cannot use a foreign divorce decree to escape bigamy proceedings in India if the divorce was granted on a ground that’s not recognised in India.

A Supreme Court bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekar on November 3 held that a change in citizenship or the fact that the second marriage took place abroad cannot alter the legal consequences of a marriage that continues under Indian law.

Here’s what to know about the case, the legal framework governing foreign judgments, and what the top court ruled in this case.

Facts of the case

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In the present case, the dispute arose after the marriage was solemnised under Hindu rites and customs in 2003. The couple eventually moved to the UK, and their relationship deteriorated. The husband then filed for divorce in a Guntur court, but his petition was dismissed. An appeal was filed in the Andhra Pradesh High Court, but that was withdrawn too. 

After acquiring British citizenship in February 2013, he approached the Cambridge County Court in August that year. The court granted divorce in January 2014 on the ground of irrevocable breakdown of marriage. He eventually went on to marry another woman in the UK in March 2014.

Also read | ‘Marriages made in heaven’: Telangana High Court rejects man’s ‘wife unfaithful’ claim

His first wife eventually filed a complaint alleging bigamy under Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code (since replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2023), a punishment for which is either seven years imprisonment or a fine. She argued that she had objected to the UK jurisdiction and that irretrievable breakdown of marriage was not a ground for divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act (HMA), 1955, which governed their marriage.

Does Indian law recognise foreign judgments?

The recognition of foreign rulings in India is governed by Sections 13 and 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC).

Section 13 lays down six exceptions under which a foreign judgment would not be considered conclusive in India. These include cases where the foreign court lacked jurisdiction, the judgment was not granted on merits, or the order was obtained through fraud. Recognition can also be refused where the foreign court refused to recognise Indian law despite its applicability.

Section 14 provides that a foreign judgment is presumed valid unless the contrary is proved, but this presumption is easily rebutted when one of the exceptions in Section 13 is shown.

Also read | Can law on false marriage promise apply in transwoman’s case? What Allahabad HC said

In matrimonial disputes, these provisions essentially mean that a divorce granted abroad does not automatically bring a marriage governed by Indian law to an end in India. The divorce decree must meet the requirements for recognition under the CPC.

Court precedents

The legal position on how India treats foreign divorce decrees was laid down more than three decades ago in Y. Narasimha Rao v. Venkata Lakshmi (1991). In that case, the Supreme Court held that a foreign divorce decree must be consistent with the matrimonial law under which the parties were married.

It laid down two principles: for a foreign divorce to be valid in India, the ground for divorce must first be recognised in India, and both spouses must have agreed to place themselves before the foreign court. If either condition is missing, the decree has no effect in India.

In Kishorekumar Mohan Kale v. Kashmira Kale (2026), the Supreme Court refused to recognise a US divorce decree on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, which is not listed under the HMA. The court dissolved the marriage itself by exercising its powers under Article 142(1), which allows the top court “to do complete justice” in any matter before it.

What the Supreme Court held in the present case

The top court held that the husband had initially approached an Indian court for divorce but, after failing to obtain relief, had withdrawn his appeal and moved to a foreign court. The UK decree was based on a ground that the Indian law does not recognise.

It said, “The foreign divorce decree was passed in contravention of the existing matrimonial law in India and on a ground that is not even recognized statutorily. This not only violates the legal threshold of Section 13 of the CPC, which every foreign decree has to pass through, but also the observations made by this Court in Y. Narasimha Rao as to the conditions required to be fulfilled by a foreign decree to be enforceable in India.”

Also read | Live-in relations a reality, law on cruelty to partner applies: Supreme Court

The bench further said that proceedings before the foreign court indicate that the wife raised objections and thus her participation could not be equated with “an unconditional submission to the jurisdiction of the foreign court”.

The husband also argued that he was a British citizen when he married the second time and the marriage took place outside India. Thus, the Indian law could not be applied to him.

The bench rejected this argument, saying that the inquiry into bigamy could not be restricted to where the second marriage took place, as it only had to consider whether the first marriage continued to subsist. “Legal consequences flowing from the subsisting marriage cannot be defeated by a subsequent change in the nationality of accused,” it said.

The husband argued that the FIR was filed after a long unexplained delay. The bench rejected this argument, observing that “bigamy is a continuing offence”, which means it’s an offence for as long as the second marriage persists. 

The court also found that the material submitted before it was not sufficient to establish that the parents of the husband had participated in facilitating the second marriage, nor was it enough to establish whether the second wife knew that the first marriage was still subsisting.
