entry.title: Why New York schools are pushing back against Google’s AI
entry.content:
Written by: Anagha Jayakumar8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 09:25 AM IST In September, New York City announced its one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI, covering nearly 600,000 public school students through eighth grade. (NYT File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Google, which has become synonymous with internet search, is in the middle of a battle with New York schools over how students can use its search engine.

The company announced on November 3 that it would turn off access to Search and its standalone artificial intelligence (AI) tools by default for K–12 student accounts, unless school administrators turn them on. Google later clarified that schools could enable Search without enabling the standalone Gemini chatbot. But schools that want to block AI-generated answers within Search would have to turn off Search itself. The changes are scheduled to take effect in early 2027.

The company’s rationale? “Search and AI are deeply integrated”, according to Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The announcement came amid wider scrutiny of Google’s push to integrate AI into Search. Just days earlier, the company had inadvertently revealed that its AI Mode generated less advertising revenue per query than traditional Search. Its insistence on retaining AI features in Search has now drawn criticism from educators and parents who want the option to turn them off.

In September, New York City announced its one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI, covering nearly 600,000 public school students through eighth grade. High school students can use AI only in approved programmes, while the city prohibits AI companion chatbots across all grades.

How did US schools become so dependent on Google?

“For the last 10–15 years Google has been trying to become a default presence in schools across the world,” Ben Williamson, senior lecturer in digital education at the University of Edinburgh, told The Indian Express.

Google’s low-cost Chromebooks have become the most widely issued student devices in the US since the company piloted them in 2010. By 2016, they accounted for 58% of mobile computing devices shipped to US schools, according to Reuters.

Schools also rely on Gmail, Google Docs and Google Classroom, where teachers can set assignments. Williamson pointed to the company’s integration with hundreds of other educational apps. Google’s single sign-on system lets students and teachers use one Google account to access those apps too.

A laptop in a language arts class where the teacher had students write argumentative paragraphs about free will and enter them into a Google chatbot that graded them on their arguments, at Southwest Miami High School, Miami, Fla., April, 2025. (Ysa Perez/The New York Times)

“All of this eventually means schools struggle to separate themselves from Google — they have become dependent on Google for all their digital needs,” Williamson added.

Concerns about Google’s growing influence in schools predate the current AI controversy. Researchers have since questioned the implications of schools’ reliance on Google’s products, while European regulators have scrutinised their use over data protection concerns. In January 2024, Denmark’s data protection authority ordered 53 municipalities to change how they shared pupils’ personal data with Google through Chromebooks and Google Workspace.

Also in Explained | How Google’s AI push is threatening search ad revenues and spooking investors

In August, the company enabled AI features by default in Google Classroom for schools that had already allowed students access to its standalone Gemini chatbot. This move sparked objections from school leaders and parents who wanted greater control over how students used AI tools.

Williamson argues that Google is now using these existing dependencies, or what he calls “lock-ins”, to push its AI products into schools.

“Many schools do not want to feel forced to use AI just because they are already using other Google products,” Williamson said. “It reduces their institutional autonomy and the freedom of educators to make professional decisions about the tools they use in classrooms.”

Why are schools concerned about generative AI?

Search engines have long used machine learning, Williamson said. “But what people are really objecting to is ‘generative AI’.”

Beyond cheating and inaccurate answers, researchers have raised questions about how reliance on AI-generated responses could affect children’s critical thinking and independent learning. A 2026 review of 22 studies on generative AI use in school education, published in Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, identified potential risks including cognitive dependence, students overestimating their own understanding, and effects on psychological wellbeing. The researchers also highlighted gaps in the evidence and recommended safeguards.

Williamson argues that “there is no clear evidence of the benefits of generative AI for students and it may even undermine their learning practices.” Google, however, claims its research found measurable improvements in student learning with Guided Learning, a feature in its Gemini chatbot.

The risks have already become a subject of litigation. The parents of a US schoolgirl have sued Google, alleging that she used Gemini on her school-provided Chromebook to plan a suicide attempt after beginning to use the chatbot at 13. They accused Google of failing to adequately warn students of its risks.

Also Read | ChatGPT for Teens an ‘unacceptable risk’ to young users: What a new report says

Google said it was reviewing the allegations and had worked with medical professionals and researchers to develop safeguards for young users.

So what exactly has Google announced now?

Google has proposed two options for schools that enable Search. One is conventional search with AI Overviews (AI-generated summaries of search results) and the option to ask questions in an AI chat. The other is search with Guided Learning, a feature in Gemini that Google says prompts students to work through a physics problem or a book report step by step before giving them an answer.

Google began piloting Guided Learning in Search at selected US schools in November. It has also made Guided Learning available globally through Google Classroom, where teachers can assign activities based on classroom material.

A test by The New York Times, however, found that the consumer version of Guided Learning produced a detailed essay in response to a school history assignment. Brit Mennuti, Google Classroom’s product lead, told the newspaper that the version being piloted in schools has additional restrictions and would let teachers review students’ chatbot transcripts.

Does Google’s decision raise antitrust concerns?

Google’s decision has also raised questions about the power it exercises over schools that depend on its services. Lina Khan, former chair of the US Federal Trade Commission, accused Google of using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting AI. On November 9, US Senator Ed Markey called on Google to reverse its decision and explain whether it could separate generative AI features from Search.

The question of whether Google can legally bundle AI features with Search has already reached the courts. In September, a US federal judge dismissed an antitrust claim by publisher Penske Media, which had accused Google of unlawfully tying AI Overviews to its search engine. The judge found that Penske had failed to sufficiently establish that Search and AI Overviews were separate products, a key requirement for an unlawful tying claim.

Also Read | Meta agrees to $17bn child safety settlement: What changes for teens on Instagram and Facebook?

Whether Google’s policy for schools raises antitrust concerns, particularly given its dominance of the search market, remains an open question.

Who gets to decide what technology children get to use?

Beyond the competition concerns, Williamson questioned how much influence technology companies have acquired over public education.

“Companies like Google have become almost like international policy authorities,” he said. “They are able to shape what happens in schools through changing how digital platforms, apps and services operate…It’s as if they can set education policy through programming code.”

He also questioned the growing commercial influence over education. “Private companies should not be able to determine what happens in public education systems,” he said.

Williamson called for stronger procurement and evaluation processes, including clear ways for schools to exit contracts and switch technology providers. He also argued that schools should be able to move their data between platforms and independently assess changes to the software they use, before companies roll out new features to millions of classrooms.

entry.title: Can a Hindu man automatically claim share in his grandfather’s property? What SC held
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 09:22 AM IST The Supreme Court in New Delhi. (Express photo by Amit Mehra) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

If a man inherits property from his father, is his son automatically entitled to a share in it under the Hindu Succession Act of 1956? Not really.

Continuing with the analogy, it is the man who becomes the absolute owner of the property and can deal with it as he chooses, including by excluding the son, according to a Supreme Court verdict last week.

Birth alone, therefore, does not mean a man can inherit his grandfather’s property — if his father is still alive and is himself an heir. The question, then, is when can a man claim a share in his grandfather’s property? And what does the law say about inheritance? We explain.

First, the facts of the case

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The case in the Supreme Court dealt with the property of one N Ramakrishnan, which was divided among his heirs following a partition suit filed by his daughter in 1993.

Ramakrishnan’s son, M Kumaran, received a plot under a compromise deed in February 1994 and sold it in April 1997. But Kumaran’s son, Rajesh, later sued his father and the buyers, claiming that the plot was ancestral property and that he had acquired a coparcenary interest in it by birth.

In Indian law, coparcenary is the group within a joint family that holds ancestral property together, with each member getting a share in it by birth.

Explained | Reading SC’s verdict on Hindu women’s inheritance rights

A trial court in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, granted a preliminary decree for partition in Rajesh’s favour. However, an appellate court set the decree aside, holding that the property had become Kumaran’s exclusive share following the partition among the grandfather’s heirs. The Madras High Court upheld that decision — and so did the Supreme Court.

The legal framework

Hindu law has two main schools, Dayabhaga and Mitakshara. Dayabhaga is followed in West Bengal and Assam, and Mitakshara is followed across the rest of India.

Under Dayabhaga, a son does not get a right in the family property by birth. His right opens only when his father dies. Until then, the father owns the property and can deal with it as he chooses.

Under the Mitakshara school of Hindu law, a son acquires an interest in ancestral coparcenary property by birth. Unlike an ordinary inheritance claim, the right does not arise only when the father dies. The son becomes a coparcener, or joint owner, in the joint Hindu family and can even claim a share in the coparcenary property.

The Hindu Succession Act has a schedule that lists who inherits and in what order. Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act states that when a Hindu male dies intestate — that is, without making a valid will — his property first goes to relatives specified as Class I heirs in that Schedule. Class I heirs include his son, daughter, widow and mother, among others.

The son of a predeceased son is included, but the son of a living son is not.

This is the distinction that lies at the heart of the present case — a man cannot claim direct succession to his grandfather’s property under Section 8 while his father is still alive and himself an heir.

Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (prior to the 2005 amendment) dealt with the devolution of a male Hindu’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property. A coparcener’s share in the joint family property did not pass by succession when he died. It automatically passes to the other coparceners in the family. The exception was where he left behind a female Class I heir such as a widow or a daughter. In that case, the share went to his heirs under the Act.

Section 19 of the Act also says that where two or more heirs inherit the property of a man who has not left a will behind, they receive it as tenants in common and not as joint tenants. This means that each heir holds an individual share that can be dealt with independently.

What the Supreme Court held

The bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal said: “The right of a son’s son in his grandfather’s property during the lifetime of his father which existed under the personal Hindu Law as enforced before the Act 1956, was not saved expressly by the legislature while enacting the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.”

Explained law | Moral obligation can become a legal one: Delhi HC on granddaughter’s property rights

The court held that Ramakrishnan’s property devolved upon his Class I heirs under Section 8 following his death. The bench noted that a grandson who is the son of a living son was not included in that category.

“A son’s son is not mentioned as an heir under Class I of the Schedule, and, therefore, he could not get any right in the property of his grandfather under the provision,” the bench noted.

The court also said that once the heirs partitioned the property, each became the exclusive owner of the share allotted to them. They inherited as tenants in common, rather than as joint tenants, and the joint coparcenary did not continue. As explained above, a tenant in common holds an individual, identifiable share in property which can be dealt with independently. The plot allotted to Kumaran under the compromise deed became his individual property, and he was entitled to sell it.

“There is no question of devolution of the property once partitioned and became exclusive individual property of the first respondent upon the appellant herein so as to recognise his right on the premise of attaining coparcenary rights with his birth,” the court said.

The grandson also argued that he had acquired coparcenary rights upon birth, and that Section 29A of the Hindu Succession Act, which was added to grant coparcenary rights to daughters, did not preserve any coparcenary character of the property following the 1994 compromise decree.

The bench rejected this argument, noting that although the grandfather’s exact date of death was not disclosed in the record, succession had opened upon his death long before the grandson was born and before the partition proceedings were instituted in 1993. The top court held that the grandson was not a surviving coparcener when succession opened.

entry.title: Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya
entry.content:
8 min readUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 08:20 PM IST A sign for the COP31 UN Climate Summit at the Istanbul Airport in Turkey. Photo: AP/Emrah Gurel/File Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Written by Indu K Murthy

Starting Monday (November 9), the next chapter of global climate action will unfold in Turkey at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) until November 20, with about 100,000 participants and heads of state gathering for a World Leaders’ Summit on November 11 and 12.

As the first COP since the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement earlier this year, COP31 removes the largest historical emitter from finance conversations, sharpening developing countries’ demand that Europe and others fill the gap. Energy security, meanwhile, has taken centre stage. The war on Iran has pushed up oil and gas prices, raising the cost of fuel and food. Supporters of a faster energy transition argue that this shows the risks of fossil-fuel dependence, while importers such as India face more immediate pressure to keep supplies affordable.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The questions that matter are how much finance will actually flow to developing countries, how adaptation will be measured and paid for, and whether mounting pressure on coal and emission targets will respect the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” (CBDR-RC).

What is a COP?

A COP is the annual meeting of countries that signed the 1992 UNFCCC. In Antalya, there will be three meetings in focus: COP31, the 21st session of the Conference of Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the Kyoto Protocol (CMP21), and the 8th session of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the 2015 Paris Agreement (CMA8).

Also read | Three steps COP should take for tangible outcomes

The Paris Agreement asks every country to submit a nationally determined contribution (NDC), essentially its own climate plan, every five years, with the shared ambition of holding warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Because decisions require consensus, a single country can hold up an agreement.

How is COP31 different from previous COPs?

COP venues rotate among the UN’s regional groups, and 2026 was the turn of the “Western European and Others” group to host. Turkey bid with Antalya, and Australia bid with Adelaide, in partnership with Pacific Island nations.

The resulting standoff led to an unusual power-sharing deal last year, making COP31 the first summit where one country hosts the meeting while another runs the negotiations.

Turkey is the formal COP31 president and host, responsible for the venue, logistics, and the “Action Agenda” of voluntary pledges and initiatives, whereas Australia has “exclusive authority” over formal talks, drafting of texts, and steering decisions. This dual leadership model is untested, and questions remain about who would have the final word if there were disagreement in the closing hours. 

What’s on the table?

COP31 is not expected to produce a landmark treaty text. The real fight is over delivery: mobilising finance, measuring progress, and accelerating the energy shift.

In terms of co-chairing consultations, India and Germany must decide on mitigation, as in how to press countries whose 2035 plans fall short of 1.5°C and what “transitioning away from fossil fuels” actually requires. On finance, France and the Philippines will work to build consensus on delivering existing finance commitments. On adaptation, the UK and Sierra Leone must chart a credible path to tripling adaptation finance and make enough headway for the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to be finalised at COP32.

A street vendor walks amid thick haze from wildfires in Indonesia on October 24, 2026. Photo: AP/Yulianus Stefan Lundju/File

Taking on newer ground, Mexico and Poland must work out how the just transition mechanism will function and what money and technical help it will give affected workers and communities. Palau and Canada handle the ocean, where Pacific Island countries want commitments written into formal decisions.

Two more items will set the summit’s tone. Turkey wants countries to pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use from about 23% today to 35% by 2035. Further, developing countries, including India, have pushed to include Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, the clause that obligates developed countries to provide finance, in the provisional agenda.

What Belém left behind

The COP30 in Belém, Brazil, closed with a package called the “Global Mutirão” (meaning, collective effort) and Antalya inherits this “to-do” list. It called for adaptation finance to be at least tripled by 2035, five years later than developing countries had wanted and without a clear baseline.

More broadly, it endorsed the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap to scale climate finance for developing countries to at least $1.3 trillion a year by 2035 from public and private sources, building on the $300 billion-a-year goal agreed at COP29 in Baku (Azerbaijan). It adopted a set of “Belém indicators” to measure progress on the GGA, created new vehicles for delivery, namely a Global Implementation Accelerator and a “Belém Mission to 1.5” to help countries carry out their plans, alongside work on a just transition mechanism.

Also read | Look beyond old climate fault lines

The most conspicuous gap concerned fossil fuels. More than 80 countries backed a roadmap to move away from oil, coal, and gas, yet the final text left fossil fuels out entirely, referring only to the 2023 Dubai “UAE Consensus”. Brazil is now steering a voluntary roadmap process outside the formal talks, and Colombia and the Netherlands have initiated the Santa Marta process — an international, plurilateral climate initiative complementing the COP process launched in Santa Marta, Colombia — in April 2026 to identify pathways for the phase-out.

Where does India stand on its climate goals?

India goes to Antalya with a new climate plan and a central seat at the table, co-chairing mitigation consultations. India’s third NDC, covering 2031-2035, was approved and submitted in April.

The new plan raises the target for reducing the emission intensity of gross domestic product (GDP) to 47% below 2005 levels by 2035, up from 45% by 2030. Emission intensity of GDP, which measures the volume of greenhouse gases (usually carbon dioxide, or CO2, equivalent) emitted for each unit of economic output or GDP, acts as a key indicator of how carbon-efficient an economy is as it grows.

The plan increases the non-fossil share of installed power capacity from 50% by 2030 (already met) to 60% by 2035 and expands the promised additional carbon sink from forest and tree cover from 2.5-3.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent to 3.5-4.0 billion tonnes. A carbon sink refers to any natural or artificial system that absorbs more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases, helping reduce the greenhouse gases responsible for global warming.

Also read | India must set a higher bar on clean energy targets

The NDC, however, ties any further ambition to “new and additional” finance and technology from developed countries. This conditionality runs through India’s negotiating line, which Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav set out at the Pre-COP in Fiji last month (October 5-8, 2026).

Yadav called for equal weight to be given to adaptation; mitigation; and the “means of implementation”, that is, finance, technology, and capacity-building. He insisted that the principle of CBDR-RC be upheld “in letter and spirit”, with no one-size-fits-all pathway imposed on countries. He backed the Article 9.1 finance discussion and argued that success should be measured by delivery on existing commitments rather than by new targets or declarations.

COP31: What to watch out for

Five questions will determine how Antalya is remembered.

The first is finance, and whether developed countries put numbers and a timeline behind tripling adaptation finance and give the $1.3 trillion roadmap a monitoring system.
The second is fossil fuels, and whether the negotiated text will include a transition away from them.

The third is Turkey’s electrification pledge, specifically how many countries sign on to the 35%-by-2035 target.

The fourth is the split presidency itself — the real stress test of a model that future COPs may copy.

The fifth is the Global South bargain, and whether India and other developing countries secure the Article 9.1 discussion and reforms to finance access in return for engaging on mitigation.

Ultimately, Antalya will be judged less on headline pledges and more on whether the promises of Paris, Baku, and Belém translate into meaningful action.

The author heads the climate, environment and sustainability sector at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

entry.title: Sensex surges, but what will it take for a sustained rally? An expert explains
entry.content:
Written by: Sandeep Singh10 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 5, 2026 03:58 PM IST Sensex jumped nearly 2,100 points to end at 79,373.18 on Thursday. (File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

A buoyant Sensex jumped nearly 2,100 points to end at 79,373.18 on Thursday amid a fall in crude  prices and hopes for a resolution to the Iran war following the US midterm drubbing for the Republicans.

Before this upsurge, however, the Sensex had traded around the 74,000 mark for around three years. A combination of factors weighed on sentiment — a weakening rupee, volatile crude oil prices, geopolitical tension, slowing growth and uncertainty over a trade deal with the US. 

Sankaran Naren, Executive Director and Chief Investment Officer at ICICI Prudential AMC, spoke to Sandeep Singh, National Bureau Chief at The Indian Express, on October 27, about what was holding the markets back and what risks should investors be watching out for. Edited excerpts from the Explained.Live interview.

What was holding the markets back?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Three years back, the markets were overvalued. That could be part of the explanation. But there are multiple reasons holding back the market.

First, is the geopolitical problem — war in Ukraine and the Gulf, and record high crude oil prices.

Second, artificial intelligence-related growth has been very high in some countries: US, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, etc. The growth rate there has been much higher than the growth rate that India can ever give. People have moved to these markets, particularly in the last two years. 

Also Read | What Democrat-controlled US Congress means for AI, trade, immigration, oil

And the third reason is that after March 2023, once the money started coming into equity mutual funds, three sets of investors started to sell. One is Indian promoters who have been launching IPO after IPO because they know that the markets are overvalued. The second is private equity companies which had invested pre-2023, which had realised that you can sell these stocks to Indian investors at a good price. And the third was multinationals who had set up businesses in India over the last 20, 30, 40 years. They realised that they should list in India because here you get valuations much higher than in your home country.

Despite the huge amount of money that we collected, all that money primarily went into these three sets of people’s pockets. And that is why markets have not delivered returns. 

Weakening rupee, volatile oil prices, rising interest rates, slowing growth: What is your biggest worry?

I am worried about the impact of AI on India, whether it will be negative or positive. It is the most important long-term view because at some point of time the war will end and when the war ends, oil will come down. At some point of time, people will not have IPOs. 

But AI can be a structural trend. And no one knows what the long-term impact of AI will be. People believe that fund managers can correctly guess the long-term impact, but we also don’t know. 

There is a talk of India becoming a $20-trillion economy say two decades from now. Are the grounds ready for that?

In the services sector, there are no other countries which are competing with us. In manufacturing, there are multiple countries that are competing, including Vietnam and Thailand.

To win in manufacturing is not as easy as winning in services. Is India working to become better every year over the previous year? Yes. But the competition is intense.

Also Read | Trump’s midterm defeat: Good news or fresh trouble for India’s trade deal?

I think we need to create manufacturing employment on a very very large scale. And that is the solution for growth to increase. And I’m sure that the government is well aware of this issue and will focus on it. But it is not as easy to create a global manufacturing hub in every area as it has been to create a global services hub. 

Assuming that the US-Iran war ends, which sectors should investors look at to maximise their returns? 

I think banking clearly will benefit a lot because the sector has been hurt by inflation and the rupee has been depreciating. Oil marketing companies should certainly benefit because they are the people who are bearing the brunt of the higher oil prices. If you look at areas like aviation for example, they are going to be benefited. But overall, we have started rate hikes and they may continue if oil is like this. But if the war ends and oil crashes, the requirement for the Reserve Bank of India to keep hiking interest rates also goes down. But we require a good fall in oil. A good fall in oil actually lubricates all parts of the economy, not just a few areas. 

These are external factors. On the domestic front, what gives you comfort and what is challenging? 

The current account deficit is under control, fiscal deficit is under control. Credit growth is booming. The automotive industry has been booming over the last year. Power demand has been booming. 

Some of the challenges include a subpar monsoon. And there is always the worry that El Niño will create more problems. 

Also Read | ‘Similar to cricket betting’: Amid India’s IPO booms, why investors need to watch out for grey markets

There are things that any country can do… the RBI realised that it is important to get insurance deposits. So, they floated an FCNR scheme and collected $127 billion of deposits. That takes care of all near-term foreign exchange issues.

Having said that, the problem of the war, and the problem of what AI leads to in the future, will remain. 

Amid these challenges, does asset allocation become much more important, given we don’t know how things are going to shape, and how long the challenges will continue given the nature of them being external rather than internal? 

Indians have got this love for equity at this point of time. And equity is inherently not a riskless asset class. That’s why if people start practising asset allocation, they will view volatility as an opportunity and not worry so much. But, if you are only invested in equity or you take positions in derivative markets on leverage, then you are very worried about everything that is happening. 

Many investors have 15-20 schemes in their portfolio. Can you simplify and tell us three classes of schemes that investors must possess at all times?

I am of the view that if you create three categories — balanced advantage, balanced hybrid, and flexi cap — you would have covered substantially. Then you don’t need to worry day-to-day about what’s happening in the market. You just keep investing in these categories and keep saving and keeping put money in these three categories because our broad approach is very clear. 

Can you take our readers through these categories briefly?

Balanced advantage is a very simple model: As the market goes up, you keep selling, and as the market goes down, you keep buying. So in 2023-24 when the market was more overvalued, it had less exposure to equity and higher exposure to debt and arbitrage. Today, because equity has become more fairly valued, it has a higher exposure to equity and a lower exposure to arbitrage and debt. 

Also Read | US midterms: Trump loses Congress. What changes for India and the world?

If you look at balanced hybrids, it’s even more simple. It says you can invest between 40% and 60% in debt, and 40% and 60% in equity. It is the quintessential asset allocation product where you’re choosing two products, and both the products have to be between 40% and 60%. 

The third category is called “flexi” cap because you can invest in all kinds of things. You can invest in large cap, mid cap, small cap, micro cap and, therefore, you are entirely investing in the entire equity market. So we call it the most unconstrained fund.

For people who need gold, I would say multi-asset is the fourth category.

What’s your advice for retail investors? 

For the first 10 years of people’s investing career, they should choose mutual funds so that they go through one cycle. They understand what is investing through balanced advantage or multi asset or flexi cap. After 10 years of investing, if you have learned quite a lot, then you do direct equity. And if you become an expert after 20, 30 years, you do derivatives.

But unfortunately, when we talk to stockbrokers, they say it is 25 to 30-year-olds who are actually trading derivatives. I do not know whether they have the knowledge and the temperament to handle it well.

Reader questions

Countries which have AI on their side, like the US, their markets are doing much better. Would you suggest that we try to invest in foreign markets?

Any market which is exuberant and where valuations are high is actually a riskier market. So, at this point of time we tell people to be careful if you are investing in the Nasdaq index because it is the best performing index in the world in the last 10 years. 

I am currently investing in mutual funds. My SIP is around Rs 25,000 a month. Should I stop it because for the past 2 years, whatever I have invested giving negative returns?

We tell people to start a SIP in flexi cap category or balanced advantage category or multi-asset category. Forget closing, we tell people to add now. That is our view. Actually, that is what we have been trying to promote at this point of time. So, I think you know, for the best benefit of SIP, you actually have to invest when the markets are down.

entry.content:
Written by: Major-General (retd) G G Dwivedi6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 3, 2026 07:57 PM IST Chinese President Xi Jinping, center attends a meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China. (Kai Naito/Pool Photo via AP) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

A key political meeting that recently concluded in China reflected President Xi Jinping’s resolve to tighten political control and reinforce the supremacy of the Communist Party of China (CPC).

The Fifth Plenary Session of the Party’s 20th Central Committee, held in Beijing from October 26–29, also addressed institutional vulnerabilities, which matter ahead of next year’s Party Congress — an all-important meeting held every five years. According to the official communiqué, the conclave focused on internal Party discipline, leadership adjustments, and preparations for the next political cycle.

For India, the implications are strategic rather than merely political. Understanding China requires looking beyond its economic strength and military hardware to its political architecture, the mindset of its leadership, and strategic behaviour.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Significance of the Plenums

During its five-year tenure, the CPC Central Committee, elected by the National Party Congress (NPC) or the national legislature, holds seven plenary sessions. These serve as important instruments for translating the NPC’s political directions into policies and decisions.

Although each plenum follows an established agenda, the 20th Central Committee (established during the 2022 Party Congress) witnessed some deviations. The First and Second Plenums focus on top leadership appointments and state institutional structures. The Third Plenum addresses major economic policies and reforms; this time delayed and held in July 2024.

Also in Explained | How Xi Jinping’s sweeping military purge echoed at a top Chinese leaders’ meeting

The Fourth Plenum, associated with Party building, was held in October 2025 and took up the task of finalising guidelines for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), an exercise normally reserved for the Fifth Plenum. Consequently, the Fifth Plenum shifted its emphasis towards strengthening CPC governance structures ahead of the 2027 Party Congress. The Sixth traditionally centres on ideology and Party discipline, while the Seventh prepares the agenda for the next NPC.

The Fifth Plenum must be viewed against the evolution of Xi’s leadership since 2012. Anti-corruption and Party discipline have been defining features of his tenure. The 20th Party Congress in October 2022 consolidated Xi Jinping’s position as China’s paramount political leader and reaffirmed his vision of national modernisation and rejuvenation. His term as the general secretary, or top leader, of the CPC was extended for a historic third time.

The record-low attendance at the latest meeting also came amid continuing leadership upheaval, marked by investigations and disciplinary action against civilian officials and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) commanders.

Fifth Plenum: Highlights and key outcomes

The communiqué outlined several guiding principles, including strengthening of Party leadership, enforcing rigorous governance across organisations, improving institutional oversight and ensuring governance through Party regulations.

Opinion | In the name of discipline, Xi has centralised power further

A consequential outcome was the adoption of a resolution reinforcing the CPC’s position that its capacity to govern itself is fundamental to its ability to govern China. The emphasis on top-down control was particularly significant.

Perhaps the most consequential development remains the continuing upheaval within the PLA. The Plenum confirmed the expulsion of 33 officials from the Party. These included senior military figures such as Zhang Youxia, former Vice Chairman of the apex military decision-making body, the Central Military Commission (CMC), Liu Zhenli, former Chief of Staff of the Joint Staff Department, Ma Xingrui, former Politburo member and Wang Haijiang, former Western Theatre Commander. This theatre also concerns the border with India.

The shrinking military leadership is evident from the CMC’s composition. Constituted with seven members in 2022, it has since seen five members removed, leaving only Xi as Chairman and General Zhang Shengmin, who oversees military discipline. The Plenum did not announce appointments to fill the vacant positions. This could reflect an effort to retain direct control and avoid potential internal challenges, particularly amid suspicions concerning officers associated with the purged figures.

The political signal

The Plenum formally announced that the 21st Party Congress would be held in Beijing in the latter half of October 2027. It will determine the composition of the CPC’s senior leadership for the next five-year cycle.

Xi’s position remains firmly at the centre of the political system and he is widely expected to seek another term. No succession arrangements have been announced. In China’s opaque political system, personnel changes and purges offer important, though not definitive, indicators of leadership priorities. In this context, Zhang Shengmin’s elevation to Politburo merits attention, although it does not settle the succession question.

The Fifth Plenum was primarily an exercise in reinforcing the foundations of Xi’s political system before the Party Congress. The underlying proposition is that the Party must strengthen and discipline itself to lead China’s rejuvenation. The unprecedented removal of senior functionaries, particularly within the PLA, highlights the continuing emphasis on political control.

However, tighter political control cannot, by itself, resolve China’s economic challenges. Weak domestic consumption, property-sector stress, local government debt, demographic decline and external technology restrictions remain structural constraints. The 15th Five-Year Plan seeks to address these issues. Excessive political control can constrain private enterprise and discourage innovation. The challenge, therefore, is to balance political authority with the flexibility required for sustained economic growth.

The centrality of national security in China’s governance framework was also reinforced. Domestic governance and external policies are increasingly interconnected. Against the backdrop of intensifying US-China competition, the leadership is expected to accelerate efforts towards technological independence, military modernisation and strategic outreach.

Closer to home, China’s territorial claims and emphasis on national security will continue to shape the environment along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). The removal of senior PLA commanders should not be interpreted as a moderation of China’s strategic objectives or a dilution of its military capabilities. India must closely monitor changes in the PLA’s command structure and operational readiness while strengthening its own defence preparedness as part of a coherent China policy.

entry.title: Delhi’s AQI is 370, but some platforms show 1,000: Why do readings differ?
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk7 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 01:03 PM IST A tanker sprays water at Kartavya Path in New Delhi on November 8, 2026. (Express photo by Praveen Khanna) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Delhi AQI: Several monitoring stations in Delhi recorded ‘severe’ air quality on Monday (November 9), a day after Diwali festivities were marked by widespread use of firecrackers despite Supreme Court-mandated restrictions.

The court had permitted only certified green crackers to be burst between 6 am and 7 am and 8 pm and 10 pm on November 7 and 8, with a complete ban returning on November 9. However, firecrackers were reportedly burst beyond the permitted hours, while illegal sales of conventional crackers had also been reported ahead of Diwali.

A thick layer of smog engulfed several parts of the city, reducing visibility on Monday morning. While Delhi’s overall AQI remained in the ‘very poor’ category, several monitoring stations recorded readings above 400, the threshold for ‘severe’ air quality. Some private monitoring platforms reported substantially higher readings, although differences in AQI scales and measurement methods mean these figures cannot be directly compared.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Over the years, The Indian Express has extensively reported on and explained Delhi’s worsening air pollution, from the factors driving seasonal spikes to how air quality is measured and the measures taken to tackle it. This article brings together those explainers to provide a one-stop guide to understanding the Air Quality Index (AQI), its impact on health, and the restrictions imposed under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).

What is the AQI and how is it calculated?

AQI is a number which measures air quality. The higher the AQI, the worse the air.

The AQI used in India was launched in 2014 as part of the government’s Swachh Bharat campaign. The colour-coded index helps explain the condition of the air and the measures necessary to mitigate the situation depending on its severity.

The index converts measurements of up to eight major air pollutants into a single number, category and colour. These include particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone, carbon monoxide, ammonia and lead.

Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya

Each pollutant’s concentration is converted into a separate sub-index based on established health-related thresholds. The highest sub-index determines the overall AQI, rather than an average of all pollutants.

There are six categories of AQI, namely ‘Good’ (0-50), ‘Satisfactory’ (51-100), ‘Moderate’ (101-200), ‘Poor’ (201-300), ‘Very Poor’ (301-400), and ‘Severe’ (401-500).

Why do private platforms show much higher AQI readings than government agencies?

While the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) recorded Delhi’s 24-hour average AQI at 370 on Monday morning, private monitoring platform AQI.in reported a reading of 955 under US standards and 787 under its Indian-standard calculation. How can the readings differ so dramatically?

The difference lies partly in how the index is calculated. India’s official AQI uses a scale that stops at 500, while some international platforms use different thresholds for pollutant concentrations and allow readings to exceed 500.

Pollution and visibility post Diwali in Noida and Delhi on Monday, November 9, 2026. Express photo by Abhinav Saha

In November 2024, atmospheric scientist Gufran Beig explained that AQI values are calculated using breakpoints, or thresholds at which pollution moves from one category to another. India’s thresholds differ from those used by some international platforms, meaning the same underlying pollution data can produce different AQI values.

Beig also questioned India’s decision to cap its AQI at 500, regardless of how much pollutant concentrations exceed that level. This means that an official reading of 500 does not necessarily indicate that pollution has stopped increasing. The actual concentration of harmful particles could continue to rise without a corresponding increase in the reported index.

However, differences in AQI scales do not explain every discrepancy. Platforms may also use different monitoring locations, averaging periods and measurement methods.

But how reliable are the measurements themselves? Click here to read how Delhi’s air quality monitoring stations work, and why their readings can sometimes falter.

What is the impact of these pollutants?

Among the more harmful pollutants are fine particles such as PM2.5, which have a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less, roughly 3% of the width of a human hair.

These particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, increasing the risk of respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses. Prolonged exposure has been linked to conditions such as asthma, chronic bronchitis, heart disease and stroke. Particulate pollution also reduces visibility, contributing to the smog seen across Delhi.

Even certified green crackers contribute to air pollution. Developed by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research–National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI), they use modified chemical formulations to reduce emissions compared with conventional firecrackers. However, they still release harmful particles and gases, particularly when burst in large numbers.

As public-health expert Sonu Goel explained in an interview with Hina Rohtaki, reducing emissions does not eliminate exposure to pollutants. Green crackers can reduce certain emissions, but their effectiveness varies with the product and pollutant measured.

Also Read | How one city in China became the fireworks factory of the world

Delhi’s winter pollution is driven by several factors, including vehicle emissions, construction dust, industrial activity and seasonal crop-residue burning. Cooler temperatures, weaker winds and atmospheric conditions that prevent pollutants from dispersing can make matters worse, as Sophiya Mathew explained in October.

How does the AQI influence government policy?

In Delhi-NCR, rising pollution levels trigger progressively stricter measures under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), implemented by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM). The four stages correspond to different AQI ranges, although authorities can invoke measures in advance based on forecasts of worsening air quality

Stage III of GRAP has been in force across Delhi-NCR since Friday (November 6), when the city’s AQI stood at 382, in the ‘very poor’ category, and forecasts indicated further deterioration.

The restrictions include curbs on non-essential construction and demolition activities, a ban on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers in Delhi and specified NCR districts, and hybrid classes for children up to Class V, subject to applicable exemptions. Measures introduced under Stages I and II also continue.

Subscribe

Stage IV, which can be invoked when Delhi’s AQI exceeds 450 or forecasts indicate that it will, introduces further restrictions, including tighter curbs on truck entry and school attendance. It has not been invoked in the current episode as of Monday morning.

For more on how GRAP works and the restrictions imposed at each stage, read our earlier explainer.

Can Delhi learn from China’s experience in tackling air pollution?

While GRAP imposes emergency restrictions when pollution levels rise, tackling Delhi’s air pollution requires sustained measures to reduce emissions at their source.

China offers one example. After facing severe air pollution in the 2000s, the country introduced stricter industrial emission controls, cleaner heating systems and measures to expand electric public transport. Research has linked these interventions to significant improvements in air quality.

However, differences in governance, energy access and sources of pollution mean India cannot simply replicate China’s approach. Click here to read Rishika Singh’s explainer on how China tackled air pollution and the lessons India can draw from its experience.

entry.title: Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy
entry.content:
Written by: Soumyarendra Barik8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 11:03 AM IST Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, speaks alongside President Donald Trump during the Investing in America event at the White House in Washington in 2025. (NYT file) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Chipmaking giant Nvidia has launched an investigation into reports that Chinese intelligence targeted its chief executive, Jensen Huang, through a woman who was a former executive at the firm Megaspeed. The controversy puts renewed scrutiny on the Singapore-based data centre operator, which American authorities have separately investigated since 2024 over suspicions that it was helping China access restricted artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

On being asked about the allegations, US President Donald Trump said, “I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he’s a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on,” he told reporters. “I hope everything’s fine,” he said, adding that Huang was an “honourable guy” and that “he probably has an excuse for ​it. ⁠You have to hear it.”

The row has spotlighted Megaspeed’s Chinese origins, its purchase of billions of dollars worth of Nvidia equipment, and allegations that the company has received financing from Chinese technology giant Alibaba, despite being registered in Singapore.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The company has also been at the centre of concerns in Washington over whether American export restrictions can effectively prevent Chinese businesses from accessing advanced AI computing power through data centres in third countries.

What are the allegations against Jensen Huang?

Recent media reports claimed that Huang had a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. In a message on Sunday (November 8), he confirmed the claims, stating, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The same day, Nvidia said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, would investigate the allegations. While the board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised, it would examine all available information.

Explained | Why ‘physical AI’ marks the next frontier in industrial applications

The allegations have also brought renewed scrutiny to Huang’s lobbying of the Donald Trump administration to ease restrictions on Nvidia’s chip exports to China. This position has drawn criticism from US lawmakers and national security officials concerned that Beijing could use advanced American AI technology to strengthen its military capabilities. Huang has repeatedly argued that supplying inferior quality chips to China would help stem the growth of its domestic industries and innovation.

But after the spying allegations, the possibility that a suspected Chinese intelligence operative had personal access to Huang has further heightened concerns over whether Beijing could have sought to influence his advocacy for easing these restrictions.

While American export controls prohibit the unauthorised shipment of certain advanced chips to China, Chinese companies can potentially obtain access to comparable computing power by renting infrastructure housed in other countries. Such arrangements are not necessarily illegal, but they have complicated Washington’s attempts to restrict Beijing’s AI capabilities.

The global AI boom has propelled Nvidia into becoming one of the world’s most valuable companies (currently valued at over $4.5 trillion), as technology giants such as Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon spend billions of dollars building AI infrastructure powered by its advanced chips. Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs) have become central to training and running sophisticated AI models, giving the company a dominant position in the market for AI computing hardware.

What is Megaspeed, and what are its alleged links to China?

Megaspeed is a Singapore-registered company that provides AI computing capacity through data centres in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia. Its origins, however, can be traced to 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud-computing company that US lawmakers have described as having links to the Chinese government. Megaspeed was previously incorporated as 7Road International before adopting its present name in 2023.

Also Read | ‘The world’s most valuable chipmaker’: How Nvidia saw a 250% surge in revenues amid AI stock rally

Despite Nvidia maintaining that Megaspeed has no Chinese shareholders and is operated outside China, its business dealings have raised questions about the extent of its links with Chinese technology companies.

According to trade records cited by The New York Times, a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. The company has reportedly supplied computing capacity to Alibaba and other Chinese businesses, allowing them to access Nvidia-powered infrastructure located outside China.

American authorities had begun examining Megaspeed’s operations well before the alleged Chinese intelligence operation involving Huang came to light.

The US Commerce Department started investigating the company in late 2024, after an official visiting one of its data centres in Malaysia reportedly found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising suspicions that the chips could be shipped elsewhere rather than installed at the facility.

According to reports, American officials subsequently examined whether Megaspeed was diverting chips to China in violation of US export controls. The investigation was transferred to the US Department of Justice earlier this year.

In October 2025, Republican Senator Tom Cotton also wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, calling for an investigation into Megaspeed’s ownership, affiliations and potential violations of American export restrictions. Cotton flagged the routing of Nvidia equipment through intermediaries, including a US subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese technology company whose parent had been placed on Washington’s trade blacklist.

What Nvidia, Megaspeed argued

Singaporean authorities have also confirmed an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed for suspected breaches of domestic laws. However, neither the American nor Singaporean investigations have publicly established that Megaspeed illegally diverted chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing, while Nvidia has maintained that its checks found no evidence of diversion.

In May 2026, short-selling firm Culper Research published a report alleging that Megaspeed had received financial backing linked to Alibaba through intermediary companies, despite claims that it was not Chinese-owned.

Citing corporate filings, Culper said Megaspeed’s balance sheet expanded from $33 million at the end of 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, driven largely by $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an undisclosed source.

Technology | Nvidia to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion: What changes for open-source AI, rivals

The report also pointed to filings showing that Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, had pledged its business as collateral to Singapore-based Apex Enterprise Solutions, whose parent company was Alibaba. Culper alleged that these arrangements suggested Alibaba-linked financing was being channelled into purchases of Nvidia-powered servers.

More broadly, Culper alleged that over 20% of Nvidia’s FY2026 compute revenue was ultimately driven by Chinese demand through Southeast Asian intermediaries and illegal chip diversion. The firm disclosed that it held a short position in Nvidia, meaning it stood to benefit from a fall in the company’s share price. Its allegations remain unproven.

The Chinese espionage allegations

The latest allegations centre on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials reportedly concluded was passing information to Beijing.

The New York Times reported that she had developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, while reports have suggested that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather information about Huang and potentially influence his position on chip exports. In his message to Nvidia employees, Huang apologised and accepted responsibility for his conduct. He did not identify the other person in his statement.

China has rejected the espionage allegations. Singapore, on its part, has clarified that it did not investigate Alice Huang over alleged intelligence ties, distinguishing that allegation from its ongoing investigation into Megaspeed.

Singaporean authorities are separately investigating Megaspeed for suspected violations of domestic laws, although the Singapore Police Force has not disclosed the specific offences under examination. The authorities have said Singapore does not enforce unilateral US export restrictions, but will act against companies using the country to circumvent foreign controls through fraudulent practices. On October 31, Singapore clarified that the Megaspeed investigation was unrelated to allegations involving former executive Alice Huang’s suspected links to Chinese intelligence, which it said it had not investigated.

Why this matters for the US-China AI race

The controversy comes amid Washington’s efforts to restrict China’s access to advanced AI technology, particularly Nvidia’s most powerful processors, which can have military and intelligence applications. Huang’s close relationship with Trump and his lobbying for exports are also under the scanner.

Three Republican chairmen of US House committees have requested a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, citing significant national security concerns over China’s access to American technology and information.

entry.title: Why revamped Agniveer scheme isn’t a return to regular recruitment of troops
entry.content:
Written by: Amrita Nayak Dutta6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 5, 2026 06:50 PM IST Agniveer recruits of the Jammu and Kashmir Light Infantry celebrate during the passing out parade of their batch, in Srinagar on May 30, 2026. Photo: PTI/File Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The Centre on Wednesday (November 4) greenlit a path for all Agniveers undergoing training in the three services to join the armed forces as regular soldiers. This marks a major overhaul of the scheme, as it would mean all Agniveers will now have an opportunity to join the three branches of the armed forces — the Indian Army, the Indian Navy, and the Indian Air Force (IAF) — as regular soldiers.

This comes just around the time the first batches of Agniveers were to complete their four-year tenure starting this month.

Agniveers refer to individuals selected under the Agnipath scheme, wherein candidates between the age of 17 years 6 months and 21 years meeting certain eligibility criteria can apply to seek recruitment in the Indian armed forces for a four-year period.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

So, does the revamp mean that the armed forces are returning to regular recruitment of soldiers as was carried out in the pre-Covid years? If not, how is the overhauled scheme different from regular recruitment of troops? We explain.

What is the overhauled Agnipath scheme?

In the first step of the scheme that the Union Cabinet cleared on Wednesday, 25% of Agniveers will be selected on merit for absorption into the services after completing their four-year tenure. This was also part of the original scheme that came in 2022.

The remaining 75%, who would otherwise exit the services with a contributory scheme package (called Seva Nidhi), will now be offered an additional two-year engagement, after which they can join the armed forces as regular soldiers, provided they are willing and meet the military’s objective selection criteria.

This means 100% of the Agniveers joining the armed forces will get an opportunity to get absorbed into the services as permanent soldiers.

Also read | Armed Forces to assess higher Agniveer retention after first batches exit

Those serving the extended two-year period will get enhanced pay as well as an enhanced contributory Seva Nidhi package if they choose not to join the armed forces after two years. They will, however, no longer have opportunities to join paramilitary forces, public sector undertakings, or other state government jobs on reservation.

Under the Seva Nidhi package, a compulsory retirement and transition fund under the Agnipath scheme, 30% of an Agniveer’s salary is deducted and deposited into the Agniveer Corpus Fund every month — a contribution that is matched by the government of India. After completing their four-year tenure, the Agniveer receives a one-time lump sum amount of approximately ₹11.71 lakh (including interest), which is exempt from income tax. Agniveers, however, don’t receive any monthly pension or gratuity benefits after their service ends.

How many Agniveers will it immediately affect?

Over three lakh Agniveers are undergoing training at various stages in the three services.

This includes around 2.8 lakh Agniveers in the Army, of whom around 19,000 will complete their initial tenure in four years. Around 2,500 Agniveers will complete their four-year tenure in the Navy this month, and another 2,900 will complete their training as part of the first IAF batch next month.

If 100% of Agniveers join as regular soldiers, does it mean the armed forces are returning to regular recruitment?

No. Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani, while briefing the media, emphasised that the Agnipath scheme will continue, albeit with the new changes introduced.

Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani during a press briefing, in New Delhi on November 4, 2026. Photo: PTI/Ravi Choudhary

So, even if 100% Agniveers are eventually absorbed into the services as regular soldiers, only 25% will first be selected to join the forces as regular soldiers after the initial four-year tenure on a merit basis, as part of the original Agnipath scheme.

Thereafter, the rest will be given the opportunity to join the forces as regular soldiers after serving a total tenure of six years under the revamped Agnipath scheme. In terms of seniority, those who join after serving the two-year extension will be placed immediately after their own batchmates who joined the regular cadre after four years.

How does it differ from regular recruitment carried out in pre-Covid years?

Under the regular recruitment scheme, which remained in place until the Covid-19 pandemic, personnel joined the armed forces as permanent soldiers from their first day of service, making them eligible for the associated benefits and pension.

A soldier could leave the forces only through voluntary retirement or after being court-martialled for an offence.

Also in Explained | Behind Agniveer retention move: More experienced manpower, training on new platforms

Under the Agnipath scheme, Agniveers can choose to leave the forces and pursue a new career, or continue serving if they aspire to a permanent career in the armed forces. Those who accept the two-year extension will have another opportunity to choose whether to leave or continue serving when that period ends.

The Agniveers will thus have the option to choose their career path at two different levels, while always having the option to join the forces as regular soldiers, provided they meet the selection criteria. They will also have the backing of the Seva Nidhi contributory scheme if they choose to pursue a different career path after four or six years.

How does 100% absorption of Agniveers benefit the military?

If 100% of Agniveers opt to join the services as regular soldiers, it may not save the government any money on pensions. It might, however, reduce the shortage of personnel in the forces on a much faster timeline, which resulted from no recruitment and regular retirements during the Covid-19 years. This is particularly crucial in post-Galwan and post-Operation Sindoor security situations.

Military officials also maintained that the scheme will foster a competitive spirit among Agniveers and reduce complacency as they strive to be among the top 25% selected. They said the multiple layers of selection will also bring quality people into the forces.

According to Gen Subramani, the scheme will give the military a pool of experienced soldiers while maintaining a youthful profile in the armed forces, with 25% young Agniveers joining the forces at the first level.

Those leaving the services to pursue other career options will gain valuable skills and training during their years in the military.

entry.title: SC says no distinction between arrest, detention: How it resets 24-hour clock
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh9 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 6, 2026 08:28 PM IST The Supreme Court directed the magistrates to record when an accused’s liberty was first curtailed, and calculate the 24-hour deadline from that time. Photo: Unsplash Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Underlining that “the Constitution does not recognize any detention dehors [outside] arrest,” the Supreme Court on Thursday (November 5) held that the 24-hour deadline to produce a person before a magistrate begins when the person is first detained and not when the investigating agency chooses to record a formal arrest.

A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar said that searches, seizures and questioning that follow an interception cannot be treated as a pause in a Constitutional safeguard. “There is no such thing called temporary disruption of liberty,” the bench said, as it set aside the Tripura High Court’s refusal of bail in a drug smuggling case.

The court directed the magistrates to record when an accused’s liberty was first curtailed, and calculate the 24-hour deadline from that time. It said that the person is produced before them after the deadline has passed, they must order their release.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Magistrates should also examine whether the detention was reasonable. Even if the accused was produced within 24 hours, they can refuse remand if they find that the person was kept in custody on unreasonable grounds.

The ruling comes amidst large-scale detentions which police describe as preventive and can last up to 24 hours, which are a regular feature of policing in the capital. While the case arose under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, it demonstrates that the label an agency uses for restraint does not decide when the clock starts.

Background of the case

The case stems from a major anti-narcotics operation conducted by the Divisional Preventive Force (DPF), Customs Division Agartala. On September 29, 2025, at 2 pm, customs officers intercepted the appellants, who were carrying a total of 60 kg of methamphetamine tablets.

Although the appellants were brought under physical control of the search team at 2 pm, the arresting officer did not sign the formal arrest memos until 11 am the following day. They were produced before the magistrate at 4.45 pm. A special judge and the High Court both refused bail.

Also in Explained | How does detention differ from arrest, what rights do detainees have?

The investigating officer had said that the men were “merely intercepted…not formally detained” at 2 pm and that the hours between their interception and formal arrest went into search, seizure, and questioning.

Legal framework

The law governing the detention of a person during a criminal investigation is laid down in three provisions in the Constitution, the Bharatiya Nyaya Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and the NDPS Act.

Article 22 is a fundamental right under the Constitution that provides for an accused to be informed about the grounds of arrest and to get legal representation. Clause (2) specifically states that a person “arrested and detained” shall be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the travel time taken to reach the court. No person shall remain in custody for more than 24 hours without the approval of a magistrate.

Section 58 of the BNSS states that a person who has been arrested without a warrant cannot be detained for longer than “reasonable”.

In practice, the terms “arrest” and “detention” are often used interchangeably. “Arrest” is a formal act of police taking a person into custody in connection with an offence, marking the beginning of criminal proceedings. Once a person is arrested, a range of constitutional and statutory safeguards immediately come into play.

More in Explained | How the Supreme Court has strengthened safeguards around arrest — and re-arrest`

The BNSS does not define “detention” per se. Instead, it gives police a set of powers that allows them to stop, remove or temporarily hold people in certain situations, including when a crime has actually taken place.

The NDPS Act gives officers the powers to search, seize and arrest people suspected of drug-related offences — Section 37 specifically places restrictions on cases involving certain serious drug offences. It governs the conditions of bail too and does not extend the time the police can keep an arrested person in custody.

Arrest vs detention

At the heart of the judgment lies the court’s interpretation of Article 22(2). It said that the phrase “arrested and detained in custody” is “conjunctive and not disjunctive”, that is, the two words are joined by “and” not “or”.

The court said that because both the terms are joined together, they are synonymous. The court held that the “sacrosanct” 24-hour countdown to produce the person before a magistrate would begin the moment their liberty is curtailed. The only time period that is excluded from the 24 hour limit is the journey to the magistrate.

It said: “The prescription of 24 hours time period would commence the moment a person is detained by the arresting authority suspecting him to have committed an offence, when his liberty is effectively curtailed…any attempt to draw an artificial distinction between ‘arrest’ and ‘detention’ would dilute or negate the fundamental protection guaranteed by the Constitution.”

Buffer zones

The bench in its 97-page judgment disapproved of the views taken by the Orissa High Court in the Aryaman Pattnayak case, the Madras High Court in the Kannan case, and the Kerala High Court in the Arun K Thomas case, saying that these decisions “do not lay down the correct law”.

The High Courts had attempted to carve out investigative procedures for law enforcement before recording a formal arrest while calculating the 24-hour deadline.

Rejecting the Orissa High Court’s view that detention becomes arrest only after a “short investigatory hold”, the Supreme Court called it “constitutionally unsustainable” and said it delved “into a realm of uncertainty”.

It also rejected the Kerala High Court’s view that the 24-hour clock remains suspended during search and seizure, saying that “creation or contemplation of such buffer zone is unconstitutional”.

The bench said that the Constitution does not recognise the concept of “temporary disruption of liberty” and that High Courts cannot invent a statutory buffer zone that freezes or suspends the fundamental rights for executive convenience.

Informal custody

The bench also said that even if the suspect is produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, Section 58 of the BNSS imposes a dual limit, that is, a 24-hour limit and that the detention within those 24 hours must be “reasonable”. It said that there was an 18-hour gap between the completion of the search on September 29 and the formal arrest the next morning. The investigating officer had not explained this delay.

“18 hours in custody without judicial oversight is a long period with misuse and abuse of authority a clear possibility. Such a period certainly cannot be construed as a reasonable period,” the court said.

On informal custody, the bench recalled Justice V R Krishna Iyer’s words in Niranjan Singh (1980). Photo: Supreme Court of India (enhanced using AI)

The court said that “remand is never a mechanical exercise” and held that if there is an unexplained gap that exists within the 24-hour window, magistrates are allowed to decline the police remand on the ground of unreasonableness alone.

On informal custody, the bench recalled Justice V R Krishna Iyer’s words in Niranjan Singh (1980) that reasons police have taken a person into informal custody but not arrested him are “terminological dubieties and unfair evasions of the straightforwardness of the law. He called such explanations as equivocatory quibblings and hide-and-seek niceties, describing those as a shady facet.”

Fundamental rights override special laws

The Tripura High Court had relied on the Supreme Court’s ruling in State of Punjab v. Sukhwinder Singh (2026), which held that the restrictions on bail under Section 37 of the NDPS Act had to be satisfied before bail could be granted.

The Supreme Court expressed reservations about this observation, saying that fundamental rights cannot be exercised under the framework of Section 37. The bench said: “These fundamental rights cannot be tinkered with so lightly, not even under the special statutes.”

Also read | On arrests declared ‘illegal’, Supreme Court’s new guardrails for re-arrest

It said that where there is a violation of Article 21 — which guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty — the restrictions under Section 37 “would have to give way”. It referred to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Union of India v. K A Najeeb (2021), which recognised that Constitutional rights could prevail over statutory restrictions on bail.

CCTV and custodial violence

The bench also linked the 24-hour limit to the need to prevent custodial violence, noting that the “worst violations of human rights take place during the course of investigation” when the police, in attempts to secure evidence or confessions, “resorts to third degree methods including torture”.

It also said that the Supreme Court directions laid down in previous rulings require CCTV cameras with audio- and video-recording and night vision in police stations and in offices of agencies such as the National Investigation Agency, the Central Bureau of Investigation, and the Enforcement Directorate, where interrogation and detention take place. The footage must be preserved for at least 18 months and longer if a complaint of custodial violence is made.
