entry.title: Global carbon emissions are set to fall. Why are India’s emissions projected to rise?
entry.content:
Written by: Pratyush Deep5 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 12, 2026 05:40 PM IST An anti-smog gun deployed at New Delhi's Rajpath after Diwali. Abhinav Saha Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decline marginally in 2026 compared with last year. But India is expected to be the only major emitter set to record an increase.

According to a new study by the Global Carbon Budget, global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall by 0.4% this year, with China, the US, the European Union and Japan expected to record declines. India’s projected rise in fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, has been pegged at 4.4%.

The projected global decline has been attributed to the expansion of solar and wind power and the energy shock triggered by the West Asia conflict.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Geopolitical upheavals and economic disruptions have previously led to temporary reductions in fossil fuel use, including in 1992, 1998 and 2009. The Covid-19 pandemic also triggered a decline in emissions in 2020. These, however, were largely one-year aberrations. Researchers behind the study caution that the projected decline in global emissions this year is also likely to be a short-term consequence of the ongoing conflict rather than a sustained structural shift.

Why is India bucking the global trend? What are the key factors driving India’s rising carbon dioxide emissions even as emissions elsewhere are projected to fall?

‘No drop in road transport emissions in India’

According to the study,  India, which accounts for around 8% of global emissions, is projected to record higher emissions growth in 2026 than its average annual increase of 3.5% over the past decade.

The study attributes part of the increase to a rebound from relatively low emissions growth in 2025, when a wet pre-monsoon period reduced demand for cooling. In contrast, a drier monsoon and higher temperatures in 2026 increased cooling demand, pushing up electricity consumption.

Also Read | COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets

Notably, India witnessed an unusual surge in power demand this summer amid persistently high temperatures and deficient rainfall, with El Niño-influenced weather conditions adding to the pressure.

This increased reliance on coal-based power generation at a time when hydropower output was lower. Between April and November 10, 2026, coal-based power generation increased by around 13.2% to 846,229.29 million units (MU), compared with 747,465.25 MU during the corresponding period in 2025.

The increased reliance on coal-based generation was also reflected in declining coal stocks at thermal power plants. Inventories fell to 19.5 million tonnes (mt) as of November 10, from around 55 mt at the beginning of April.

“The Indian economy continues to grow strongly with an emphasis on infrastructure development. Since the government fixes petrol and diesel prices, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has not led to a drop in road-transport emissions, but consumption of other oil products declined,” the study said.

Also Read | COP31: 2026 could end up as one of the four warmest years ever

An analysis of government data shows that while domestic consumption of overall petroleum products declined by 2.24%  in January-October 2026, consumption of transport fuels continued to increase. Petrol consumption increased by 6.61% to 37.15 million tonnes from 34.85 million tonnes, while diesel consumption increased by 5.76% to 80.86 million tonnes from 76.46 million tonnes over the same period.

India’s industrial emissions

Anubha Aggarwal, analyst at the research organisation Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), said contributions from the power sector to CO2 emission remained flat for two years till June 2026.

A CREA analysis found that India’s CO2 emissions in the first half of 2026 increased 3.7% year-on-year in because of an increase in emissions from steel, cement and other sectors.

Power-sector CO₂ emissions in the first half of 2026 were back at the level of two years earlier — a 2.2% decline in the first half of 2025 reversed by a 2.3% rise during the first half of this year. CO₂ emissions from oil and gas fell 7% year-on-year, despite higher demand for diesel and petrol.

Also Read | Breach of 1.5 degree Celsius temperature threshold now ‘unavoidable’: Emissions Gap Report

“For two years till June 2026, all of the growth in India’s electricity demand has been met by clean energy, and that has halted the rise of coal power for the first time in half a century. The challenge now is industry, where coal dominates and electricity makes up a smaller share of energy use than in almost any other G20 economy, so unless steel and other energy-intensive manufacturers begin to electrify, rising output will keep pushing India’s total emissions up even as the power sector stabilises,” Aggarwal told The Indian Express.

entry.title: Total Chess, explained: Inside the made-for-TV tournament reimagining the sport
entry.content:
Written by: Amit Kamath5 min readBudapestUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 07:25 PM IST Magnus Carlsen at the Total Chess event in Budapest. (X/Total Chess) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Chess has never been a particularly television-friendly sport. Over the years, organisers and officials have tried to introduce elements such as live screens and commentary to bridge the gap with the viewer.

The latest attempt, however, is a reimagining of chess competitions themselves. Meet Total Chess — a plan for a “complete” new world championship in the sport. An ongoing pilot event in Hungary’s capital of Budapest is laying the grounds for the new format, trying to turn it into a made-for-TV product.

So how does Total Chess differ from usual competitions? Will playing in it be more difficult? What will a tournament look like? We explain:

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is Total Chess? How is it different?

Simply put, the Total Chess World Championship Tour that starts next year will have four events around the year in different cities, with the first three events having 24 players each and the finale having four players fighting it out to become the FIDE World Combined Champion. The idea is to crown the most complete chess player in the world.

Chess currently has three formats — classical, rapid and blitz. And each has its own world championship: the Classical World Championship (the most prestigious, and chess’s equivalent of Test cricket), the Rapid World Championship (comparable to ODIs) and the World Blitz Championship (closest to T20s, with players starting with 10 minutes or less on the clock).

But at Total Chess, players will have to be good at all three formats. To be clear, the event will involve a modified version of classical, called fast classical.

Also Read | Chess tries a faster classical, and Vaishali pays for it in Budapest

As Hungarian chess legend Peter Leko told The Indian Express: “I’ve been in the chess world for 35 years at the highest level. I used to think I have seen enough and I know what’s happening. And then suddenly there’s this Total Chess World Championship and suddenly everything is new! I don’t know what to expect.”

What will a Total Chess tournament look like?

Each tournament leg will have a group stage where the 24 players are divided in four groups of six each. Each player faces the other member of the group twice in fast classic. Over the five days, they play two fast classic games a day. What’s also interesting is that each leg of Total Chess will start with a pre-tournament nine-round blitz event that will help determine rankings in a group in case of tiebreaks.

India’s Vaishali Rameshbabu at the event. (Total Chess/ Michal Walusza)

Which players are playing in the Total Chess pilot event?

There are 24 players in the pilot event including five-time world champion Magnus Carlsen. From India, there are three players in action: Praggnanandhaa, Vaishali and Arjun Erigaisi.

What’s fast classic chess?

At the Total Chess pilot in Budapest and for the four events of the tour next year, players will play a format called fast classic instead of classical chess.

This is simply an accelerated form of classical chess, with players starting a game with 45 minutes on their clock and getting a bonus increment of 30 seconds each time they make a move. In classical chess, players usually start a game with 90 to 120 minutes on the clock, with increments for each move made.

Will playing in the Total Chess events be more difficult?

Yes. Playing two fast classic games a day for five days straight will be physically and mentally taxing, says Leko. While players do play multiple games a day at rapid and blitz tournaments, those don’t count in standard ratings.

But at Total Chess, not only are players entering the unknown with a time control most of them haven’t played before, they are also under pressure to do well to preserve their standard rating. This is something that most players are protective about.

“It plays with your mind, it’s not just an incredible show event but the rating is also on the line. Because every game, every move, everything matters. The biggest trick that normally allows you to play many rapid or blitz games in a day is that it does not count for (classical) rating. So you take it lighter. If you’re not so well prepared for an opponent, that’s okay. When rating points are on the line, you realise that these fast classical games are equally important as any classical game for which you prepare for so many hours,” says Leko, who is also the coach and mentor of Vincent Keymer, who’s playing in the Total Chess Pilot event.

So how do you prepare for the two fast classic games each day?

Leko explains that the name of the game at the Total Chess events will be energy conservation.

“If you prepare for the first game too much, then you might lack energy to play the second game. If you are already thinking about the second game before playing the first game, that’s also super dangerous. I think the players’ strategy will be to conserve energy. I believe that none of the players will really be preparing for both games in a day because that would be suicidal.”

(The writer is in Budapest at the invitation of Total Chess)

entry.title: Videocon and the Venugopal Dhoot case: What happens when a person is declared bankrupt
entry.content:
Written by: Dheeraj Mishra8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 12, 2026 06:29 PM IST Dhoot is the former promoter and director of Videocon Industries. (File) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) on November 5 declared former Videocon Industries promoter and director Venugopal Dhoot bankrupt. The tribunal found Dhoot liable as he was the personal guarantor for loans worth Rs 12,668 crore granted by the State Bank of India (SBI) to his companies.

This was a rare move — very few loan default cases in India have reached the stage of bankruptcy.

Once a business titan, Dhoot now stands to lose control of his companies and assets held in his name, unless the order is stayed or set aside by an appellate tribunal or court. Even holding the position of a company director requires one to not be bankrupt.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Another recent case relating to personal guarantees was that of Essel Group founder Subhash Chandra, whose repayment plan with a 99.97% “haircut” was approved by the NCLT in August. Later, a five-member special bench stayed the order.

What happens when a person is declared bankrupt? How often does a loan default case reach this stage? And how much money can be recovered once bankruptcy is declared? We explain.

How a person is declared bankrupt

First, let’s understand what the terms insolvency and bankruptcy mean. Insolvency occurs when a person or company is unable to repay debts when they fall due. Bankruptcy is the formal legal process through which an insolvent individual is declared bankrupt, allowing their assets to be distributed among creditors to repay outstanding debts.

In India, such matters are governed by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), which came into existence in 2016. While banks use the law to recover their loans, the government promotes it as a rescue ladder for a company in financial distress.

When a company fails to pay its loans, its creditors can approach the NCLT to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) to recover their money. If this effort fails, the company is liquidated and its assets are sold to repay the loan.

Also Read | Who is Venugopal Dhoot?

Banks have one more option — to go after the person or promoter of a company who has provided a personal guarantee for the company’s loans. This is called the personal insolvency resolution process (PIRP), which came into force in December, 2019.

Now, the question that arises is: How do these different processes work? The answer: They work sequentially as well as simultaneously.

Say a company owes a bank Rs 100. The bank has two options. It can initiate CIRP and PIRP simultaneously, but its total claim in both processes put together cannot exceed Rs 100. 

Alternatively, the bank can first initiate CIRP through the NCLT. Let’s say it recovers Rs 70 through the resolution process. The bank can then file a PIRP petition to recover the remaining Rs 30.

It is when these two processes fail to ensure recovery of money by creditors that the third stage kicks in — bankruptcy. In other words, bankruptcy is the liquidation of the personal guarantor. 

What is the Venugopal Dhoot case?

Dhoot’s case relates to loans granted to Videocon Industries Ltd and Videocon Telecommunications Ltd between 2010 and 2012 by SBI and its associated banks, which were merged in April 2017. Dhoot had unconditionally guaranteed repayment of all the liabilities.

When the companies defaulted, the SBI issued demand notices to Dhoot in February 2018. The notices, however, yielded no relief for the bank. 

From the archive | Videocon gets Rs 3250-crore loan from ICICI Bank, bank CEO’s husband gets sweet deal from Venugopal Dhoot

Following this, the creditors filed a petition in the NCLT for the initiation of the CIRP, which was admitted in June 2018. Later, 12 more companies of the Videocon group were brought under the process by the tribunal. The creditors filed a claim of Rs 72,078 crore, of which around Rs 65,000 crore was admitted for the resolution process.

The NCLT approved a resolution plan submitted by Twin Star Technologies Ltd in June 2021. However, the NCLAT set it aside in January 2022, as it offered creditors only Rs 2,962 crore — a haircut of over 95%. The appellate tribunal sent the matter back to the committee of creditors for a fresh resolution plan. In the meantime, Twin Star challenged the NCLAT order in the Supreme Court, whose judgement is pending. 

The bottomline, therefore, is that all of Videocon’s dues to the bank are still due. 

Also Read | Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.5-crore settlement: What are ‘haircuts’ and how high can they get?

Separately, after the NCLT approved the resolution plan in May 2021, the SBI, which has the highest outstanding exposure to the Videocon Group among lenders, filed a petition to initiate the PIRP process against Dhoot. Indeed, the tribunal initiated PIRP against Dhoot in April 2026 after he failed to submit a repayment plan in connection with SBI’s loans.

But this, too, failed. Dhoot’s offer of Rs 600 crore was rejected by creditors because it was contingent on the future development of a Siliguri project and offered nothing upfront.

The tribunal terminated the PIRP in July 2026 — and thus came the bankruptcy of Venugopal Dhoot.

What will happen to Venugaopal Dhoot now?

Dhoot’s entire estate will now be vested with a bankruptcy trustee appointed by the NCLT. What does this mean?

Essentially, Dhoot will have to submit details of all assets, sources of income and net worth held in his name to the trustee. These assets will then be sold, much like in a liquidation process, to repay creditors. Even in the case of Dhoot’s residential properties, there are limits to what he can retain.

An analyst, however, said that this IBC provision has largely remained untested so far since very few cases reach the third stage and the recovery is very low.

Also Read | How latest amendments to Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code promise a swifter resolution process

“The bankruptcy of a personal guarantor has largely remained untested under the IBC. It takes a very long time to reach this stage and recovery is also very low. In the case of companies they have hard assets and business on the ground, through which the lenders can recover their loans faster. In the case of an individual, discovery of their actual net worth continues to be a challenge,” said Prateek Kumar, a partner at corporate law firm Khaitan & Co.

Data from the IBC regulator, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), shows that bankruptcy cases are indeed few. Only 310 applications seeking to declare guarantors bankrupt have been filed since 2019, when the provisions relating to insolvency resolution and bankruptcy of personal guarantors were implemented.

Also Read | How Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.25-crore resolution proposal sailed through

On the other hand, 5,186 applications have been filed for the initiation of PIRP — a process that precedes bankruptcy. Of these, only 64 cases resulted in the approval of repayment plans, while creditors realised just 1% of their admitted claims.

In the case of company insolvency, the NCLT admitted 9,166 applications for the initiation of CIRP since 2016, according to IBBI. Of these, resolution plans were approved in 1,484 cases, while liquidation was ordered in 3,074 cases. A total of 1,333 applications were withdrawn under section 12A, 1,410 cases were closed on appeal or review or settled, and CIRP is ongoing in 1,865 cases.  

Under resolution plans, creditors realised an average of 30.52% of their admitted claims, whereas in liquidation cases, the realisation was only around 4%. 

Clearly, the data shows that the recovery in personal insolvency has remained low, in comparison to the resolution of companies.

entry.title: Gokul dairy: The controversy over elections to Maharashtra’s largest milk cooperative
entry.content:
Written by: Sadaf Modak7 min readMumbaiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 02:14 PM IST Gokul has an annual turnover of nearly Rs 4,000 crore and a network of 4.41 lakh milk producers across an estimated 1,810 villages in Kolhapur district. Photo: X/@GokulMilk Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The elections to the board of Maharashtra’s largest dairy cooperative, Gokul, and the events that followed have been at the centre of controversy. On Tuesday (November 10), the candidate of the BJP-led Mahayuti alliance was elected the cooperative’s chairman, with the Opposition claiming that the ruling alliance had “usurped power”, with some farmer leaders also joining the protest.

This came a day after the Bombay High Court’s Kolhapur bench refused to grant a stay on the state government’s decision to give voting rights to four government-nominated directors on the Gokul dairy board. The court will hear the case next on November 25.

Why Gokul dairy matters

Gokul is a major political and economic institution in western Maharashtra. It has an annual turnover of nearly Rs 4,000 crore and a network of 4.41 lakh milk producers across an estimated 1,810 villages in Kolhapur district.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Control over it gives political parties influence over rural households and the vast network of farmers, many of them marginal producers who depend on regular milk payments for household income.

The Gokul election

In the board election held on October 19, a panel led by Congress MLC Satej Patil (Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi) won 13 of the 25 director seats. The Mahayuti-backed panel (Chhatrapati Shahu Shetkari Vikas Aghadi) won the remaining 12.

In the subsequent board meeting to select the chairperson, the 12 Mahayuti members initially stayed away from the meeting. It was claimed that as per Gokul’s existing bylaws, this meant that the required quorum for the chairperson’s selection couldn’t be met.

To break this deadlock, the 13 Satej Patil-allied panel members subsequently held a separate meeting and declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar the chairman. The Gokul administration, however, said that this decision was not recognised, prompting the Patil-led group to approach the High Court. On November 2, the court directed that the elections be held on November 10, with notices to all 25 elected members to remain present.

Also read | How BJP-led Mahayuti secured Gokul dairy weeks after losing board election

Then, on Friday (November 6), the state government approved and issued an ordinance, giving the government the power to appoint five directors to cooperatives with an annual turnover over Rs 500 crore, with four of them having voting rights. The ordinance amends Section 73AAA of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, which earlier stated that nominated and government-designated directors cannot vote in the election of a chairman or other office-bearers. The ordinance states that the members shall not be eligible to be elected as office-bearers of the committee but gave four of them voting rights.

The ordinance introduced one government officer, not below the rank of the assistant registrar of cooperative societies, and four “having such requisite experience relating to the work of the Society and such qualifications, as may be specified by the government” to be nominated on the board. Accordingly, five members were appointed.

This tilted the dairy’s board in favour of the Mahayuti. In the elections held on Tuesday (November 10) to choose the chairperson, the Mahayuti panel candidate, Rajesh Patil, won 16 votes — 12 from the elected board, four from the government appointees — and defeated Chuyekar’s tally of 13.

‘Changes in rule after the game has started’

Chuyekar and others filed an interim plea before the High Court, seeking that the ordinance be quashed and set aside, calling it arbitrary, against the Constitution and stating that it has been issued in “colourable exercise of powers”. The petitioners said that the ordinance passed after the elections cannot apply now, calling it “patently illegal as it changes the Rule after the game has started”.

By introducing four government-appointed voters, the petitioners claimed that ‘artificial voters’ were created and this was done ‘to unsettle the democratic process’, when no such law was brought into effect for 30 years. The petitioners also referred to provisions of the Act, which says that no nominee of the government shall be entitled to vote in any election of office-bearers of such a committee.

‘Government not an outsider’

The state government submitted that a law introduced by the legislature cannot be stayed unless the law passed is absurd. It said that no irreparable loss will be caused if a stay is not granted, and that the government itself is not an outsider but concerned with the interest of such cooperative societies, with elections being just one part of its functioning.

Also read | BJP lost election to Maharashtra’s largest dairy. Then why is it still fighting for control?

It also said that Gokul is not the only society on which the ordinance will apply, and that there are four such cooperative societies in the state, so the government’s decision cannot be said to be selective.

The state government also argued that such a proposed ordinance was already under consideration by the government, with a communication between the government departments, dated October 16 — three days before the election — annexed. It also submitted that the ordinance is for a limited duration, since it requires to be passed by the state Assembly or it lapses.

Why the court refused to grant stay

According to the vacation bench of Justice Neeraj P Dhote, the regular Division Bench that heard the main petition on November 2 had specified that any steps taken by the parties during the pendency of the plea would be subject to its outcome. So, all the steps — including the ordinance and the chairperson elections — would depend on the court’s final decision. The vacation bench noted that no case for stay or any interim relief was made out.

The court also noted that the decision for the ordinance was already under consideration and that there were three other similar societies with an annual turnover of more than Rs 500 crore. It said that hence the ordinance prima facie cannot be said to have been tailor-made for Gokul.

Also read | NCP’s Rajesh Patil elected chairman of Maharashtra’s largest dairy; Opposition cries foul

The court also considered various judgments cited by both sides on the judiciary’s powers to strike down such laws passed by the legislature, one stating that mere possibility of abuse of a provision of law doesn’t invalidate a legislation. It said that since the ordinance is under challenge, the presiding officer shall keep a separate ballot box for the government nominees and the elected members and preserve all relevant documents.

A former CJI’s legal opinion

A day before the ordinance was passed, a legal opinion sought from former Chief Justice of India B R Gavai by the Patel-allied panel was emailed to the Chief Minister, the Chief Secretary and the Cooperation Department Secretary. Although Gavai stated that he was only giving opinion on the information submitted before him, he said that since the High Court had ordered for the chairman’s election to be held, such an ordinance before the elections would amount to “direct interference in the judicial process”.

On the proposed change in the law to give voting to nominated members, he had said that such an action “would be hit by the doctrine of manifest arbitrariness and would amount to colourable exercise of powers”. Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said that the former CJI had not been given a full picture, and that the election cannot take place without a requisite quorum.

entry.title: Why Sonia Gandhi chose a Milan hospital over Tata Memorial for cancer surgery
entry.content:
Written by: Anonna Dutt4 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 12, 2026 03:27 PM IST Sonia Gandhi's personal memoir, Belonging, chronicles her journey from her marriage to Rajiv Gandhi and adjustment to Indian life to the tragedies that shaped the Gandhi family. Photo: PTI Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

From her bouts of asthma and allergies, to her fight against breast cancer, and the fall during a rally that resulted in a broken shoulder — Sonia Gandhi has recounted it all in her recently published memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love.

The Congress leader recounts how while floating in and out of consciousness after the fall, she had seen Rajiv, smiling at her as if to say everything will be fine. She said that Sheila Dikshit, who was by her side at the time, noticed her smile. “(She) told me later that she noticed me suddenly smile in the middle of the tension-racked flight — I’m sure it must have been that moment,” she wrote in the memoir.

Talking of her experience with cancer, she revealed that she underwent treatment in Milan, Italy and Rotterdam in the Netherlands — and not at the renowned cancer hospital Memorial Sloan Kettering in New York, as many had suspected. Here’s what to know.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the Milan hospital Sonia chose for her cancer treatment?

While Gandhi was under treatment in India, she chose to undergo surgery in 2010 at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan. It is one of Europe’s leading anti-cancer institutes — a hub of global expertise dedicated to patient care and cutting-edge clinical research, which led to the institute developing a breast-conserving surgical technique now used worldwide. It also integrated plastic surgery as part of breast cancer care, set up one of the first nuclear medicine departments in the world, and took a lead on developing low-dose CT screening protocols for lung cancer.

The institute was founded by the breast-cancer specialist Dr Umberto Veronesi, known for inventing the breast-conserving cancer surgery quadrantectomy, where only a fourth of the breast tissue is removed. He was the one to operate on Sonia. A renowned oncologist, Veronesi had served as Italy’s Minister of Health between 2000 and 2001 and as a Senator between 2008 and 2011.

Also read | Sonia Gandhi understands Modi’s ‘discomfort’ with elite, attacks his Sangh ideology

“Afterwards, still groggy from the anaesthesia, I saw Dr. Veronesi with them by my bedside. How relieved I felt to hear him announce, ‘Non c’è niente da preoccuparsi, tutto è andato bene e non ci sono residui’ (No need to worry, everything has gone well and there are no residues),” Gandhi recounted in her memoir.

One year after her surgery, follow-up tests detected a growth in her pancreas. She was then recommended surgery at Erasmus teaching hospital in Rotterdam under the well-known pancreatic surgeon, Dr Casper van Eijck.

Younger than Dr Veronesi, Gandhi remembers him as “exuberant and lively personality, but as a doctor equally kind and caring”. He told her she was fortunate that the tumour was detected at a precancerous stage, for which Gandhi thanked her doctors at Delhi’s Sir Ganga Ram Hospital.

Why did Sonia Gandhi choose to go there?

There were several reasons she chose the centres she did for her surgery.

First was a matter of privacy. “A question arose… Should I undergo the surgery here, at the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, or abroad? … the thought of my illness being discussed in the media was painful to me — even infuriating. True, I had become a public figure, but did that mean I wasn’t to be allowed even a modicum of privacy?” she wrote.

Also read | Pressured by Congress, Sonia Gandhi said ‘yes’ to PM post. How Rahul reacted

Second, it was the proximity to her family. She writes that the institute situated on the outskirts of Milan was a good option for her sisters, Nadia and Anouchka, would be close by.

How did Sonia Gandhi deal with Delhi’s pollution?

With asthma and allergy flare-ups, Delhi’s toxic and hazardous air was a challenge for her.

“The surgeries left me feeling somewhat fragile. I found an escape from Delhi’s winter ordeal in Goa, where I went for a few days a number of times along with family or friends. It was therapy: long walks on the deserted beach morning and evening, cycling along paths laid between beautiful trees and shrubs, sitting outdoors breathing in the fresh air.”

entry.title: What is China’s Singles’ Day, and how is AI changing the world’s biggest shopping festival?
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk7 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 07:21 PM IST A woman passes by a shopping advertisement for the Singles' Day sale promotion in Beijing (AP Photo) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

In China, November 11 has been a day for single people to celebrate their relationship status. What began as a celebration among university students over three decades ago has become one of the world’s biggest shopping events and has drawn millions of consumers to online platforms with discounts and celebrity-led promotions.

The festival, however, is changing. It has expanded to include a month-long sales campaign while e-commerce companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to persuade shoppers to make purchases. Chatbots recommend products, while virtual try-on tools offer shoppers a more personalised experience.

The technology push comes at a time when Chinese consumers are becoming more cautious about spending. A prolonged property downturn and fatigue with year-round discounts have made it harder for retailers to generate the excitement that once defined the festival.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The Associated Press reported that sales during the 2026 Singles’ Day campaign had crossed 1 trillion yuan ($154 billion) by October 31, broadly in line with the corresponding period last year. The festival’s record sales in 2025 were nearly 1.7 trillion yuan ($254 billion).

So, how did a celebration of singlehood become a global retail phenomenon, and what does Singles’ Day look like today? Here’s a look.

What does Singles’ Day in China entail?

Celebrated on November 11, Singles’ Day takes its name from the date 11/11, with the four ones representing people without partners.

It is believed to have originated at Nanjing University in 1993 and was initially termed Bachelors’ Day. Male students began marking the occasion by treating themselves to gifts, organising social gatherings and celebrating their single status.

The observance spread beyond university campuses over time and came to be an occasion for all single people — including women — to celebrate their independence.

The occasion also offered an alternative to festivals that traditionally placed greater emphasis on couples and families. For many young people, it became a way of celebrating singlehood rather than viewing it as a social disadvantage.

How did Singles’ Day evolve into a commercial staple?

The transformation into a consumer-focused celebration began in 2009, when e-commerce giant Alibaba turned November 11 into a day-long online shopping festival.

The marketing pitch played on the original idea of the day by suggesting that even without a partner, people could treat themselves by shopping. According to a Quartz report, Alibaba promoted the event with the message: “Even if you don’t have a boyfriend or girlfriend, you can at least shop like crazy.”

The strategy drew criticism. Zhang Hailan, a folklore researcher at East China Normal University, argued in 2015 that Alibaba had turned an occasion associated with the social stigma of being single into a celebratory shopping experience.

The strategy worked. Other retailers joined in, and the event grew in scale, with companies investing in advertising, celebrity appearances, livestreamed performances and interactive shopping experiences.

In 2023, Alibaba kicked off its Singles’ Day campaign with a group of livestreamers, including popular online influencer Austin Li Jiaqi, known as the “Lipstick King”, and actor-singer Allen Lin Yilun. During the first evening of presales, 12 livestreamers each generated more than 100 million yuan ($14 million) in sales volume by midnight, according to figures released by Alibaba.

Such large-scale shopping events are not limited to China. In 2019, Amazon hosted a live concert for its Prime members featuring performers including Taylor Swift and Dua Lipa ahead of its Prime Day sale.

Over the years, Singles’ Day expanded beyond Alibaba to include rival platforms such as JD.com and social commerce platforms such as Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Is Singles’ Day big today?

Singles’ Day is widely regarded as the world’s largest online shopping festival, having grown far beyond its origins as a one-day sale.

Alibaba’s gross merchandise value (GMV) rose from 52 million yuan ( 7.6 million) in 2009 to 168.2 billion yuan (25.3 billion) in 2017. The festival subsequently expanded beyond Alibaba, with third-party estimates tracking sales across China’s major e-commerce platforms.

According to Bain & Company, total Singles’ Day GMV rose from 840 billion yuan in 2020 to 1.115 trillion yuan in 2022 and 1.442 trillion yuan in 2024.

Retailers have extended the promotional period from a single day to several weeks, making year-on-year comparisons less straightforward. Alibaba and JD.com have also stopped disclosing their overall festival transaction values.

The AP reported that total Singles’ Day sales in 2025 reached nearly 1.7 trillion yuan. For the 2026 campaign, cumulative sales had exceeded 1 trillion yuan by October 31, according to retail data platform Syntun, broadly matching the pace of the previous year.

The event’s expansion has also changed how its success is measured. Rather than a single day’s shopping frenzy, it is now a prolonged contest among e-commerce companies to attract consumers, retain merchants and increase purchases across multiple platforms.

How is AI changing Singles’ Day shopping?

One of the biggest changes to the festival is the growing integration of artificial intelligence into the shopping experience.

According to a November 11 Reuters report, Alibaba, JD.com and PDD Holdings are increasingly using AI-powered tools to attract consumers. These include chatbots that recommend products, virtual try-on features, automated discount searches and shopping assistants that can help customers complete purchases.

Alibaba’s Taobao and Tmall platforms have incorporated AI tools that allow shoppers to research products and find deals. JD.com’s AI shopping assistant, Dongdong, attracted nearly 80 million users seeking shopping advice during this year’s festival, more than three times the figure recorded last year.

The shift is also visible on social commerce platforms. On Douyin, AI-generated chatbot links accounted for around 5% of purchases in October, according to data from WPIC Marketing + Technologies. For more considered purchases, such as dietary supplements, the proportion exceeded 20%.

AI is also emerging as a product category in its own right. Alibaba said sales of AI toys on its platforms crossed 100 million yuan within a year of the category’s launch. Sales of AI companion robots increased nearly fivefold year-on-year in the second half of October, while sales of AI token packages, prepaid credits that allow customers to use AI services, rose more than 700% between October 15 and November 5, compared with September 15 to October 5, according to Alibaba’s Tmall platform.

However, the growing dependence on AI also presents challenges for retailers. Brands that fail to appear in AI-generated recommendations or product searches could lose visibility among consumers.

Whether these technological changes will translate into significantly higher overall spending remains uncertain. Reuters reported that Singles’ Day sales rose just 2.4% between October 7 and October 31, according to Syntun.

The festival’s enormous scale has also raised environmental concerns. The volume of deliveries generates transport-related emissions, while discarded plastic packaging adds to waste.

Chinese authorities and retailers have sought to address these concerns by promoting recyclable packaging and more sustainable delivery practices. JD.com, for instance, introduced measures to reduce packaging waste during earlier editions of the festival.

entry.title: Sairang Express accident: What leads to train derailments?
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 13, 2026 09:24 AM IST Recovery work is underway after coaches of the Kolkata-Sairang Express (Train No. 13125) derailed at Digaru Railway Station, in Kamrup, Assam (ANI Photo) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The locomotive and five passenger carriages of the Mizoram-bound Kolkata-Sairang Express were derailed near Digaru station in Assam’s Kamrup district on Wednesday (November 11).

The Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR) said in a statement that the train was being received at the station to give precedence to another train during which the loco pilot lost control of the machine’s speed.

NFR said there were no injuries and all passengers were safe, though some local accounts suggest a few passengers suffered minor-to-moderate injuries. Also, a video that surfaced online — purportedly filmed from inside the train — claimed that the emergency brakes did not work. This claim is yet to be verified.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What really happened to the Sairang Express?

Around 6.54 am on Wednesday, the Kolkata-Sairang Express was being received at Digaru so that another train could be given precedence. Here, giving precedence means to delay or hold the original train so that another, higher-priority train can pass through.

But the Sairang Express’s loco pilot was allegedly unable to maintain speed and lost control, which resulted in the train going off the tracks.

Besides loss of control, how else can trains be derailed?

A 2022 performance audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India concluded that derailments accounted for nearly 75% of all consequential train accidents between 2017 and 2021.

In an analysis of 1,129 cases, the report stated that 422 cases were attributed to engineering such as track maintenance, 275 cases were classified as operating errors, 182 cases as mechanical errors, and 154 cases of human errors by loco pilots.

One of the more notable findings, however, was the fact that in 63% of cases, inquiry reports were not submitted within the prescribed time. Of the reports submitted, there was delay in acceptance by the relevant authority in 49% of the cases.

Also Read | SC order on train insurance: Who is eligible, and what compensation can you receive?

A 2017 report by The Indian Express also highlighted that openly accessible data from that time showed that 40% of all rail accidents in the nation were cases of derailment — lower than the number the CAG’s 2022 audit revealed.

To understand derailments, the three broad categories to consider are mechanical failures, operational or human failure, and geotechnical instability.

Why do mechanical and operational failures occur?

Of the 422 cases attributed to engineering, track maintenance was the major factor for derailment in 171 cases. Track maintenance spans multiple areas and a mechanical failure can involve physical defects in the rolling stock — any vehicle that moves on a track — or even the tracks themselves.

Rails may face breakage or fracture owing to multiple reasons, some of which are metal fatigue, defective wheels, extreme temperature variation and inadequate routine maintenance. Taking a sample of 517 machines over four years, the 2022 CAG report concluded that of 7,54,820 total available machine days, the machines remained idle for 16% of the time — or 1,20,135 days.

Table 1

Operational and human errors, on the other hand, encompass signalling, crew actions, and dispatching. Signalling systems regulate movement to prevent conflicting paths, but communication failures, procedural violations, or incorrectly handled points and crossings can route a train into an unsafe alignment.

Similarly, human errors such as misinterpreting signals or operating beyond safe driving thresholds compound these operational risks.

How geotechnical instability plays as much of a role in track stability

The engineering underneath the railway tracks is critical. Derailment is caused by misalignment of rails and sleepers — the heavy rectangular support laid perpendicular underneath railway tracks to hold the steel rails in place — because of problems with the foundation on which it rests.

The three main components supporting railway tracks are the steel rails, concrete sleepers holding the rail, and the ballast. Ballast, which consists of crushed stones well-graded between 20- 56 mm in size, provides necessary strength and stability for the track to maintain geometry.

Also Read | Before Kanchanjunga Express: Major train accidents of the last decade

But these stones break down over time owing to train loads, allowing foreign contaminants to accumulate in the gaps. This manifests a condition known as “ballast fouling”, which changes the ballast’s mechanical behaviour for the worse and in some ways, is the first step in the sequence of derailment.

Excessive fouling reduces drainage capacity, leading to moisture retention. This moisture causes track-bed erosion, which renders the ballast ineffective in providing uniform support, causing uneven shifts to concrete sleepers. This leads to deformities in the track’s alignment and geometric profile.

To counter this, the Indian Railways utilises “deep-screening”, a process that involves lifting the track, removing fouled ballast, cleaning it, and restoring the track bed.

When locomotive pilots become a source of concern

Human error as a factor, however, cannot be forgotten. For the Wednesday incident, the loco pilot’s inability to control the vehicle’s speed has been cited as the official cause until now.

The 2022 audit also revealed that human agency — spanning train crew, operating staff, and maintenance personnel — acts as a critical vulnerability in railway operations.

Table 2

Of the 1,129 inquiry reports, 154 derailment cases were attributed directly to loco pilots, where bad driving, over-speeding, and braking anomalies were primary risk factors.

The report also pointed to recurring instances of Signal Passing at Danger — when a train moves past a stop signal or exceeds its movement authority without permission — as a major precursor to collisions. These highlight systemic pressures on running staff, such as duty hours exceeding limits and a lack of real-time aid like Train Protection and Warning Systems.

entry.title: How PM Rajiv Gandhi endorsed the making of ‘Ramayan’ — and lost power
entry.content:
Written by: Abhinav Chakraborty9 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 12, 2026 09:32 PM IST It was a Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi that allowed Ramanand Sagar’s TV show to be telecast on Doordarshan. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (enhanced using AI) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Even as the first instalment of the two-part Ramayana grossed over Rs 800 crore worldwide within its first week of release, the film’s casting of the actor Arun Govil in a key role served as a callback to the 1980s television adaptation of the epic.

Govil plays Dasharatha — the king of Ayodhya and Rama’s father — in the new film, but his most memorable role was playing Rama in the 1987 TV version, which made him and the other principal cast members household names.

But the TV show Ramayan also arrived at a time when the country was increasingly gripped by rising communal fervour, and it became not just a pop culture phenomenon but a catalyst in India’s broader sociopolitical theatre — one that changed the political fortunes of the country’s two biggest national parties and even led to the incumbent Prime Minister, Rajiv Gandhi, losing power in the subsequent general election. We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Why Ramanand Sagar wanted to make Ramayan

Ramanand Sagar, who was born as Chandramouli Chopra in Asal Guruke near Lahore in 1917, started his cinematic journey in Lahore’s film industry and moved to Bombay (now Mumbai) after Partition. He began writing for Hindi films and made his name with Raj Kapoor’s Barsaat (1949), before moving on to directing. Although his early directorial ventures didn’t work, he found success in the 1970s and 1980s with films like Arzoo (1971), Charas (1976), Prem Bandhan (1979, and Baghavat (1982).

But Ramanand, according to Prem Sagar’s 2019 book An Epic Life: Ramanand Sagar, had long wanted to pursue what he had once called his “life’s mission: to bring to mankind the virtuous story of Maryada Purushottam Shri Ram”. He had harboured the idea for decades, since he’d witnessed the impact of the film Ram Rajya (1943) on audiences — with “crowds filling the streets, overcrowded theatres beholden by beloved ‘Ram’”.

Also read | Ramayan: Look at the show from the moral prism, not religious

Prem Sagar wrote that Ramanand saw television as “the right medium for his creativity and the future of mass media communication”, which was not tied to box-office returns and where the makers were free to express their philosophy.

Moreover, the growing presence of TV sets in Indian households and the increasing stranglehold of a Dubai-based mafia on the film industry forced Ramanand to move to television. Although he initially ran into production hurdles for Ramayan, the success of Ramanand’s first TV venture Vikram Aur Betaal (1985-86) — starring Govil as the protagonist, King Vikram) in 1985-86 — gave him much-needed confidence in his vision for the epic saga.

Why Rajiv Gandhi supported the making of Ramayan

Although he was sworn in as Prime Minister in 1984 after the assassination of Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi stormed to power in the general election that followed shortly with the Congress winning a record 404 seats.

But Rajiv’s tenure at the helm, despite his secure mandate, appeared to be riddled with insecurities. In her book How Prime Ministers Decide (2023), journalist Neerja Chowdhury wrote: “Naiveté marked the early prime-ministerial actions of Rajiv Gandhi. Earnest and well-meaning, his response to the Shah Bano judgment by the Supreme Court of India in April 1985, giving alimony to an aggrieved Muslim woman, proved to be his undoing. The choices he made unleashed forces that overwhelmed him despite his brute majority in parliament.”

According to Chowdhury, two of Rajiv’s decisions after the Shah Bano verdict accelerated the BJP’s growth in national politics, rising from just two seats in 1984 to 85 seats in the 1989 election.

First, his government’s passage of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, to undo the Shah Bano judgment was perceived as appeasement of a minority community.

Second, to placate the majority Hindu community, he engineered the opening of the locks at Ayodhya’s disputed Babri Masjid site so that Hindus could offer prayers there. This happened as the Ramjanmabhoomi movement to build a Ram Temple in Ayodhya, led by the Hindu right-wing outfit Vishwa Hindu Parishad, was gathering steam across the Hindi heartland.

“Rajiv Gandhi’s twin decisions set off forces which were to fashion the politics of the next three decades. It finally led to the installation of the BJP on the Delhi throne in 2014 with a clear majority,” Chowdhury wrote.

A still from Ramanand Sagar’s Ramayan (1987). Photo: IMDb

Part of Rajiv’s attempts to become a “king of Hindu hearts” was perhaps his inclination towards allowing the telecast of Ramayana on the public broadcaster, Doordarshan (DD).

“…[T]here were whispers that Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi himself had suggested that the DD authorities telecast the great Indian epics like the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and that these epics were our cultural heritage and needed to be shown with pride and in all their glory. The conjecture was that the judgement of the Shah Bano case was perhaps influencing his political decisions. The prime minister may have been advised that the judgement in the case had had a negative countereffect on the Hindu vote bank of the Congress Party,” Prem Sagar wrote. “In order to please the Hindus, and at the same time not antagonise the Muslims, the telecast of the greatest epics seemed a perfect political antidote.”

Then Union Minister of Information and Broadcasting (I&B), V N Gadgil, and senior Congress leader H K L Bhagat (who later became I&B Minister in Rajiv’s government) had warned Rajiv of the possibilities of telecasting a Hindu mythological serial such as Ramayan on DD. According to them, it would generate an atmosphere in favour of the fledgling Ramjanmabhoomi movement by instilling a “sense of pride in the Hindu community” and raise the possibility of the BJP coming to power.

But Rajiv didn’t pay heed to these concerns — in fact, a bureaucratic reshuffle saw all those in the I&B Ministry opposed to the telecast shunted to other ministries. Even Gadgil had been replaced in November 1986 by Ajit Kumar Panja, who was more receptive towards the telecast.

The first episode was finally telecast on January 25, 1987, and it went on for 78 episodes until July 31, 1988, with close to 650 million viewers — an Indian television record to date. “On Sunday mornings, the streets in Indian cities would be deserted, with families glued to their TV sets to watch the Ramayan, with many paying obeisance to their TV sets. As H K L Bhagat had predicted, the TV serial created a religious fervour amongst the Hindus of an unprecedented kind,” Chowdhury wrote.

Also read | In the telling of Yash’s Ravana, Ramayana finds its footing

A January 2025 paper, “Ancient Epics in the Television Age: Religious Identity and the Rise of Hindu Nationalism in India” by a team of development economists including Dean Yang of the University of Michigan, found that areas with higher exposure to Ramayan — that is, higher TV signal strength when the show aired — experienced significant cultural and political changes.

For instance, parents in those areas became more likely to give their newborns traditional Hindu names, while households increased adherence to vegetarian diets. The cultural shift also led to a rise in communal violence and also provided a fillip to the BJP’s political fortunes, especially in state Assembly elections.

According to the researchers, these effects were not owing to general TV access but to the TV show Ramayan in particular. “Our findings reveal that media portrayal of religious narratives can have lasting effects on cultural identity, intergroup violence, and electoral outcomes,” Yang said in a press statement.

Arvind Rajagopal, a noted professor of media studies at New York University, also expressed similar views in an interview about his book Politics after Television: Hindu Nationalism and the Reshaping of the Indian Public (2001). He pointed out that while it was the Congress that greenlighted the telecast of Ramayan and opened the locks of the Babri Masjid, “whatever gains accrued for the Congress from these moves, the net beneficiary was the BJP”.

The aftermath

By early 1989, Rajiv Gandhi’s personal image had taken a beating in the form of corruption allegations in the Bofors guns scandal. Although a group of his party leaders had broken away under the leadership of V P Singh (who would go on to succeed Rajiv as PM), the Opposition at the time was not exactly a united one.

Chowdhury wrote that Rajiv was advised to advance the general elections due at the end of 1989 (polling was eventually held in early November), as the Opposition had not yet regrouped and “striking early would help Rajiv get the better of an Opposition on the offensive”.

Also, the Intelligence Bureau (IB), India’s internal intelligence agency, had assured Rajiv that the Congress would win 300 seats (it won 197) — this was the same IB that told Indira Gandhi in 1977 that her party would win 330 to 350 seats.

As it turned out, both mother and son were trounced in the elections that followed. Although the Congress emerged as the single largest party in 1989, Rajiv chose not to stake claim, thereby paving the way for the National Front — a coalition led by V P Singh’s Janata Dal and comprising both the BJP and Left parties — to form the government.

entry.title: Karakoram-2026: How China and Pakistan are deepening military ties — and what it means for India
entry.content:
Written by: Major-General (retd) G G Dwivedi6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 05:13 PM IST A drill during Karakoram-2026. (Screenshot from video posted by China Military Bugle) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

China and Pakistan’s longstanding partnership, while not a formal alliance, has emerged as a defining feature of the regional security architecture.

Over the years, their military cooperation has deepened, moving beyond defence acquisitions and joint exercises towards greater functional integration and interoperability. 

In this context, the countries’ recently concluded joint exercise, Karakoram-2026, marked a significant milestone — it involved the participation of regular army formations from both countries. Notably, the exercise was conducted in Xinjiang, which borders Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

Why the Karakoram-2026 exercise matters

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Karakoram-2026, held from October 14-22 in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, was the first joint-army level exercise between People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and Pakistan Army. 

It expanded on the earlier naval, air and counterterrorism exercises (Sea Guardian, Warrior and Shaheen series). The focus was on challenging high-altitude operations, relevant to the PLA’s Western Theatre Command which oversees the border with India.

Also Read | Why India lost the 1962 war with China, and the lessons that endure

Phase One of the exercise, up to October 19, involved troops from both sides practicing specialised tactics, close-quarter combat and unmanned aerial vehicle (or drone) operations. Phase Two entailed joint command, mixed formations and combat teams undertaking counterterrorism clearance operations, joint manoeuvres and coordinated fire drills. 

The equipment used was Chinese, including small arms, armoured assault vehicles, infantry fighting vehicles and support systems, such as artillery, drones and anti-manned systems. The Chinese Ministry of National Defence described Karakoram-2026 as an opportunity to deepen cooperation and tactical integration between the two armies. 

The China-Pakistan Nexus: Its genesis and core pillars 

The China-Pakistan nexus refers to the longstanding strategic, economic and military partnership between the two countries. It dates to the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement under which Pakistan ceded the Shakasgam Valley, part of Gilgit-Baltistan, to China, thus cementing the strategic alignment. 

Also Read | India-China face-off in Arunachal: What lies behind the border tensions

The subsequent decades witnessed China’s growing role in building Pakistan’s nuclear and missile programme which altered the regional strategic balance and security dynamics, primarily hedging against India. Today, China treats Pakistan a strategic priority, central to its South Asia policy.

 The core pillars of China-Pakistan nexus are:

  • Military supplies: China is Pakistan’s dominant arms supplier, accounting for roughly 70-80% of its imported military hardware. Major acquisitions include J-10C and JF-17 fighter aircrafts, Type 054 A/P frigates, Hangor-Class Submarines, HQ-9, 16, 17 series air defence systems, and Wing Loom drones.
  • Defence co-production: Both nations regularly collaborate on co-producing military equipment including fighter jets (J-10C and JF-17), main battle tanks (Al-Khalid), missiles, naval platforms, electronic and surveillance systems. Pakistan gets access to advanced technology while China gets to consolidate its defence-industrial outreach. 
  • Information: Information and space are other arenas of close cooperation; encompass intelligence sharing, cyber warfare, satellites (Bei Dou for navigation) and information cum narrative alignment, through initiatives like China-Pakistan Information Corridor.
  • Infrastructure: The collaboration extends to infrastructure and strategic projects such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and Gwadar Port under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
  • Drills: The two countries regularly conduct bilateral and multilateral drills; the scope has significantly enlarged over the years.

Expanding architecture of military cooperation

The Karakoram-2026 exercise must be viewed against the expanding profile of the China-Pakistan defence cooperation — from a buyer-supplier arrangement towards deeper military integration. 

It follows a joint patrol conducted by Chinese and Pakistan security personnel at Mantika Pass, at an altitude of 4,700 metres (near Khunjrerab Pass), in the upper Hunza area of Gilgit-Baltistan, reflecting the operationalisation of the border management mechanism and a growing institutional engagement.

In May 2025, when India launched aerial strikes (Operation Sindoor) targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, the collusion between Beijing and Islamabad came into sharp focus. There was strong evidence that China accelerated the deliveries of PL-15 E air-to-air missiles, air defence and electronic platforms into Pakistan’s military structure during the crisis. 

Also Read | Why India should observe China’s Fifth Plenum, as Xi Jinping tightens political control

Lt Gen A S Chaudhary, Director General of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations, had claimed in an interview with Bloomberg that China-made weapon systems performed extremely well during the four-day conflict with India.

The change of government in Bangladesh also adds a new dimension to defence and diplomatic ties in the region. Islamabad, Dhaka and Beijing may not have formed a strategic trilateral, but they are leveraging the China-Pakistan strategic framework. 

Bangladesh has advanced plans to purchase J-10CE fighter jets from China and its pilots will be trained by Pakistan at Jessore airbase, near the Siliguri corridor. There are also discussions regarding integration of air defence radar systems and upgrading Bangladesh tank fleet with Chinese technology and Pakistani expertise. High-level exchanges between the Pakistani and Bangladesh militaries are a distinct departure from the past isolation.

Strategic implications

Karakoram-2026 takes the China-Pakistan relationship a step further. Beyond equipment familiarisation, the joint training facilitates the exchange of operational experience, standardisation of procedures, command and control coordination and interoperability. Incidentally, there are intelligence reports that Pakistan Army officers are posted in key Chinese military formations in the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and Joint Staff Department of the Central Military Commission (CMC).

The significance of Karakoram-2026 lies in the changing character of the China-Pakistan military cooperation. The joint training of mixed formations, growing integration of the Chinese platforms into Pakistan’s military inventory and increasing military engagement in the Xinjiang-Karakoram region have critical strategic significance. India needs to closely monitor the evolving China-Pakistan military relationship, both as an integrated two-front challenge and in the larger regional context.

The expanding China-Pakistan nexus, therefore, compounds India’s security threat on the Northern border. For Delhi, the challenge is no longer just to contend with two adversarial neighbours but to prepare for the strategic consequences with a coherent national security strategy that addresses the convergence of Chinese and Pakistani military capabilities.

entry.title: Delhi air pollution: How cloud seeding works — and doesn’t work
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk7 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 07:14 PM IST The plane that was used in Delhi's cloud seeding trials last year. (IIT via AP) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

In Diwali’s aftermath, the Delhi government may be planning to carry out cloud seeding trials to induce artificial rain over the region amid high levels of air pollution, The Indian Express had recently reported. Two trial runs are already learnt to have been conducted near the airport.

But this is not Delhi’s first brush with the experiment. On October 28, 2025, the Delhi government conducted two back-to-back cloud seeding trials, in which a team from IIT-Kanpur flew a small aircraft over parts of Delhi and released silver iodide and salt particles in flares. 

The experiment, however, was not exactly a success. An Indian Express report from that year found that air quality improvements on Tuesday began hours before the cloud seeding operation, and that pollution levels fluctuated and even rose afterwards. What’s more, Delhi received no rain, while Noida and Greater Noida received only 0.3 mm.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

How does cloud seeding work? What went wrong last time? And what could be the outcome of a fresh experiment around this time?

What is cloud seeding?

Cloud seeding refers to introducing substances such as silver iodide or sodium chloride into a particular class of clouds to artificially trigger rain.

Cloud seeding experiments began to be carried out around the world after American chemist Vincent Schaefer and his colleagues at General Electric in New York made the first snowstorm in a laboratory freezer in 1946.

Also Read | Nearly seven decades ago, a bid to seed clouds in New Delhi

Generally, water vapour condenses around small particles in the air to form the droplets that make up a cloud. These droplets collide and grow; as they get heavy and the cloud gets saturated, it rains.

In case of cloud seeding, the seed particles are “cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), a particle on which water vapour condensates” or “ice nuclei particles, a particle on which water freezes”, the 2024 document said. CCNs have an affinity for water vapour to form cloud droplets or ice particles, respectively. Ice crystals grow faster than drops, and they enlarge and fall.

How is cloud seeding carried out?

To induce rain artificially, clouds are usually injected with salts like silver iodide, potassium iodide, or sodium chloride, which is the ‘seed’. These salts are expected to provide additional nuclei around which more cloud droplets can form. They are dispersed into the cloud either using aircraft or through generators on the ground.

Rockets, drones or flares can be used for dispersal. In Delhi’s case, flares were deployed, which are pyrotechnic material and burning agent compressed inside a tube and attached to the wings of an aircraft. These flares dispense the seeding material into the clouds.

Also read | What is smog and why does it blanket Delhi every winter?

Last year, eight flares were used, each weighing around 2 to 2.5 kg. It took about two to two-and-a-half minutes to drop each flare into clouds that had 15 to 20% humidity.

How exactly does rain from cloud seeding improve air quality?

In India, cloud seeding has mostly been tried to deal with drought-like conditions, with varying results. 

A 2024 document by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune mentioned experiments conducted over 100 km inland from the west coast of India over many years (Murthy et al., 2000). They found that certain conditions produced an increase in rainfall of 24% at 4% level.

Generally, rain ends up washing away some pollutants, such as PM 2.5 and PM 10. 

An article from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) explained the process thus: “As a raindrop falls through the atmosphere, it can attract tens to hundreds of tiny aerosol particles to its surface before hitting the ground. The process by which droplets and aerosols attract is coagulation, a natural phenomenon that can act to clear the air of pollutants like soot, sulfates, and organic particles.”

What conditions are needed for cloud seeding?

First, cloud cover and clouds of a certain type are necessary. 

M Rajeevan, former secretary of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, earlier told The Indian Express, “Cloud seeding can only happen if there is a sufficient number of clouds and a particular depth to these clouds. Inside, there needs to be an adequate number of cloud droplets. Cloud seeding is done to increase the radius of the cloud droplets so that they will grow bigger and because of gravity, they will come down as rainfall. But with a clear sky, you can’t do it.”

Also Read | Express view on cloud seeding in Delhi: A damp squib

In winter, clouds form over Delhi when a western disturbance moves over the region. These are storms that originate in the Caspian or Mediterranean Sea and bring non-monsoonal rainfall to northwest India.

However, they may be inadequate for the purposes of cloud seeding. Sachchida Nand Tripathi, Professor at IIT Kanpur, had said, “In winter, you don’t see the kind of clouds that are needed for seeding, but western disturbances are the way through which clouds form. Even if clouds are there, you need to see what their height is, what their liquid water content is.”

What does this tell us?

That cloud seeding may not work in Delhi in the post-autumn months. The moisture content of late autumn clouds are insufficient to wash away the particulate matter in Delhi’s air.

Even when it does work, there should be “a significant amount of rain so it washes away pollutants,” Gufran Beig, founder project director of the government’s System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting And Research (SAFAR), earlier said. “It will only be temporary, but if at all it is successful, it will break the flow of pollutants.”

Also Read | Cloud seeding can’t be a reliable fix for Delhi’s winter pollution: IIT-Delhi study

Apart from concerns about the efficacy and the temporary effect, doubts have been cast over the strategy to target the effect rather than the cause of air pollution — vehicular pollution, industrial emissions, and dust around the year, with stubble burning, weather conditions and fireworks during the winter months worsening the situation in areas in and around Delhi.

A study carried out at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi concluded that cloud seeding cannot be a “primary or reliable strategy” to manage winter air pollution in Delhi as the capital is climatologically unsuitable for it.

Cloud seeding, the study says, “should be viewed, at best, as a potential high-cost, emergency short-term measure, contingent on stringent forecasting criteria”. 

It underscores that “sustained emission reduction remains the most viable and necessary long-term solution” to the problem of air pollution.

entry.title: What is smog and why does it blanket Delhi every winter?
entry.content:
By: Explained Desk5 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 11:06 AM IST A water tanker sprays water to curb air pollution at Kartavya Path in New Delhi on Monday. (Express Photo/Praveen Khanna) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Days after Diwali, the Delhi-NCR region remains blanketed in smog, the thick haze that returns every winter as pollutants accumulate in the air. This year, firecrackers added to the problem, accounting for over 71% of Delhi’s fine particulate pollution in the early hours following Diwali, according to an assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune.

But what causes this recurring winter phenomenon, how is smog different from fog, and why is Delhi particularly vulnerable?

What is smog, and how is it different from fog?

Smog, derived from ‘smoke’ and ‘fog’, occurs when pollutants accumulate in the air, often reducing visibility. These include fine particulate matter, such as PM2.5 and PM10, and gases released by vehicles, industries and other sources.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Some pollutants, including nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, can also react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone. This process produces what is known as photochemical smog, which is more common in sunny conditions.

Delhi’s winter smog, however, is particularly associated with the accumulation of fine particulate matter under weather conditions that prevent pollutants from dispersing.

PM10 refers to particles measuring 10 micrometres or less in diameter, while PM2.5 refers to finer particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less. These particles can include dust, soot and smoke, as well as substances formed through chemical reactions involving gases in the atmosphere.

Fog, on the other hand, consists of tiny water droplets suspended close to the ground. It forms when moist air cools and water vapour condenses into droplets, reducing visibility.

Also in Explained | Delhi’s AQI is 370, but some platforms show 1,000: Why do readings differ?

Unlike fog, smog contains harmful pollutants that can affect human health. Fog and smog can also occur together.

Why does smog worsen in Delhi during winter?

A tanker sprays water mist along Anand Vihar to suppress dense smog and maintain air quality after Diwali celebrations, in New Delhi on Monday. (Express Photo by Amit Mehra)

Delhi’s winter smog results from a combination of pollution, geography and weather conditions that prevent pollutants from dispersing. The problem worsens as temperatures fall and wind speeds decline.

During warmer months, rising air and stronger winds help disperse pollutants. In winter, however, cooler temperatures and weaker winds reduce the movement and mixing of air, allowing pollutants to accumulate closer to the ground.

Another important factor is temperature inversion, a phenomenon in which a layer of warmer air forms above cooler air near the surface. Under normal conditions, warm air rises and carries pollutants upwards. During an inversion, the warmer layer acts like a lid, trapping colder air and pollutants close to the ground.

Delhi’s location in the Indo-Gangetic Plain, where pollution from several states can accumulate, adds to the problem. These conditions can persist for days, allowing pollutants to build up and produce the thick smog that regularly blankets the region during winter.

Where does Delhi’s air pollution come from?

Delhi’s air pollution comes from several sources, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, construction activity, road dust and the burning of waste and biomass. These contribute to pollution throughout the year, although their relative shares vary with the season, weather conditions and location.

During the post-monsoon months, smoke from agricultural residue burning in neighbouring states can add to the pollution already present in Delhi’s air.

Also Read | COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets

Before Diwali, other sources such as biomass and waste burning, vehicle emissions and secondary organic aerosols contributed substantially to Delhi’s PM2.5 pollution.

After Diwali, however, firecrackers became the dominant contributor. Using real-time scientific data, IITM Pune’s analysis showed that firecrackers contributed 71.1% of the PM2.5 concentration in Delhi’s air between 1 am and 9 am on November 9 (Monday), immediately after the celebrations wound down. Their contribution was lower, at 43.4%, during the same hours on November 8, and just 5.6% on November 7.

Why does smog linger, and what makes it dangerous?

Smog can persist for several days when pollutants continue to accumulate in the atmosphere, even after temporary sources of emissions, such as firecrackers, have subsided.

One of the biggest concerns is particulate matter, particularly PM2.5. These particles, measuring 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter, are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs. Some can also enter the bloodstream, affecting organs beyond the respiratory system.

Exposure to polluted air can cause irritation of the eyes and throat, coughing and breathing difficulties. It can also aggravate asthma and other respiratory conditions. Long-term exposure to fine particulate pollution is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, lung cancer and chronic respiratory illnesses.

Children, older people, pregnant women and those with pre-existing heart or lung conditions are particularly vulnerable. However, prolonged exposure to high levels of pollution can affect otherwise healthy people too.
