entry.title: Third time’s the charm? What US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks could yield, the role India can play
entry.content:
Written by: Arav Shah8 min readNew DelhiNov 11, 2026 06:30 AM IST US Envoy Steve Witkoff (right), speaks during the coordination meeting before the trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in Abu Dhabi. (AP Photo) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

US President Donald Trump announced earlier last week that he had met with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy at the White House and that a “big, beautiful agreement” over the war in Ukraine was on the horizon.

Trump’s words, however repetitive they might have been in spirit, were supplemented by US envoy Jared Kushner, who stated on Thursday (November 5) that US officials in Brussels held “productive and substantive discussions” with Ukraine and NATO.

Scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10, delegations from all three nations will sit down over the next two days for the third iteration of the US-mediated peace talks. They face the task of wrapping up the nearly five-year-long war — now the deadliest conflict that Europe has seen since the Second World War.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is likely to be on the bargaining table, and what is not? Do the US midterm results affect the talks? And how will the question of a broader European security architecture be broached?

First, what happened during the earlier round of talks?

In May-June 2025, Ukrainian and Russian officials met for their first direct talks after the 2022 war began in Istanbul, Turkey.

This Turkey-mediated meeting was marked by a 28-point US-Russia peace plan that included Ukraine permanently denouncing NATO membership and a total prohibition on Ukraine’s long-range arsenal — a demand that was denied by Zelensky. It was also met with a swift counter-proposal by the European bloc, which demanded a “robust, Article 5-style security guarantee” mirroring that of the NATO agreement. Article 5 encapsulates the principle of collective defence, where an attack on any member is considered an attack on all.

Russia’s proposal also outlined sweeping domestic reform, such as an armed personnel cap, and ultimately, no common ground was reached.

Subsequently, the next meeting came about in February 2026 in Geneva. Here, Moscow firmly insisted that Ukraine formally cede the entire Donbas region before it would even entertain a cessation of hostilities. Kyiv explicitly rejected these terms, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s delegation demanded an unconditional ceasefire, and the talks stalled again.

Any further action was marred by the fact that only days later, the US — alongside Israel — was embroiled in a conflict against Iran, severely depleting its diplomatic capacity and shifting its focus elsewhere.

How is the bargaining table positioned now?

The two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi are expected to focus on the three broad questions of territory, post-war security guarantees and the future security architecture of Europe.

Notably, Russia — and Putin — have remained steadfast in insisting that no European delegation be present, despite the Trump administration having suggested that a new European security “framework” may be tabled.

The most immediate sticking point remains the question of territory. Russia currently controls Crimea, which it annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and substantial parts of eastern and southern Ukraine. Moscow has also claimed the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions as Russian territory. Their principal demand remains that Ukraine withdraw from Donbas, allowing the surrender of territory that may have otherwise not been captured.

Ukraine has repeatedly rejected such demands. According to Reuters, US negotiators believe a compromise on territory may be possible, with both sides making limited concessions.

Another concern for Ukraine is whether Russia could launch another military offensive in the future, which is why Kyiv has demanded security guarantees as non-negotiables to peace.

Ukraine previously sought NATO membership, arguing that the alliance’s collective defence clause would provide protection. From Russia’s perspective, though, NATO’s eastward expansion presents a threat to its security, and has been read as a reason for its 2022 invasion.

What about the broader question of European security?

One of the more significant aspects of the current negotiations — besides the exclusion of Europe — is Russia’s insistence that the discussions extend beyond the immediate conflict.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on November 10 that defining the parameters of a future European security architecture before addressing the specifics of the Russia-Ukraine conflict was reasonable.

Also Read | C Raja Mohan writes: At Abu Dhabi, new diplomatic push on Ukraine, high stakes for India and world

European leaders, however, have argued for the opposite sequence. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, has maintained that wider security discussions should follow a ceasefire in Ukraine.

The disagreement matters because a potential settlement that limits NATO’s presence in eastern Europe or restricts Ukraine’s future security choices could have unseen consequences.

European governments are also concerned about being excluded from negotiations that could directly affect their security. Representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, the European Union, and NATO have been involved in separate discussions with US and Ukrainian officials in Abu Dhabi.

Could the US midterm results affect the negotiations?

The US midterm elections have introduced another variable into the negotiations. Trump’s Republican Party was on the receiving end of a ‘blue wave’ that saw the Democrats win control of the US Congress. Come January, when new members are sworn in, Democratic lawmakers have indicated that they could push for greater military assistance to Ukraine and tougher sanctions on Moscow.

For Russia, the results have raised questions about whether Trump’s negotiating position could face greater domestic opposition.

A change in US Congress, however, does not automatically translate into a change in US foreign policy. The extent to which a Democratic-controlled Congress can influence Trump’s approach will depend on its ability to secure bipartisan support for legislation, funding and sanctions.

The immediate negotiations, meanwhile, remain in the hands of the Trump administration.

What role is India expected to play?

A day before the Abu Dhabi negotiations began, Zelenskyy spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, briefing him on preparations for the trilateral meeting. Hours later, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also spoke to his Russian counterpart.

Zelenskyy specifically urged India to identify the steps it could take, and the dialogue it could pursue with other world leaders, to help bring the war to an end. He also pointed to food security as a possible area of cooperation, with India expressing readiness to mediate in establishing food corridors through the Black Sea.

Also Read | From calling for peace in Russia-Ukraine and beyond, Delhi is now working for it

Earlier in October, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had described an Indian proposal for a limited ceasefire as the most comprehensive among the proposals received from several countries.

The broad contours of the Indian proposal, reported earlier by The Indian Express, involve three elements: reducing attacks around the Black Sea to allow the movement of Ukrainian agricultural exports, a halt to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and Ukraine refraining from attacks on Russian positions along the line of contact.

What happens if the talks fail?

A failure to reach an agreement would not necessarily bring the diplomatic process to an end.

The US could continue engaging the two sides through separate channels, while negotiations on issues like prisoner exchanges and the safety of commercial shipping could continue independently.

However, the lack of progress on territory and security guarantees would leave the central dispute unresolved. For Ukraine, a failed negotiation would mean continuing to seek military and financial support from the US and Europe while attempting to prevent further Russian advances. For Moscow, it would mean continuing its military campaign while retaining its stated negotiating demands.

The consequences would also extend beyond the battlefield. Continued attacks on energy infrastructure, ports, and commercial shipping could deepen disruptions to international trade, affect agricultural exports, and add to Europe’s security concerns.

entry.title: Can states levy a tax on sales tax? The 30-year-old legal question SC has now settled, explained
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 08:17 PM IST A seven-judge constitutional bench of the Supreme Court last week closed a reference that has been pending for around three decades, holding that it had become infructuous and no longer required an answer. (Express) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Can a state impose a tax on a tax that a dealer already owes? The Supreme Court has reiterated that states can levy a surcharge calculated as a percentage of sales tax payable by dealers, holding that such a levy is essentially an additional sales tax and not a separate tax on tax.

In doing so, a seven-judge Constitution Bench has closed a reference that had been pending for nearly three decades, ruling that the question had already been settled by a 1974 judgment.

Background of the case

A surcharge is an additional levy imposed over and above an existing tax. The legal question before the Supreme Court was whether states could impose such a surcharge on the sales tax payable by dealers, or whether doing so amounted to an impermissible ‘tax on tax’.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The dispute arose from a 1990 amendment to Odisha’s Sales Tax Act, which required dealers with a gross turnover exceeding Rs 10 lakh to pay an additional 10% of the sales tax they owed.

The dealers challenged this provision, and argued that the surcharge was a “tax on tax”. They reasoned that the surcharge is measured on the tax payable and not on turnover, hence it is not a tax on the “sale or purchase of goods.” The dealers argued that it falls outside Entry 54 of list II of the Seventh Schedule, which empowers the states to tax the sale or purchase of goods but does not authorise them to impose a tax on sales tax that is already payable by the dealer.

Also Read | When can the Income Tax Department reopen a taxpayer’s assessment?

The state maintained that the surcharge was only an increase in the rate of sales tax for a particular class of dealers. The fact that it was calculated as a percentage of the tax payable instead of turnover did not change the nature of the levy.

Previous cases

The Orissa HC upheld Section 5A following two Supreme Court rulings that had previously upheld a similar additional sales tax levies. Previous Supreme Court rulings have also adjudicated on similar points.

In S. Kodar v. State of Kerala (1974), a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld a Tamil Nadu law that imposed an additional tax of 5% on the sales tax payable by dealers whose annual turnover exceeded Rs 10 lakh. The court held that the levy was an increase in sales tax, not a separate tax on income. It said, “the fact that quantum of additional tax is determined with reference to the sales tax imposed would not alter its character.”

This position was reiterated in the Hoechst Pharmaceuticals (1983) ruling, in which a three-judge bench upheld a 10% surcharge on sales tax payable by dealers with an annual turnover exceeding Rs 5 lakh. It said a surcharge is “nothing but a higher rate of tax to raise revenue for general purposes.”

In the India Cement case (1990), a seven-judge bench struck down a cess imposed on mineral royalty, saying that “royalty is a tax” and a cess on royalty was beyond the State’s legislative competence. Dealers challenging the sales tax surcharges relied on this ruling to argue that a tax calculated on another tax was unconstitutional.

The Orissa HC bench referred the matter to a larger bench in 1998, seeing a possible conflict between Hoechst and India Cement rulings. In 1999, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court in Arjun Floor Mills referred the matters to a seven-judge bench, noting that the earlier constitutional bench ruling in S. Kodar would also have to be considered.

Also in Explained | SC says no distinction between arrest, detention: How it resets 24-hour clock

In State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries (2004), a five-judge bench suggested that the observation in India Cement that royalty was a tax was an inadvertent error. The issue was eventually settled in the Mineral Area Development Authority ruling (2024) where a nine-judge bench held that “royalty is not a tax. Royalty is a contractual consideration paid by the mining lessee to the lessor for enjoyment of mineral rights.”

What the Supreme Court has now said

The bench held that the question of whether states could levy an additional sales tax as a percentage of the sales tax payable had already been settled by the Supreme Court in Kodar ruling and said there was no reason to revisit this decision.

The bench rejected the dealers’ argument that surcharge calculated on sales tax amounted to a “tax on tax”, saying the argument confused what was being taxed with how the tax was calculated. The subject of the levy remained the sale or purchase of goods. That the surcharge was calculated with reference to the sales tax payable did not change its character.

It said, “A surcharge of 10 per cent upon a sales tax levied at the rate of 10 per cent of the turnover is, in substance, nothing but an additional levy of 1 per cent upon the turnover. The subject of the surcharge remains the sale or purchase of goods; the only difference lies in the arithmetical route by which the quantum is reached.”

The court also rejected the argument that the surcharge was effectively a tax on dealer’s income. It said that the liability depended on turnover, not profit. Even a dealer who made losses would have to pay the surcharge if their turnover crossed the prescribed limit. The ruling said, “A levy which is payable irrespective of the existence of income, and which bears no relation to the quantum of income, cannot, by any stretch, be characterised as a tax on income.”

The bench also said that the India Cement ruling relied on by the dealers dealt with a different issue regarding a cess on mineral royalty and the limits of state power in a field covered by central legislation. It had not held that every levy calculated on another levy was unconstitutional. The nine-judge bench in the Mineral Area ruling had held that royalty was not a tax but a contractual payment for the right to extract minerals. The Supreme Court bench said that this removed the basis of apparent conflict between India Cement and S. Kodar.

The bench also noted that the reference concerned the state’s taxing powers under the pre-GST regime. The 101st constitutional amendment, which introduced the GST in 2016, narrowed Entry 54 of the state list to specified goods, replacing the broader power states’ previous ability to tax the sale or purchase of goods. Since the surcharge in question related to old sales tax laws, the bench said the reference had little prospective significance

The CJI, writing for the majority, declared the reference as infructuous since the legal question was already addressed in S. Kodar.

“The continued survival of a reference depends upon the continued existence of the doubt which occasioned it. Where the doubt has been authoritatively dispelled, in the interregnum, whether by a subsequent decision of a Bench of greater strength, by a legislative or constitutional amendment, or otherwise, the reference ceases to serve the purpose for which it was made. To answer it in such circumstances would be to render, in substance, an opinion on a question that no longer requires an answer, and to wastefully occupy a larger Bench’s time in restating the settled law,” the court said.

The majority did not decide every individual challenge. It left open whether Punjab could impose a surcharge on industrial units exempt from sales tax under Section 30-AA, and whether proceeds of the Punjab Social Security Cess could be transferred directly to a separate fund without first being credited to the state’s Consolidated Fund under Article 266.

Justice K V Viswanathan authored a separate opinion holding that S. Kodar remained good law. He directed that the Odisha and Punjab sales tax appeals be placed before an appropriate bench for decision in accordance with S. Kodar. He said that the Punjab Social Security Act appeals should be separated and placed before an appropriate division bench.

entry.title: Why the bid to impeach Pete Hegseth failed, and what could happen next
entry.content:
Written by: Anagha Jayakumar8 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 09:50 AM IST A demonstrator holds a sign reading "ARREST HEGSETH" near the US Capitol ahead of a procedural vote related to the potential impeachment of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington, D.C., US, November 10, 2026. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday called moves to impeach him a “farce” that would fail. Hegseth made the ⁠comment ​at a news conference a day after US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles ​of impeachment ​against him — including over alleged violations of the law in handling the Iran war.

However, the Republican-controlled House voted 211–204 on Tuesday (November 10) to refer Massie’s impeachment resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively halting the effort. The vote followed a motion introduced by Republican Congressman Darrell Issa and did not require lawmakers to decide on the eight charges against Hegseth.

The move comes a week after the Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Under a two-legislative-day procedural deadline, the House could take up the resolution as early as Wednesday (November 11), during the outgoing Congress’ lame-duck session, which we have explained here. While Democrats have expressed support, President Donald Trump and Hegseth have rejected the move.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Massie has accused Hegseth of knowingly executing unlawful orders, arguing that his actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors”, the constitutional grounds for impeachment.

In his ⁠first Pentagon news conference since May, Hegseth said attempts to ‌impeach President Donald Trump had failed and added: “They will fail again.”

“This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” he said. Referring to the Iran war, he ⁠said, “I stand ⁠beside every one of these operations. I was proud ⁠to ‌execute them, and I would ​do it again tomorrow.”

Why is Hegseth facing impeachment?

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at a White House roundtable on cybercrime in Washington, October 21, 2026. (Alex Kent/The New York Times)

Massie’s 34-page resolution lists eight articles of impeachment, covering military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean and Pacific, as well as allegations involving civilian casualties and freedom of speech.

Iran war (Articles I–III): Three articles concern the war that the US and Israel launched against Iran on February 28, 2026. Massie alleges that Hegseth violated provisions of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 by conducting military operations without congressional authorisation, continuing them despite a congressional resolution seeking the withdrawal of US forces, and disregarding statutory time limits on unauthorised hostilities.

Civilian casualties (Article IV): Massie accuses Hegseth of dismantling safeguards intended to minimise civilian casualties during military operations. The charge specifically cites the deadly February 28 strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, alleging that the weakening of these safeguards contributed to civilian deaths.

Strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats (Article V): The resolution alleges that Hegseth authorised extrajudicial killings in US military strikes on vessels suspected of drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean. It also cites strikes on survivors and failures to rescue people left at sea.

Free speech (Article VI): Massie accuses Hegseth of suppressing the free-speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly in connection with his remarks about unlawful military orders.

Venezuela (Article VII): The resolution alleges that Hegseth participated in the unlawful use of military force to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Yemen (Article VIII): Massie alleges that Hegseth authorised military operations in Yemen without the congressional authorisation required under US law.

This is not the first attempt to impeach Hegseth. In December 2025, Democratic Congressman Shri Thanedar introduced two articles of impeachment accusing him of murder and conspiracy to murder in connection with US military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats, and the unlawful mishandling of classified information. Democratic lawmakers also introduced a separate resolution in April 2026 seeking his impeachment.

What is War Powers Resolution, and why does it matter here?

Under the US Constitution, Congress has the power to declare war, while the President serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 was enacted to place limits on a president’s ability to conduct military operations without congressional authorisation.

The law requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying troops into hostilities. Unless Congress authorises the operation, US forces must generally be withdrawn within 60 days, with a possible additional 30 days for their safe withdrawal.

Also Read | Trump tells Congress hostilities in Iran have ‘terminated’. Does War Powers Act still apply?

Trump subsequently argued that the April 7 ceasefire with Iran had ended hostilities and effectively stopped the 60-day clock, which was set to expire on May 1.

Legal scholars, however, questioned this interpretation. Jasmine Farrier, a political science professor at the University of Louisville, pointed to the difficulty Congress faces in enforcing the law following a 1983 Supreme Court ruling against legislative vetoes. Congress must now pass legislation to stop military operations, which the President can veto.

The continued US military presence near Iran also raised questions about whether hostilities had actually ended. On April 19, a US warship fired at an Iranian-flagged cargo vessel attempting to breach the American blockade, despite Trump’s assertion that there had been no exchange of fire since the ceasefire.

Massie’s resolution now accuses Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution on three counts: initiating hostilities without congressional approval, continuing military operations despite a congressional direction to withdraw, and disregarding the statutory deadline for ending unauthorised hostilities.

Can a Defence Secretary be impeached?

Yes. Under the US Constitution, federal officials, including Cabinet secretaries, can be impeached for “treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanours”.

The House of Representatives can impeach an official by a simple majority, formally bringing charges against them. Removal from office, however, requires a separate Senate process, where conviction needs a two-thirds majority of senators present. The Senate can also vote to disqualify a convicted official from future federal office.

Only two Cabinet secretaries have been impeached so far: William Belknap in 1876 and Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. Neither was convicted by the Senate.

Former Secretary of Homeland Security Mayorkas was impeached by the House of Representatives in February 2024, and charged with “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust” over his handling of immigration and border security by the Republican-majority House. However, the charges against him were dismissed by the Democratic-majority Senate in April, without a full trial.

Explained Archives | Donald Trump impeached, what happens next

Donald Trump himself has been impeached twice. In 2019, the House of Representatives impeached him on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. In 2021, he was impeached again for incitement of insurrection following the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. The Senate acquitted him on both occasions, illustrating the distinction between impeachment by the House and conviction by the Senate.

Could Hegseth actually be removed?

Massie introduced his resolution on November 9 using a procedure that allowed him to force House consideration within two legislative days. However, Republican Congressman Darrell Issa moved to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, which the House approved by 211 votes to 204 on November 10.

Of those who voted, 210 Republicans and one independent supported the referral, while Massie was the only Republican to oppose it, alongside 203 Democrats. Another 18 lawmakers, including 11 Democrats and seven Republicans, did not vote. The referral effectively stalls the impeachment effort during the outgoing Congress, without requiring lawmakers to decide on the eight charges.

Massie, who lost his re-election bid, has said he hopes the move will persuade Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control of Congress in January. He argued that Democrats could otherwise pursue a more extensive impeachment process next year.

Even if Democrats pursue impeachment after assuming control of the House, removal would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate. They would therefore need substantial Republican support to secure the 67 votes required for conviction if all senators are present.

entry.title: COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets
entry.content:
Written by: Amitabh Sinha7 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 08:20 PM IST COP31 President Murat Kurum and Turkish Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu at a high-level roundtable on integrating health into global climate action. (Photo: X/@COP31) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The annual United Nations Climate Change Conference, or COP31, this year comes amid a troubling reality check.

According to two reports released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) earlier this year, the window of opportunity to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is firmly shut now. The best the world can now hope for, the reports say, is to restrict the temperature rise to 1.7-1.8°C. This is the first time that any scientific assessment of climate change has made such an assertion.

One might have therefore expected the COP31 climate conference, which began in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday (November 9 and runs till November 20), to focus on finding ways to put the world back on track. However, the conference is unlikely to deliver any outcome that can be considered a breakthrough on this front.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The 1.5°C target did not suddenly become unattainable this year. It was always a difficult target, and years of inadequate climate action have finally led scientists to conclude that it can no longer be achieved. No outcome from COP31, however ambitious, can reopen that window of opportunity.

Delinked from reality

In terms of expected outcome and impact, COP31 could turn out to be one of the most inconsequential COPs in recent years, though not because of any shortcoming of its own.

COPs, in general, have always underperformed. These annual year-ending two-week conferences, which attracted the largest gatherings of global leaders until not so long ago, have only produced low-ambition outcomes. In the last two decades, its most important success has been finalising the 2015 Paris Agreement, which defined the climate targets and framed the broad rules for international climate action.

Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya

But COPs have had a poor record in convincing the member countries — virtually the entire world till the United States decided to walk out — to do enough to achieve those targets. COPs take decisions only through consensus, and there is no way to force laggard nations to do more.

The result has been a widening gap between what is required to achieve the targets set in the Paris Agreement and the actions actually taken by individual countries. The gap has grown so large that COPs no longer seem interested in even pretending to catch up. Any outcome that enables incremental progress towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and prevents further backsliding, is now considered a good outcome.

By this metric, the success of COP31 would rest on being able to build on the decisions taken in past COPs, particularly in Brazil last year, to keep pushing for decarbonisation and energy transition.

Not irrelevant

Despite this poor record, it would be a mistake to conclude that COPs have become entirely irrelevant.

There is no denying that it is this very process of international climate negotiations under the UN framework that has put the world on a path of decarbonisation, however slow the progress might have been. The accelerating adoption of renewable energy, and the thousands of climate actions being taken by a variety of actors around the world, both state and non-state, can also be attributed to this process. Many of these actions also offer a range of collateral benefits, including energy security, poverty reduction, improved livelihoods, pollution reduction, and improved food security.

Climate change has largely disappeared from the agendas of other major global and regional forums, thanks to multiple wars, rapidly evolving technological threats, and new demands for energy use. While several immediate challenges have emerged in recent years, the problem of climate change has not disappeared, as evidenced by the growing number of large-scale climate disasters. COPs remain the only major global stage that continues to focus on climate change.

The COPs are still the only forum where developing countries can demand greater accountability from the developed world, which bears the primary responsibility for addressing climate change. Nepal was recently promised US$ 20 million from the newly-established Loss and Damage Fund for recovery and reconstruction efforts after the devastating flash floods in August. While the allocated sum is only a fraction of what Nepal needs to rebuild after the disaster, there is no other international forum where it could have demanded and received this kind of funding without any strings attached and within a short span of time. There is also a possibility that Nepal could receive more money from the Fund.

That is why countries see merit in continuing with this COP process, despite its threat of irrelevance and possible disintegration, following the withdrawal of the US from the Paris Agreement and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

Reality check

Most countries appear to have reconciled with the reality that not just the 1.5℃, but even the 2℃, target might be breached in the coming decades, unless some really unexpected technology intervention takes place.

Also Read | Delhi’s AQI is 370, but some platforms show 1,000: Why do readings differ?

The 1.5 degree and 2℃ targets were arbitrarily chosen temperature limits with no intrinsic value behind their choice. The climate impacts were evident even at 1.2℃ warming, though there is no denying that the severity and frequency of extreme climate events have steadily increased with the continued rise in temperatures.

It could be argued that the temperature targets set in Paris were too ambitious to start with. The actions necessary to achieve them were never consistent with the political and economic realities of the world and the competitive nature of international coexistence. Achieving these goals was predicated heavily on an appeal to the moral force and good conscience of the countries, and largely delinked from the political and economic interests and compulsions. The concerns of the developing countries, particularly their need for rapid economic growth, were never adequately accounted for.

This tension was evident even when the Paris Agreement was being finalised. The Agreement was hailed as a major breakthrough for climate action. The unflattering reality, however, was that developed nations had succeeded in freeing themselves from the responsibilities placed on them by the 1997 Kyoto Protocol. The Paris Agreement was not a victory for climate action, but a successful effort by the developed nations to preserve their dominance and economic interests. The stated goal of achieving the temperature targets mentioned in the Agreement was largely an obfuscation.

In the last few years, countries have increasingly dropped the pretence that they are actively pursuing the temperature targets of the Paris Agreement. Countries are now preparing themselves to deal with the impacts of climate change, rather than chase a temperature target that has never been within reach. At the same time, it is important for the countries to make sure that they give up only targets, not climate action itself.

entry.title: US Congress lame-duck session explained: Key bills Republicans may push before January 2027
entry.content:
Written by: Arav Shah5 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 10, 2026 12:50 PM IST The floor of the US Senate - one of the two chambers comprising Congress (Wikimedia Commons) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in last week’s midterm elections, dealing a major setback to President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. But Republicans still have roughly seven weeks to advance their legislative agenda before the newly elected Congress takes office.

The 120th US Congress is scheduled to assume office on January 3, 2027. Before that, however, the Republican-controlled 119th Congress must contend with several pressing legislative matters, including government funding and defence spending Any bills that are not passed into law before the current Congress ends will have to be introduced afresh in the next Congress.

This final period, known as the ‘lame-duck’ session, gives Republicans one last opportunity to advance their priorities before handing control of Congress to Democrats. Which bills are likely to take priority, and does the outgoing Congress face any restrictions on its powers? We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the lame-duck period?

The ‘lame-duck’ period refers to the period between federal elections and the newly elected members taking office.

The members of Congress retain all their legislative powers until January 3, including the ability to vote on and pass bills. Any bill left unpassed, regardless of how far it has progressed, is considered dead, and the legislative process must be restarted if lawmakers wish to pursue it in the next Congress.

Also Read | What are US midterms, why these elections matter to India

It is also a period during which lawmakers due to be replaced operate in a lower-stakes environment since the question of re-election has already been answered. The term ‘lame-duck’ refers more to the waning political power of the sitting Congress than to any limitation on its constitutional powers.

What is the progress on pending legislation?

Several legislative proposals remain on the agenda. The immediate priority is government funding.

Each year, the United States Congress must pass 12 appropriations bills that provide federal agencies with the authority to incur obligations and make payments for government functions such as defence, transportation, healthcare and education. The funding cycle begins on October 1 each year.

Also Read | US midterms: Will Democratic control of Congress bring relief to Indian H-1B holders?

Currently, federal agencies are operating under a temporary arrangement, known as a continuing resolution (CR), under Public Law 119-103, which expires on December 11. Congress was unable to agree on full-year funding before the October 1 deadline, necessitating the interim arrangement. Should Congress fail to agree on a budget or pass another CR, a funding lapse will begin on December 12. This may force federal agencies to suspend non-essential operations.

Three of the 12 appropriations bills have been cleared by the full House. The Senate, meanwhile, has yet to report any of its versions of the 12 bills, with disagreements over overall spending levels and President Trump’s proposed defence budget holding up negotiations.

Congress may also seek to address healthcare funding extensions, infrastructure and permitting reforms, and outstanding presidential and judicial nominations.

How about defence spending? What does this mean for the Iran War?

Given the US military’s involvement in the Middle East this year, defence remains another priority for Congress.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is an annual law that sets out defence policies and authorises spending for the US Department of Defense (DoD). For FY2027, a version of the NDAA has been cleared by the House of Representatives and is currently awaiting Senate approval.

Congress must reconcile the House and Senate versions before sending a final bill to Trump for approval.

The implications of the NDAA extend beyond routine military expenditure. The Iran War, which began on February 28, 2026, has placed considerable pressure on American military resources, particularly its stockpiles of precision-guided munitions and missile interceptors.

Also Read | After US midterm wipeout, will Trump resume Iran war? An expert explains

The Trump administration has already sought additional funding to address these requirements. In June 2026, the White House submitted a supplemental defence funding request of approximately $67.1 billion for the Department of Defense, covering military operations against Iran as well as other defence priorities. This included funding for operational costs, replacement of damaged or depleted equipment, and accelerated munitions production.

Democrats, however, have questioned the scale of the administration’s defence spending demands. Under the new Congress, the NDAA could also become an avenue for lawmakers to seek greater reporting on military operations, weapons stockpiles and the use of defence funds

What restrictions does the outgoing Congress face?

Constitutionally, there are no special restrictions imposed on a lame-duck Congress. Until the 119th Congress concludes its term, its members retain the same legislative authority they had before the midterm elections.

There are, however, several practical and procedural constraints:

  • Currently, Congress has limited time to complete its agenda. The second session of the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, leaving little room for prolonged negotiations.
  • A bill must ordinarily secure approval from both the House and Senate in identical form before it is presented to the President. Disagreements between the chambers can therefore delay legislation.
  • Even if Congress passes a bill, Trump can veto it. Congress can override the veto only with a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
  • The Republicans’ electoral defeat weakens their bargaining position.

The lame-duck session is therefore a political contest over which policies the outgoing Republican majority can secure before Democrats assume control on January 3, 2027.

entry.title: Gender identity vs biological sex: How a new plea in SC seeks to reopen debate
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh6 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 11, 2026 09:10 PM IST Members of the transgender community and their supporters protest against the Transgender Bill at Jantar Mantar on March 29, 2026. Photo: Abhinav Saha Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

A plea filed in the Supreme Court challenges provisions of the Transgender Persons Act that allow a person to obtain official documents recognising a gender different from the one assigned at birth, arguing that this could affect protections and benefits specifically meant for women.

The plea was filed by the India chapter of the Women’s Declaration International (WDI), a UK-based organisation that advocates for preserving sex-based rights for women. WDI was formed to lobby nations to maintain language protecting women and girls on the basis of sex rather than gender or gender identity.

WDI India filed a plea in the Supreme Court challenging Section 7 of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and Rule 7 of the Transgender Rules, which allows a person seeking a change in gender certificate. The plea has also sought consideration of the NALSA judgment that recognised a transgender person’s right to determine their gender identity.

Here’s what to know.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What the 2014 NALSA judgment said

In the landmark 2014 judgment in NALSA v. Union of India, the Supreme Court distinguished a person’s biological sex and their gender identity. It said that while biological characteristics include genitals, chromosomes, and secondary sexual features, gender also involves a person’s self-image and their psychological or emotional sense of identity.

“Both gender and biological attributes constitute distinct components of sex,” the court said, adding that discrimination on the ground of sex under Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution also included discrimination based on gender identity. 

Also in Explained | Transgender Persons Amendment Act 2026: Looking back at a decade of legal battles over gender identity

The court said that a person’s gender could not be determined only by their biological characteristics. It said that an individual’s own understanding of their gender should be given primacy. It said that “determination of gender to which a person belongs is to be decided by the person concerned”. The court also located this right within the guarantees of personal liberty and dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution.

It also held that a person could not be required to undergo surgery, sterilisation, or hormonal treatment to have their gender identity legally recognised. “No one shall be forced to undergo medical procedures, including SRS (sex reassignment surgery), sterilization or hormonal therapy, as a requirement for legal recognition of their gender identity,” the order said. 

What experts say

Senior Advocate Jayna Kothari told The Indian Express that the petition sought to reopen a question that the Supreme Court had already addressed through its recognition of gender identity. “What it tries to argue is that trans women cannot be considered as women,” she said.

Kothari said that the Supreme Court had made it clear that gender identity was distinct from biological sex and was to be determined by the individual. As per this understanding, undergoing surgery or hormonal treatment was not a condition for identifying as a man or a woman, she said.

The petition also argued that allowing transgender women to compete in women’s sporting categories could affect competitive fairness, particularly in contact sports, because of the physiological differences between biological males and females. Kothari said that such an argument claims that “no benefits given for women should be given to trans persons”, as this goes beyond sports since sporting bodies in India and abroad had mechanisms to address participation-related concerns.

Kothari said transgender persons continued to face discrimination in accessing public services, education and employment despite the legal protections recognised by the Supreme Court. “There is a huge struggle that they are facing and fighting for all their basic rights. When all these issues are pending, and now new issues are raised, that the rights given to them as women should be taken away, that just undermines their status even more.” 

Also read | Proposed changes to Transgender Persons Act turn back the clock on rights and dignity

Swarupa Deb, faculty at the National Law School of India University, Bengaluru, told The Indian Express that such an argument appears to treat transgender persons as a “risk to be managed”, rather than as individuals entitled to equal rights and citizenship. She said the concerns raised around prisons, hostels and sporting opportunities brought back memories of an earlier period when transgender persons were viewed as potential carriers of HIV and treated as a group that needed to be excluded or segregated.

Deb said that implications could extend beyond the courtroom, particularly as social media could shape public opinion even before the court arrives at a decision. “Public attitude is something that is going to harden very fast,” she said, adding that transgender persons from poorer and marginalised sections, particularly in rural and Adivasi communities, and those dependent on begging and sex work could be most affected.

She said that uncertainty was already affecting how some transgender persons accessed healthcare. People in her circles were becoming apprehensive about visiting doctors, while some medical professionals who had earlier been sympathetic were also worried about the implications of treating them.

“At least NALSA had given some sort of safety net. The 2019 legislation, however bad it was, had given some kind of safety net. If this goes on, everything will be taken away,” she said, adding that community groups were advising transgender persons to preserve their identity documents and remain in touch with reliable legal aid organisations in case they faced harassment and assault.

entry.title: Why Mumbai airport plans to shift flights to Navi Mumbai by destination, not airline
entry.content:
Written by: Sukalp Sharma7 min readNew DelhiNov 9, 2026 07:09 PM IST The first international arrival at Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA) landed from Abu Dhabi on July 15, 2026. (Express photo by Narendra Vaskar) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Mumbai International Airport Limited (MIAL), which operates Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA), announced on Monday (November 9) that it will pursue a destination-based approach to reduce capacity at the airport.

The decision follows resistance to MIAL’s proposal last week to suspend or shift flights serving 14 destinations to Navi Mumbai from the summer 2027 schedule until 2029, when Terminal 1 redevelopment is expected to be completed. The original plan would have required 46 Indian and overseas airlines to split operations between the two airports, which are both operated by Adani Group entities.

MIAL’s original proposal involved suspending or shifting 265 of the 770 weekly international departure slots at CSMIA from the last week of October, representing roughly a third of international departures. The revised arrangement reduces the number of affected foreign carriers from around 40 to 12, but the airlines that will have to relocate their services remain opposed to the move.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads. Preparations at Navi Mumbai International Airpot, ahead of its inauguration in 2025. (Express photo by Narendra Vaskar)

The development has reignited the dispute between airport operators and airlines, raising questions about how the transition should be managed, and whether airlines can be forced by airport operators to relocate services to another airport. The airlines which will be affected by MIAL’s latest move have approached the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) to clarify whether it had approved the airport operator’s move not to allocate slots to them for the next summer schedule.

There is no domestic precedent for moving flights from a major metropolitan airport to a secondary airport or temporarily suspending slots. Most airport shifts in India have been from older airports to greenfield facilities, and involved moving all or most of the commercial traffic to the new airport. Even in the case of Delhi and Mumbai airports, which were brownfield expansions by private sector operators, slots were largely maintained during the redevelopment phase.

What exactly is the Mumbai airport proposing?

MIAL is proposing to reorganise international traffic by destination rather than by airline. Under this arrangement, all flights serving the 14 identified destinations would operate from Navi Mumbai, instead of individual airlines splitting their operations between the two airports. The approach is expected to simplify scheduling and reduce passenger confusion, according to sources.

The 14 destinations identified by MIAL are Bahrain, Dammam, Dhaka, Doha, Fujairah, Jakarta, Jeddah, Kathmandu, Kuwait City, Madinah, Muscat, Ras Al Khaimah, Riyadh, and Sharjah. Citing that Indian airlines IndiGo, the Air India group and Akasa Air have decided to serve these destinations from Navi Mumbai instead of Mumbai, MIAL justified suspending their slots at Mumbai.

However, connecting passengers could face difficulties. Someone arriving at CSMIA on a domestic flight and connecting to an international service from NMIA would have to travel between the two airports.

This proposal was part of a capacity-management exercise at MIAL, which was necessitated by the redevelopment of CSMIA’s ageing Terminal 1. T1 handles domestic traffic, while Terminal 2 handles all international traffic and some domestic traffic as well.

CSMIA is India’s most capacity-constrained large airport, handling approximately 55 million passengers across both terminals. Terminal 1, commissioned in 1964, has an annual passenger-handling capacity of about 15 million, and its redevelopment is expected to increase this to around 20 million passengers annually.

According to the airport operator, the redevelopment is necessary to address structural concerns associated with the ageing terminal. Structural audits conducted by Structwel in 2017 and IIT Bombay in 2024 flagged concerns with the existing infrastructure.

Explained | Lie-flat business class seats, premium economy: IndiGo goes upscale with wide-body aircraft

The broader capacity-management exercise is expected to affect five million passengers at CSMIA. The transfer of international services to the 14 identified destinations by Indian carriers alone is expected to account for about three million passengers annually. The remainder is expected from the 12 overseas airlines serving these destinations.

MIAL plans to offset some of this capacity reduction by accommodating the affected domestic passengers from Terminal 1 in Terminal 2, and by shifting international flights away from Terminal 2.

Why did Mumbai airport change its proposal?

The immediate reason for the change was resistance from foreign airlines to splitting their operations between the two airports, which would have involved additional costs and logistical complications. After the MoCA intervened last month and asked MIAL to defer the redevelopment and work out a transition plan with airlines, the Adani-operated airports worked out an arrangement with Indian carriers to shift services to the 14 destinations to Navi Mumbai.

MIAL’s destination-based approach appears to be an attempt to address at least one of these concerns. Relocating entire routes rather than selected flights of individual airlines could make scheduling easier and reduce passenger confusion.

The 12 affected overseas airlines are Qatar Airways, Saudia, Air Arabia, Gulf Air, Kuwait Airways, Oman Air, Riyadh Air, Flyadeal, Flynas, Jazeera Airways, SalamAir, and Nepal Airlines, according to an analysis of flight schedules between Mumbai and the 14 identified destinations. Some large global airlines like Emirates, Air France, and KLM, which had publicly commented against the earlier plan to split operations between CMIA and NMIA, won’t be affected by the new destination-based proposal.

What objections have foreign airlines expressed?

Airport slots are particularly valuable at CSMIA given the limited availability of runway and terminal capacity. The airport has two intersecting runways, meaning only one can be operational at any given time. CSMIA is among the world’s most congested single-runway operations airports.

Also Read | Why are so many helicopters crashing in Uttarakhand? The risks explained

Under internationally accepted slot-allocation practices, airlines that operate their slots consistently and meet prescribed utilisation requirements are usually allowed to retain historical priority for those slots. MIAL’s proposals to reduce international capacity at Mumbai ran into conflict with the slot allocation convention.

This spurred the objection to the proposed capacity cut by the Airline Operators’ Committee (AOC)-Mumbai, which represents carriers operating from CSMIA. While the committee expressed its support for the redevelopment and capacity augmentation at Terminal 1, it alleged that MIAL had taken an arbitrary, unilateral decision. The AOC questioned the rationale behind the original proposal and asked whether this complied with the applicable guidelines from MoCA and the International Air Transport Association (IATA).

Airlines have argued that shifting operations or suspending services could affect their historical slots at Mumbai as well as interline and codeshare arrangements with Indian carriers. MIAL and its parent Adani group have assured carriers that their historical slots will be respected once the redeveloped Terminal 1 is commissioned in 2029.

Following MIAL’s November 5 slot allocation decision, AOC-Mumbai again wrote to MoCA, seeking clarification on whether the operator had the ministry’s approval to withhold slots from affected foreign airlines for the next summer schedule.

As both CSMIA and NMIA are operated by entities belonging to the Adani group, it is effectively assuming a significant role in determining how traffic is distributed between the two airports. From the operator’s perspective, managing the facilities as a coordinated aviation network could ease congestion and improve efficiencies and capacity utilisation. Airlines, however, would be concerned about the implications of an airport operator effectively exercising control over which destinations should be served from which airport.

entry.title: When can the Income Tax Department reopen a taxpayer’s assessment?
entry.content:
Written by: Amaal Sheikh7 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Nov 9, 2026 06:25 PM IST The I-T Department cannot reopen a taxpayer’s assessment simply because it wants another look at it. (Magnific) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

The Supreme Court has allowed the Income Tax Department to reopen assessments of Chetan and Nitin Sabharwal, sons of former Chief Justice of India YK Sabharwal, over shares sold for Rs 255 crore and subsequent property purchase in Delhi’s Sikandra Road.

A bench comprising Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran on October 28 upheld the 2015 notices that reopened the brothers’ earlier assessments. The court held that the notices were based on “tangible material”, citing the I-T Department’s investigative unit report.

It said that the alleged overvaluation of shares and the use of proceeds to acquire another asset could involve “a diversion of income, accessable to tax under the guise of sale proceeds.” Here is what the case is about, and what the law says on reopening taxpayers’ assessments.

What were the transactions in question?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In 2007, the brothers and two other shareholders signed share purchase agreements with GYS Real Estate Pvt Ltd, wherein they agreed to sell their shares in Pawan Impex and SVIIT Software Pvt Ltd for Rs 255 crore.

Each of the four sellers was entitled to a quarter of the consideration. The final payments were lower after the buyer deducted the company’s outstanding loans and other costs.

When Chetan filed for his income tax return in 2008-09, he declared a loss of Rs 90.37 lakh. The return also showed around Rs 37.64 crore received from the buyer under “sundry credit,” an accounting entry that included amounts payable by the buyer under the share sale transaction. The department examined the transaction and completed Chetan’s scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, accepting his declared income.

Explained | What changes with the new Income Tax rules? All you need to know

Nitin’s returns, however, were only processed under Section 143(1), which is a routine processing of returns that involves checks and certain permitted adjustments. It is not the same as a detailed scrutiny assessment of the taxpayer’s claims and transactions under Section 143(3).

The brothers used proceeds from the share sales for purchasing a residential property on Sikander Road. Chetan had also claimed exemption from long-term capital gains tax if the proceeds from the sale of certain assets were invested in a residential house.

The issue resurfaced after an I-T Department investigation raised questions about whether the shares had been sold at values substantially higher than the underlying land and buildings. In 2015, the assessing officer issued notices under Section 148 to reopen the brothers’ assessments, saying that a “substantial amount has escaped assessment during assessment years 2008-09 and 2009-10.”

The brothers challenged the notices, saying that the department was seeking to revisit already examined issues. The dispute before the SC was about whether the department had a legally valid basis to reopen the assessment.

When can a taxpayer’s assessment be reopened?

The I-T Department cannot reopen a taxpayer’s assessment simply because it wants another look at it. Section 147 of the I-T Act, 1961, allows an assessing officer to do so only when he “has reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year.”

The law sets a time limit on this power. If an assessment has already been completed after scrutiny under Section 143 (3), the department generally cannot reopen it after four years from the end of the relevant assessment year. But it can do so if the income escaped assessment because the taxpayer failed to make a return or “to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment.”

The law also requires the officer to record the reasons for reopening an assessment before issuing a notice under Section 148, to ensure that the decision is based on reason rather than vague suspicion.

An important safeguard is the rule against the Assessment Officer’s “change of opinion” in the case. In CIT v Kelvinator of India Ltd (2010), the SC said that without this check, “In the garb of reopening the assessment review would take place.” In ITO v Techspan India (2018), it said that Section 147 gives the department the “power to reassess and not the power to review.”

The distinction matters, as under Section 143(1), a return is only processed, and an intimation is sent to the taxpayer. That doesn’t mean that the department has examined every transaction or claim in the return. Under Section 143(3), the assessing officer examines the return, calls for information, and completes an assessment after scrutiny.

What the SC held

In the latest case, the court explained what the law means by an officer having “reason to believe” that income has escaped assessment. It said that when the officer does not have to prove at the time of issuing a notice that tax has definitely been evaded, the officer must have some material to support the belief that income may have escaped assessment.

Explained Law | Why SC said ‘creamy layer’ verdict can’t reopen past appointments

The bench said “reason” means “cause or justification.” At the notice stage, the question is whether “there was relevant material on which a reasonable person could have formed the requisite belief.” The officer can only rely on direct and/or circumstantial evidence.

It said, “It is not any and every material, however vague and indefinite or distant, remote and far-fetched, which would warrant the formation of the belief relating to escapement of income. If there is no rational and intelligible nexus between the reasons and the belief, so that, on such reasons, no one properly instructed on facts and law could reasonably entertain the belief, the AO could not have reason to believe that income had escaped assessment.”

The brothers argued that the alleged overvaluation of shares could not by itself mean that income had escaped assessment. They also objected to the department relying on the treatment of capital gains in later years. The SC rejected this, saying that the recorded reasons covered not just the share valuation but also the gains being “adjusted in future years” and the exemption claimed.

The bench said that the transactions could involve “a diversion of income, assessable to tax under the guise of sale proceeds,” especially since the sale price was above the actual value of sale.

The brothers also argued that the department was revisiting matters it had already examined. The SC said that change of opinion arises only when the officer has applied their mind to an issue and formed a view during the original assessment. Merely accepting a return does not mean every transaction or claim in it was examined.

Both the brothers’ cases were treated differently. On Nitin’s returns being processed under Section 143(1), the court held that “the question of change of opinion, does not arise.” On Chetan’s return, which had to be scrutinised under Section 143(3), the court said the assessment order is “a bare acceptance of the returned income as it is.”

It found no indication that the officer had examined the share valuation, the purchase of property, or the treatment of capital gains. The assessment order from 2009-10 also contained no discussion of the long-term capital gains.

The court also noted that the information about the alleged undervaluation had emerged from a subsequent investigation and was not available to the officer during the original assessment and therefore held that reopening of assessments did not amount to a change of opinion.

entry.title: Can Eisenkot unseat Netanyahu: Path ahead, and one major roadblock
entry.content:
By: New York Times7 min readUpdated: Nov 8, 2026 09:39 PM IST Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger, during a campaign event in Haifa, Israel, Sept. 23. (Amit Elkayam/The New York Times) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT AI Narration Listen 00:00 0.5x 0.75x 1x 1.25x 1.5x 2x

Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief, has been given a chance to form a new government, after he was recommended for the task by parties that won 67 seats in the 120-seat parliament.

But completing that mission and replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may well be the toughest assignment of Eisenkot’s career so far.

The ideologically and ethnically diverse factions that recommended him for prime minister include left-wing, right-wing, centrist and predominantly Arab parties. Most would have to break seemingly ironclad campaign promises to unite behind Eisenkot, no matter how he arranges them into a governing coalition.

But the pressure is on him and his allies to do just that because the alternatives, in their view, are far worse.

A failure to form a government could send Israel to another round of elections. It would leave Netanyahu in his job as prime minister in the meantime, with all of the advantages of incumbency. And the opposition would be unlikely to perform as well as it did in October, when thousands of expatriate Israelis flew home to vote.

A unity government in which Eisenkot and Netanyahu share power, such as by taking turns as premier, seemed far-fetched before Election Day and seems unthinkable now. Some of Eisenkot’s campaign promises left wiggle room, but he was adamant in saying that Netanyahu, as the person with ultimate responsibility for defending the country on Oct. 7, 2023, when it suffered its worst attack in history, was unfit to continue in government.

But what kind of government can Eisenkot form?

He starts with 48 members of parliament, thanks to his own center-right Yashar party (21), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s centrist Together party (12), Yair Golan and the left-wing Democrats party (8), and Avigdor Liberman’s right-wing but secular Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party (7).

That is more than Netanyahu’s coalition can count on: After an ultra-Orthodox party, United Torah Judaism, refused to recommend him for prime minister, Netanyahu’s coalition has only 46 seats.

To form a bigger coalition, let alone a majority in parliament, Eisenkot’s options include partnering with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which together have 13 seats, or the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats. Either route is deeply problematic, according to opposition lawmakers, operatives and advisers, most of whom insisted on anonymity to discuss coalition talks.

Here is a look at Eisenkot’s possible path forward, and at one major roadblock standing in his way.

First, Take Control of Parliament

Until a new government is formed, Netanyahu remains a caretaker prime minister. But parliament is another story. Lawmakers will be sworn in on Tuesday, and Eisenkot is working to arrange for the election of a new speaker to replace Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu loyalist.

If he is successful, that could put Eisenkot’s allies in charge of key legislative committees. And it could allow his anti-Netanyahu bloc to begin enacting legislation — fulfilling key campaign promises and demonstrating Eisenkot’s ability to get things done.

The lowest-hanging fruit, insiders say, would be to repeal laws passed by Netanyahu’s coalition, such as controversial judicial changes allowing more political control over the appointment of judges and curbing the attorney general’s powers.

Equally important would be to deliver on a core campaign promise by all the opposition leaders to establish a national commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures that preceded the Oct. 7 attack.

Liberman Rules Out the Arab Parties

Eisenkot this past week began speaking of the need to form a “national emergency government” — an important rhetorical shift.

“If it’s an emergency, you do things you wouldn’t do otherwise,” said Nimrod Novik, a senior fellow of the Israel Policy Forum who was an adviser to former Prime Minister Shimon Peres.

The Arab parties’ 19 seats would give Eisenkot a solid majority, but bringing them into a government could cost him other allies.

For now, the question is moot: The Joint List, an amalgam of three smaller Arab parties that together won 11 seats, has ruled out joining a government, though it could provide support from the outside and enable a minority government to function. The United Arab List, or Raam, which won eight seats, has not. But Eisenkot has insisted that any party joining his government must declare Hamas a terrorist organization.

Raam’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has refused to do so, though he condemns all terrorist acts. But he did say Thursday that Hamas and all other Palestinian factions should be disarmed.

Even if Abbas were to satisfy Eisenkot, however, Liberman, the Yisrael Beiteinu leader, has repeatedly ruled out a government that includes Arab parties or even relies on their support from the outside.

That leaves relying on the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties.

A Deal With the Ultra-Orthodox?

This, too, is fraught with peril. The most important issue for the Haredim is to protect their young men, who now account for about 1 in 4 draft-age teenagers, from conscription into the military and punishment for draft evasion. But with the Israeli army overstretched, a core campaign promise of Eisenkot and his opposition allies was to compel Haredi men to share the sacrifice of defending the country.

Liberman has now chosen to break that promise but not his vow to keep Arab parties out of government.

On Friday, he wrote on social media that while he remained dead set on replacing Netanyahu, avoiding new elections and spurning any partnership with the Arab parties, “on all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise, and to understand that you cannot have it all. This includes the issue of the conscription law as well.”

Eisenkot was not entirely absolutist in his campaign rhetoric about drafting the ultra-Orthodox, but Bennett, of the Together party, was adamant about it and would have to accept going back on that pledge.

Eisenkot could also find it difficult to strike a deal with the Haredi party leaders, who are far more experienced at coalition negotiations than he is, and whose voters have grown steadily more right-wing and nationalist in recent years.

Eisenkot Considers a Minority Government

With 48 votes to Netanyahu’s 46, Eisenkot said Friday that he planned to form a minority government, at least initially. That would mean that the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties abstain from the vote to form the government.

But he also said he would invite every political party — without exceptions — to join his government, now or later, provided it embraced his terms: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values in the Israeli Declaration of Independence, requiring universal national military or civilian service, and agreeing that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.

Liberman, however, is again standing in the way. On Friday, he ruled out forming a government with anything less than a 61-seat majority.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a government, Netanyahu would be given a chance next. But if he failed, there would be a short period before new elections are called in which anyone in parliament — including Liberman — could become prime minister by enlisting the support of 60 other lawmakers.

On Friday, Eisenkot appeared to allude to Liberman’s resistance — and possible ulterior motives.

“Anyone who seeks to delay or sabotage the formation of a government for personal rather than substantive reasons,” he wrote on social media before the start of the Sabbath, “will be remembered by history as someone who failed to rise to the occasion and failed to act to save Israel in a time of national emergency. They will not be forgiven.”
